name: Tennessee Lookout
title: Tennessee on pace for another surplus in 2026-27, as House Speaker proposes narrow grocery tax cut
description: Tennessee’s revenue officials predict the state is on pace for another billion-dollar surplus, giving state lawmakers and Gov.-elect Marsha Blackburn more room to navigate budget negotiations.  The estimates were given as part of the department’s presentation to the State Funding Board, which will make an official recommendation on the bottom-line financial [...]
text:
Tennessee revenue officials are projecting another surplus in 2026-27. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)Tennessee’s revenue officials predict the state is on pace for another billion-dollar surplus, giving state lawmakers and Gov.-elect Marsha Blackburn more room to navigate budget negotiations. 
The estimates were given as part of the department’s presentation to the State Funding Board, which will make an official recommendation on the bottom-line financial numbers lawmakers and the governor can use to shape next year’s budget. 
Economists and state officials told the state funding board Monday that they expect state revenues to increase by 3.5% to 4.5%, essentially keeping pace with inflation. This growth follows last year’s $1.2 billion surplus, which lawmakers can spend later this year. 
For years, officials have conservatively estimated revenues, allowing the state to experience a “surplus” used for things like road funding, tax cuts and a reworking of the education funding formula.
Don Bruce, a professor at the University of Tennessee’s Boyd Center for Business and Economic Research, said the state continues to struggle to project its franchise and excise taxes on business. 
This year the state is projecting a $700 million surplus in franchise and excise taxes. Three years ago, volatility in franchise and excise taxes on business led the state to miss its revenue projections, leaving it to find a way to plug a nearly $600 million budget hole. 
“It could go anywhere from up to down double-digit percentage points,” said Bruce, referring to future business tax revenues.  
Tennessee does face at least some increasing costs. After the federal One Big Beautiful Bill legislation, the state is expected to have to cover around $170 million in its shared costs of the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, SNAP.
Tennessee House Speaker Cameron Sexton kicked off the legislative season Monday by introducing a bill to cut the sales tax on milk, eggs and bread. Lawmakers won’t convene until January, but can file legislation through the end of the year and into 2027.
Sexton’s narrowly tailored tax cut comes after Democrats have pushed for years to eliminate the food sales tax on all groceries. A bill introduced by two Democrats in 2025 would have eliminated the grocery sales tax. 
Eliminating all sales tax on groceries would cost about $1.2 billion in state and local tax revenue, according to legislative fiscal revenue officials at the time.
Tennessee is one of the lowest-taxed states in the nation, but a 2024 ThinkTennessee report found that lawmakers have steadily shifted more of the tax burden from corporations to people through a reliance on sales taxes, leaving low-income families with a “higher tax burden than wealthier families and businesses.” Tennessee also made multibillion-dollar corporate tax cuts in 2023 and 2024. 
No estimates yet show how much Sexton’s proposed tax cut would cost. Sexton’s bill is also a caption bill and will likely undergo significant changes before passage. 
The proposed legislation also follows Democrats flipping six state House seats in the 2026 election. Republicans now hold a 68-31 supermajority in the state House. 
The state funding board will issue its final prediction of state budget growth at a meeting on Nov. 23. 
State Treasurer David Lillard said he would caution the board in its revenue projections because so much of the predicted business tax revenue increase is based on estimated payments, and not actual collections. 
“We don’t want to be caught off guard,” Lillard said.

title: North Dakota land trusts to produce record distribution to schools, universities
description: The North Dakota agency responsible for managing state trusts announced Monday a record payout is expected during the next budget cycle.  The Department of Trust Lands, responsible for managing the Common Schools Trust Fund and 12 other permanent trusts, will distribute $762 million in earnings for the 2027-2029 biennium.  The payout will include more than [[...]
text:
Gov. Kelly Armstrong, right, Secretary of State Michael Howe, center, and Land Commissioner Joseph Heringer, left, listen to a presentation during a meeting of the Board of University and School Lands meeting on Dec. 11, 2025. (Photo by Jacob Orledge/North Dakota Monitor)The North Dakota agency responsible for managing state trusts announced Monday a record payout is expected during the next budget cycle. 
The Department of Trust Lands, responsible for managing the Common Schools Trust Fund and 12 other permanent trusts, will distribute $762 million in earnings for the 2027-2029 biennium. 
The payout will include more than $722 million from the Common Schools Trust Fund, which helps fund K-12 education. That’s about 24% higher than the contribution during the 2025-2027 budget cycle. 
Annual bonuses proposed for North Dakota teachers to improve recruitment, retention

“These record distributions will provide crucial support for educational institutions and students in classrooms across our great state, from kindergarten to college,” Gov. Kelly Armstrong said in a statement. Armstrong chairs the Board of University and School Lands.
The Common Schools Trust Fund collects revenue from several sources including oil and gas royalties, surface property rents and the income derived from investing these funds. It was valued at $9.3 billion as of June 30.
The state constitution requires 10% of the five-year average value of the trust’s assets to be distributed to K-12 schools each biennium. The trust fund contributed nearly $585 million, or 24% of the state’s per-pupil funding responsibility, during the 2025-2027 biennium. 
The agency also manages a dozen other trusts that distribute funding each biennium. The 2027-2029 biennium’s distributions include $10.6 million for North Dakota State University and $8.4 million for the University of North Dakota, as well as payouts to other education institutions. 
The distributions will also include $3.9 million for the Youth Correctional Center, $2.5 million for the State Hospital and $1.2 million to the North Dakota Veterans Home. 
“These historic distributions reflect the Land Board’s commitment to responsible stewardship and ensuring North Dakota’s trust assets deliver lasting value,” said Joseph Heringer, land commissioner. “By carefully managing these resources, we are strengthening educational opportunities across the state and investing in a brighter future for generations of North Dakotans.”
The Legacy Fund, another state investment portfolio that is managed by a different agency, is expected to have a record $894 million distribution for 2027-29. The Retirement and Investment Office’s preliminary estimate provided to lawmakers in August is 30% higher than the last payout from the Legacy Fund. 
North Dakota Monitor reporter Jacob Orledge can be reached at jorledge@northdakotamonitor.com.

name: Colorado Newsline
title: 34% of Colorado households are cost-burdened, new state housing​ study finds
description: Over one-third of Colorado households spend more than 30% of their income on housing, with a heavier strain on the state’s renters, according to a statewide housing needs assessment released Monday. text:
A tower of downtown Denver residences is seen on Feb. 18, 2023. (Quentin Young/Colorado Newsline)Over one-third of Colorado households spend more than 30% of their income on housing, with a heavier strain on the state’s renters, according to a statewide housing needs assessment released Monday.
Nearly 34% of households were cost-burdened under that definition as of July 1 this year, including 49% of renters and 25% of homeowners. The lower the income level, the higher the share of cost-burdened households. Colorado tends to have a higher share of cost-burdened households than other states, according to separate research from Harvard.
The State Demography Office released its first statewide housing assessment as part of a requirement under 2024 legislation to analyze current housing stock and estimate statewide needs for the next 10 years.
“Behind every data point are families hoping for stability and an affordable place to put down roots. The data from the HNA will be critical for us to be able to successfully map out a plan for Colorado’s housing future,” Maria De Cambra, the state Department of Local Affairs executive director, said in a statement.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The assessment comes amid a surge of new statewide housing policies passed by a Democratic majority in the state Legislature and championed by outgoing Democratic Gov. Jared Polis. New laws from the past four years include efforts to increase density near public transit routes, make it easier to build accessory dwelling units and reform the state’s construction defect laws for condos. Voters also approved Proposition 123 in 2022 to fund various affordable housing projects.
A new Legislature and governor take power starting in January. Gov.-elect Phil Weiser, a Democrat, has a goal to add 40,000 more affordable units in the state by 2035 through policies like down payment assistance and development permitting reform.
“I think it might be a good time for some reflection, and an opportunity to take a look back and see, one, how far we’ve come and think through and maybe even measure the efficacy of some of these policies,” Brian Rossbert, the executive director of Housing Colorado, said.
But the upshot from the report is that affordability has declined over the past decade. State researchers estimate that a household needs to make $153,000 annually to afford a median-priced home at $547,900. Renters need to make $72,900 to afford the average apartment. The last time an average household could afford a median-priced home without being cost burdened was 2014. Put another way, the gap between income and how much a household needs to buy an average home is around $50,000 today, while it was just $2,600 in 2013.
“This gap has sidelined many households from becoming homeowners and has also been a driver in the increased supply of homes for sale,” the report says. Over the last three years however, home prices have remained relatively stable and incomes have risen slowly, shrinking the gap.
The area median income for a Colorado household of four people is $127,800.
“Affordability is one of the most dynamic elements of the housing conversation, the report says. “Developers can choose to build high-end housing in the single-family and multifamily space, but if households cannot afford to live there, the increase in supply will not solve the housing need for a community.”
There are 2.75 million housing units in the state, and 64.1% of those are occupied by owners. More houses are on the market than in any year since at least 2012, and the number of new multifamily units has exceeded demand over the past year. Mountain resort communities and the Front Range especially have a surplus of apartment units. Demographers found demand for market-rate renter housing on the Western Slope and Eastern Plains.
The report estimates an affordable housing shortfall of around 106,000 units. That would allow a 5% vacancy rate and reduce the number of residents — mostly young people — who are living with roommates or “doubling up” because they can’t afford not to. Last year, demographers estimated that the state needs 34,100 more housing units per year to prevent the shortfall from growing. They revised that this year to 34,950 per year to account for annual housing inventory losses.
Another figure in the report is an annual demand of 30,600 units over the next 10 years to support a projected population growth.
Additionally, as Colorado’s population ages, there will be more housing needs for older adults and people with disabilities. Demographers estimate there will be 238,000 more people with disabilities through 2036.
“This (assessment) gives us a little bit of a North Star in the housing community of a goal to work towards, which we haven’t had,” Rossbert said. “Since my time on the Affordable Housing Transformational Task Force back in 2021, we were always trying to put our finger on what the actual unit shortage is, and then how do we direct resources in the best way possible to meet that shortage. And this gives us a starting place.”

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: Meet North Carolina’s US House members for the 120th Congress
description: North Carolina appears to be sending 10 Democrats and four Republicans to Washington in January.
text:
The U.S. Capitol on Oct. 1, 2025. (Photo by Shauneen Miranda/States Newsroom)After a blue tsunami swept the state during the 2026 midterm elections, North Carolina appears to be sending 10 Democrats and four Republicans to Washington in January. 
In unofficial results, since not all county elections boards have completed their count yet, Democrats appear to have flipped six seats in N.C. They’ve also gained a majority in both chambers of Congress. 
North Carolina’s U.S. House delegation during the 119th Congress consisted of 10 Republicans and four Democrats, after three Democratic incumbents opted not to seek reelection due to Republican redraws of their districts to favor Republicans. In the 118th, there was a 7-7 split for the 14-member delegation. 
District 1: Don Davis (D)
U.S. Rep. Don Davis (Photo: House.gov)
U.S. Rep. Don Davis held off a gerrymander to secure his third term in the U.S. House, where he’s represented the 1st Congressional District since 2023. The district covers the northeastern part of the state and some of the outer exurbs of the Triangle area. 
Aiming to secure another seat in Congress, state Republican lawmakers redrew the district in 2025 to include more GOP voters. It didn’t work — Davis still beat Republican Army veteran Laurie Buckhout in a rematch of their 2024 matchup.
The 2026 race broke records to become the most expensive U.S. House general election in history. 
This time, Davis won by 10,285 votes, according to unofficial results from the State Board of Elections. It’s a larger margin than 2024, where 6,307 votes separated the two.
A moderate Democrat, Davis has supported increased funding for crop insurance and pricing for local farmers, and opposed job cuts at Seymour Johnson Air Force Base in Goldsboro. 
He served in the Air Force and attended the U.S. Air Force Academy, Central Michigan University, and East Carolina University. 
District 2: Deborah Ross (D)
U.S. Rep. Deborah Ross (Photo: House.gov)
U.S. Rep. Deborah Ross easily won reelection to the 2nd Congressional District, which covers most of Wake County and some of its surrounding suburbs. She’s held the seat since 2021. 
Ross trounced Republican Eugene Douglass, winning more than three-quarters of the vote in the heavily Democratic district. 
The Democrat was a member of the North Carolina House of Representatives from 2003 to 2013. She’s a former civil rights attorney who strongly supports public education, affordable healthcare, and fighting climate change. 
She lives in the Boylan Heights neighborhood in Raleigh, and attended Brown University and the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill. 
District 3: Greg Murphy (R)
U.S. Rep. Greg Murphy (Photo: House.gov)
U.S. Rep. Greg Murphy appears to have narrowly won reelection to the 3rd Congressional District, a seat he’d held since 2019. The district covers most of North Carolina’s coast. 
Murphy leads Democratic challenger Raymond Smith by 233 votes or 0.09 points, according to unofficial results from the State Board of Elections. That’s after Republican lawmakers moved some Republican voters out of his district and into the 1st in an attempt to unseat Davis. 
The race could be subject to a recount.
A urologist, Murphy co-chairs the House GOP Doctors Caucus and is the only practicing surgeon in Congress. He’s a social conservative who introduced legislation to ban giving federal funds to graduate medical schools that offer diversity, equity, and inclusion training.
Murphy was in the North Carolina House of Representatives from 2015 to 2019.
He lives in Greenville and holds degrees from Davidson College and the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill. 
District 4: Valerie Foushee (D)
U.S. Rep. Valerie Foushee (Photo: House.gov)
U.S. Rep. Valerie Foushee coasted to victory in the 4th Congressional District, which she’s served since 2023. The heavily Democratic district covers all of Durham and Orange counties, as well as parts of Chatham and Wake counties. 
Foushee won nearly 80% of the vote, defeating Republican Max Ganorkar. 
She’s an original cosponsor of Medicare for All at the federal level, and fought to expand Medicare in North Carolina. 
Prior to Congress, Foushee was elected to the North Carolina House in 2012 and was subsequently appointed to serve in the Senate in 2013, which she did until 2023.
She graduated from the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill. 
District 5: Chuck Hubbard (D)
U.S. Rep.-elect Chuck Hubbard (Photo: Courtesy Hubbard campaign)
Chuck Hubbard appears to have unseated longtime incumbent Virginia Foxx in a surprise upset, although the race could be subject to a recount. He’ll represent the 5th district, which covers the central western portion of the state. 
Hubbard leads Foxx, who’s served since 2005, by only 99 votes in unofficial results. He’s attending freshman orientation in Washington this week. 
The Democrat is a former journalist and newspaper publisher who wants to expand access to affordable healthcare and support public education. He said he was inspired to run for Congress by his daughter Meredith, who is a member of the LGBTQ+ community.
Hubbard graduated from Wofford College and lives in Wilkesboro. 
District 6: Cyril Jefferson (D)
U.S. Rep.-elect Cyril Jefferson (Photo: Courtesy Jefferson campaign)
High Point Mayor Cyril Jefferson defeated GOP freshman Addison McDowell in the 6th district, located in the north central part of the state. 
The district was drawn to be a safe Republican seat, but Jefferson beat McDowell by 6,264 votes, or 2.28 points, according to unofficial results. 
As mayor, Jefferson helped launch a business initiative called Thrive High Point, which has raised over $3 million to support local entrepreneurs. 
He was the youngest mayor elected in High Point’s history. He’s at freshman orientation in Washington this week. 
District 7: David Rouzer (R)
U.S. Rep. David Rouzer (Photo: House.gov)
U.S. Rep. David Rouzer has represented the deep-red 7th Congressional District since 2015, spanning the southern portion of the state. 
Rouzer beat Democrat Kimberly Hardy by 2,425 votes or 0.76 points, according to unofficial results from the State Board of Elections. The race could be subject to a recount.
He’s an arch-conservative who opposes abortion and same-sex marriage. He’s a founding member of the Congressional Coastal Communities Caucus, as well as the Primary Care Caucus.
Rouzer represented Johnston and Wayne counties in the North Carolina Senate from 2009 to 2013.
He attended North Carolina State University. 
District 8: Mark Harris (R)
U.S. Rep. Mark Harris (Photo: House.gov)
U.S. Rep. Mark Harris, a beneficiary of the state legislature’s new map for the 2024 cycle, appears to have held onto his seat in the 8th Congressional District. It covers the southern Piedmont area and is heavily Republican. 
Harris received 5,179 votes, or 1.77 points, more than Democrat Colby Watson, according to unofficial results. 
He supports efforts to cut spending and root out waste, fraud, and abuse. In his first term, he served on the Agriculture, Education, and Judiciary committees.
Harris is a pastor and previously ran unsuccessful bids for the U.S. Senate and U.S. House.
He holds degrees from Appalachian State University and Southeastern Baptist Theological Seminary.
District 9: Richard Ojeda (D)
U.S. Reps.-elect Chuck Hubbard, Jamie Ager, and Richard Ojeda at freshman orientation in Washington on Nov. 8, 2026. (Photo: Ojeda campaign on X)
Richard Ojeda unseated National Republican Congressional Committee chair Richard Hudson in North Carolina’s 9th Congressional District. 
The district was drawn to be a safe Republican seat, but Ojeda won 6,015 more votes than Hudson, who’s held the seat since 2013, according to unofficial results. 
The Democrat is a retired Army major who previously served in the West Virginia Senate. There, he played a prominent role in the 2018 statewide teacher strike. 
Ojeda, who pronounces his name with a hard “J”, will be the first Hispanic member of Congress from North Carolina. 
He graduated from West Virginia State University and Webster University. 
District 10: Pat Harrigan (R)
U.S. Rep. Pat Harrigan (Photo: House.gov)
Along with Harris, U.S. Rep. Pat Harrigan is the only other Republican freshman to survive the blue wave in the Tar Heel State. The 10th district, which is heavily Republican, is located in central and western North Carolina.
He beat Democrat Ashley Bell by 3,029 votes, or 1.03 points, according to unofficial results. 
Harrigan supports enforcing immigration laws, strengthening border security, and combating human trafficking and drug smuggling. 
He’s a firearms manufacturer and military veteran. 
Harrigan attended the U.S. Military Academy. 
District 11: Jamie Ager (D)
Jamie Ager at Hickory Nut Gap Farm in Fairview on Oct. 13, 2026. (Photo: Christine Zhu/NC Newsline)
Democrat Jamie Ager is a fourth-generation farmer from a political family. He easily won North Carolina’s 11th Congressional District, which covers Western North Carolina.
Although the district was drawn to favor a Republican, Ager led Republican state Rep. Jennifer Balkcom by nearly 16 points. 
He owns Hickory Nut Gap Farm in Fairview and gained national prominence for an ad featuring his monthly barn dances. He’s a centrist who brands himself as a “Mountain Democrat.”
The district has been reliably red for most of the past 35 years. After disgraced incumbent U.S. Rep. Chuck Edwards withdrew, the North Carolina Republican Party picked Balkcom as his replacement. 
A combination of candidate quality and the blue wave led to Ager’s dominant performance out west. Ager’s grandfather Jamie Clarke held the seat from 1983 to 1985 and 1987 to 1991. 
Ager graduated from Warren Wilson College. 
District 12: Alma Adams (D)
U.S. Rep. Alma Adams (Photo: House.gov)
U.S. Rep. Alma Adams won the greatest percentage of votes in North Carolina’s U.S. House races. She’s served the deep blue 12th Congressional District, covering northern and eastern portions of Charlotte and surrounding areas, since 2014. 
With Foxx’s defeat, Adams will become the longest-serving member of North Carolina’s congressional delegation. She received more than 80% of the vote. 
Adams supports reproductive freedom, strengthening the middle class, and has sponsored progressive policy proposals during her tenure in Congress. 
She was appointed to the North Carolina House in 1994 and served until 2014. 
Adams holds degrees from North Carolina A&T State University and Ohio State University. 
District 13: Paul Barringer (D)
Paul Barringer, the Democratic nominee running for North Carolina’s 13th Congressional District, poses with his dogs, Billy and Penny, at an early voting site in Clayton on Oct. 27, 2026. (Photo: Christine Zhu/NC Newsline)
Paul Barringer eked out a win over GOP freshman Brad Knott in North Carolina’s 13th district, besting Knott by 7,652 votes, or 2.41 points. 
Known for its gerrymander, the district curves around Raleigh, spanning from Caswell County in the north to a thin piece east of Raleigh before going down to Lee County. The district was drawn in 2023 to be a safe Republican seat.
Last fall, Barringer rode his bike from his home in Lee County to Yanceyville, in the northwestern part of the district. A straight shot would be 66 miles, but through the district, Barringer said he rode for 183 miles.
It’s led to plenty of time on the road while campaigning. Barringer went over 350,000 miles on his 2006 Toyota Land Cruiser in October, he told NC Newsline. 
Barringer is a moderate who’s been a healthcare consultant and attorney. He grew up on his family’s tree farm in Lee County. 
He holds degrees from Davidson College, the University of North Carolina School of Law, and Princeton University. 
District 14: LaKesha Womack (D)
Lakesha Womack. right, and Shivawn Mitchell, left. pose with campaign sign. (Photo: Courtesy Womack campaign)
LaKesha Womack beat Republican freshman Tim Moore in a massive upset. She’ll represent the 14th district, which covers areas west of Charlotte.
Moore, the former Speaker of the North Carolina House, was one of the leaders of the Republicans’ 2023 redistricting efforts and carved out a district favorable for himself. Womack leads by 6,415 votes, or 2.22 points.
She founded Womack Consulting Group, helping small businesses and faith-based organizations with strategic plans.
After moving to North Carolina in 2016, Womack and her young son became unhoused when a medical emergency left her hospitalized in intensive care. She has an outstanding felony charge for allegedly failing to return a rental car on time in 2019. 
Womack ended the campaign with only $4,792.77 in cash on hand, according to her pre-election report filed with the Federal Election Commission. 
She graduated from Vanderbilt University.

name: Alabama Reflector
title: Report: Alabama parole rates declined in fiscal year 2026
description: Alabama’s parole rates fell this year after rising in 2025, according to a report released last month. The ACLU of Alabama’s Parole Watch reported that the Alabama Board of Pardons and Paroles granted parole to about 19% of parole applicants for fiscal year 2026, which ended on Sept. 30. That was down from 23% in […]
text:
A court clerk swears in people to testify before the Pardons and Parole Board hearing in Montgomery, Ala., on Wednesday, Feb. 8, 2023. A new report found that the rate of parole grants fell to 19% in fiscal year 2026. (Stew Milne for Alabama Reflector)Alabama’s parole rates fell this year after rising in 2025, according to a report released last month.
The ACLU of Alabama’s Parole Watch reported that the Alabama Board of Pardons and Paroles granted parole to about 19% of parole applicants for fiscal year 2026, which ended on Sept. 30. That was down from 23% in 2025.
“We did see a rise in the parole grant rate, but it went back down, so that was disappointing to us,” said Nichelle Cunningham, a paralegal with the ACLU of Alabama who attends the parole hearings. “I do think the board dynamic has changed. I do not disagree with that. I do think this board is more fair, but the numbers are not reflecting that.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
In an Oct. 27 statement, the Alabama Board of Pardons and Paroles did not dispute the report’s estimates on parole grant percentages, but said the number of people paroled overall had increased.
“Overall, 613 inmates were granted parole in FY 26 — a 4% increase from FY 25 and an 8% increase from FY 24,” the parole board said.
It also defended its parole decisions by saying it is following the guidelines.
“The Board maintains a concurrence rate, or the percentage of cases where the Board’s decision matched that of the suggested outcome from the parole guidelines, above 85 percent for FY 26,” the parole board said in its statement.
Groups such as the ACLU of Alabama have become concerned with the low parole rate for the past several years. Following changes to the parole process in 2019, parole grants fell from 55% in 2017 to 8% in 2023. Several criminal justice reform advocacy groups criticized former parole board chair Leigh Gwathney, appointed in September 2019, for the drop.
At a Joint Prison Oversight Committee meeting in October 2024, Gwathney could not answer pointed questions she was asked by lawmakers on the committee about why the conformance rate, the frequency that the parole board decisions match the recommendations from the parole guidelines, was only about 25%.
Ivey appointed Hal Nash, the chief corrections deputy for Jackson County, in July 2025 to replace Gwathney after her term had expired. Parole rates increased to about 30% for the three months after he was appointed to the parole board, but then decreased.
The report also said that parole decisions are nearly identical for people assessed to be low risk to commit another crime versus those considered a moderate risk.
The report said low-risk individuals were paroled at 26.1% in 2025 while the grant rate for those considered moderate risk was 25.2% in 2025, according to the ACLU report.
The report also pointed to a racial disparity in the parole grant rates. In 2026, white applicants were granted parole 20.9% of the time, while Black applicants received it in 18.4% of cases. In 2025, white applicants received parole 24.2% of the time while Black applicants were granted parole 20.3% of the time. The disparity has declined from 2021 when the ratio of whites who were paroled to Black applicants who were paroled was 2.5. It was 1.1 in 2026.
To address the disparities, the ACLU of Alabama indicated in its report that it wants lawmakers to pass a bill to allow applicants to participate virtually in their parole hearings.
The parole board currently only hears from the family and supporters of applicants who get to speak two minutes on their behalf. Those who typically oppose parole, such as the Alabama Attorney General’s Office and Victims of Crime and Leniency, also get two minutes to present their case.
“That starts with basic reforms, like allowing incarcerated individuals to speak for themselves at their own hearings. Legislation allowing this practice was approved by lawmakers last session but was killed by pocket veto,” said Alison Mollman, legal director for the ACLU of Alabama, in a statement that accompanied the report. “We are hopeful lawmakers and other stakeholders will consider implementing virtual participation options again next session.”
A message was sent to the Alabama Attorney General’s Office seeking comment.  Wanda Miller, executive director of VOCAL, said in an interview on Monday that “we do protest parole on behalf of the victims, the victims of these inmates.”
Miller said the organization only protests paroles for violent offenders where there is a victim or where another person is harmed, and does not consider the risk assessment.
“I don’t really put those in a category of low risk or high risk,” Miller said. “That is something the parole board does. I can’t really speak to how they make those decisions.”
The report referred to SB 157, sponsored by Sen. Will Barfoot in 2025, that would allow parole applicants to participate in their parole hearings. He then sponsored SB 240, largely the same bill, in 2026, but Ivey introduced an executive amendment that lawmakers did not consider, which doomed the bill.

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: Second officer charged with theft from state Fraternal Order of Police
description: A second former officer of the state Fraternal Order of Police has been charged in connection with thefts from the Frankfort-based lobbying organization. Federal prosecutors charged Bryan Bogard, former treasurer of the Kentucky FOP, on Wednesday with one count of wire fraud. Prosecutors filed a plea agreement along with the document charging Bogard, an indi[...]
text:
A second member of the Kentucky Fraternal Order of Police has been charged with theft. (Getty Images) A second former officer of the state Fraternal Order of Police has been charged in connection with thefts from the Frankfort-based lobbying organization.
Federal prosecutors charged Bryan Bogard, former treasurer of the Kentucky FOP, on Wednesday with one count of wire fraud.
Prosecutors filed a plea agreement along with the document charging Bogard, an indication he plans to plead guilty.
The court file says the case is related to one involving Kevin Ryan Straw, who pleaded guilty to wire fraud earlier this year.
According to Bogard’s plea agreement, he was treasurer of the Kentucky FOP at times.
The deal says that between January 2020 and September 2024, Bogard “devised a scheme to defraud” the state FOP by withdrawing cash from its accounts and charging personal expenses to the organization.
Those expenses included travel, jewelry, supplements, meals and purchases from Amazon.
The one specific purchase cited in the plea deal was to Tiffany & Co. for jewelry in December 2023. Prosecutors cited that in support of the wire-fraud charge.
All told, Bogard misappropriated $30,839 — $9,359 in cash withdrawals; $18,014 in personal expenses charged to the state FOP credit card; $1,837 in unauthorized restaurant expenses; $1,066 in unauthorized Amazon purchases and subscriptions; and $562 in unauthorized vehicle expenses, according to the plea deal.
After the problem was detected, Bogard returned $4,000 to the state FOP.
His plea deal calls for him to repay the remaining $26,839.
Bogard was a lieutenant with the Covington Police Department at the time the investigation became public last year, according to published sources. Sebastian D. Torres, executive director of external affairs and counsel for the city of Covington who said Bogard retired from his job with the city while under investigation.
Wire fraud is punishable by up to 20 years in prison, though it’s unlikely Bogard’s sentence will be that long under his plea deal.
An arraignment date for Bogard had not been set as of Thursday.
In the related case, Straw, of Lexington, admitted misappropriating money from FOP Metropolitan Lodge 32 in Louisville and from the state FOP.
Straw, who was a probation and parole officer for the Kentucky Department of Corrections from 2012 to 2020, was president of the Metro Lodge 32 at times and also served vice-president and government affairs chair for the state FOP, according to the court record.
Straw admitted he withdrew $49,760 in cash from a Metro Lodge 32 account in 2024 for his own use.
In 2023 and 2024, he also charged personal expenses to the state FOP credit card and filed false vouchers to get reimbursed for travel expenses that he didn’t actually incur, totaling $57,064, according to court records.
Between 2021 and 2024 he also defrauded at least 10 people by claiming he could get significant returns on money they invested through him, when in fact he had no qualifications as an investment advisor and spent people’s money on personal expenses, according to the charge against him.
That fraud totaled $80,200.
U.S. District Judge Robert E. Wier sentenced Straw in August to 27 months in prison and to pay restitution of $187,164.
Straw’s attorney, Benjamin D. Allen, said in a sentencing document that Straw is determined to repay the victims as quickly as possible.

name: Virginia Mercury
title: Virginia elected a woman governor. The state Constitution still says ‘he.’
description: Virginia has its first woman governor, but its constitution still describes the office as a man’s job.  Abigail Spanberger’s election last year renewed attention to outdated laws governing voting rights, campaign finance safeguards and the K-12 funding formula. But after her election and 11 eventful months in state politics, there has been no notable effort [...]
text:
Virginia Gov. Abigail Spanberger gives her first speech after being sworn in on Jan. 17, 2026. (Photo by Charlotte Rene Woods/Virginia Mercury)Virginia has its first woman governor, but its constitution still describes the office as a man’s job. 
Abigail Spanberger’s election last year renewed attention to outdated laws governing voting rights, campaign finance safeguards and the K-12 funding formula. But after her election and 11 eventful months in state politics, there has been no notable effort to address them, especially compared with other states.
Joan Porte, president of the League of Women Voters of Virginia, said the state Constitution should be revised accordingly.
“It’s important for Virginia to catch up with the times,” said Porte. “We’ve been behind the times on so many things, and I just think it’s important that this language be updated and become gender-neutral, and go with the flow, go with the time.”
Virginia’s constitution includes gender-specific references to the governor, including “he shall hold office” and “he shall communicate to the General Assembly.” Masculine pronouns appear throughout the language describing the office and its responsibilities.
A similar issue surfaced in Maine when the state elected its first female governor, Janet Mills, in 2018.
Maine passed a bill in 2019 to remove gendered pronouns from references to the governor and chief justice, replacing them with wording focused on the office — for example, repeating “the chief justice” instead of using “he” or “him.” 
The bill also directed Maine’s Office of the Revisor of Statutes — responsible for preparing, editing, organizing and publishing the state’s laws — to plan updates across the state’s other statutory titles. At the time, staff estimated it could take 10 to12 years to review all 40 titles.
 Maine’s lesson

Maine House Majority Leader Matt Mooman said he was glad the measure passed unanimously without political theatrics, adding that it was “awesome” to see people from both parties agree that Maine’s laws should recognize women leaders.
“It’s important for all people to see themselves in their government,” Mooman said. “To recognize that they can participate in their government, their government will care about them, listen to what they have to say, and that they too can serve in those roles if they want to someday.”
Mooman said one lesson from the process was that the phrase “gender neutral” confused some people. Clearer language, such as “updating laws so they don’t assume everyone is a man,” may better communicate the change.
Lawmakers also recognized that updating every statute would require much more staff work, so it made sense to phase the work into the revisor’s regular schedule.
Overall, he viewed the change as a small but meaningful way to help people see themselves in government.
 Public support is key, study shows

Efforts to make state constitutions gender-neutral cut across party lines and raise a broader question about how states describe public office.
In 2018, South Dakota elected its first woman governor, Republican Kristi Noem, who pushed to change male references to the governor in the state Constitution. However, after lawmakers passed the amendment, residents rejected it in November 2024.
Researchers later examined how information about South Dakota’s proposed 2023 constitutional amendment to replace male-specific pronouns with gender-neutral language affected public reaction.
The results showed that public support for a gender-neutral constitutional language may depend significantly on how the change is explained.
Using a survey of 727 registered voters, researchers found that Republicans were generally less supportive than other political groups, primarily because of preconceived notions about gender-neutral language and pronouns.
Those views included arguments among conservatives that the measure is an attempt to advance LGBTQ+ or nonbinary gender policies, as well as discomfort with nonbinary pronouns.
However, explaining the amendment’s purpose increased support, particularly among women, independents, and Republicans.
 What’s next

Spanberger’s administration has not publicly stated its stance on the matter, and no legislation proposing a gender-neutral constitutional amendment has been introduced.
The closest measure was introduced by Del. David Reid, D-Loudoun, in 2019 and successfully reintroduced in 2020, amending the state law to recognize “chairwoman,” “chair,” “chairperson” and “chair-at-large,” in addition to “chairman,” as legally permissible titles for the head of a county board.
Also in 2020, Del. Marcus Simon, D-Fairfax, introduced a successful measure to replace gender-specific terms such as “husband” and “wife” with gender-neutral terminology in the state code.

name: Virginia Mercury
title: JLARC: Data center tax break accounts for 60% of Virginia’s incentive spending
description: Virginia spent more than $7 billion on economic development incentives over the past decade, with 60% going to a data center exemption that helped stall budget negotiations earlier this year.  The incentives include tax exemptions and project grants, according to the latest review by the Joint Legislative Audit and Review Commission.  “Data center growth in [...]
text:
Data center in Prince William County, VA. (Photo by Shannon Heckt/Virginia Mercury)Virginia spent more than $7 billion on economic development incentives over the past decade, with 60% going to a data center exemption that helped stall budget negotiations earlier this year. 
The incentives include tax exemptions and project grants, according to the latest review by the Joint Legislative Audit and Review Commission. 
“Data center growth in the state has resulted in dramatic increases in spending estimates on the exemption beginning in fiscal year 2021,” Ellen Miller, JLARC’s chief economic development and quantitative analyst, told lawmakers Monday.
JLARC analyzed the incentives to determine the state’s return on investment. From fiscal year 2021 through fiscal year 2025, Virginia spent $4.5 billion on the sales and use tax exemption for data centers. 
Amount invested by Virginia in economic development incentives in FY16-FY25. (Joint Legislative Audit and Review Commission)
The exemption allows data center companies to avoid the state’s 5.3% tax on the frequent computer system replacements needed to upgrade technology within the facilities.
It is by far the largest incentive offered by the state. The next largest, Manufacturing Single Sales Factor Apportionment, cost Virginia $254 million over 10 years, accounting for just 4% of total spending. The Virginia Business Ready Sites Program followed at $223 million from fiscal year 2016 through 2025.
“Growth in the data center exemption spending was greater than spending on other incentives, more than doubling between FY23 and FY25,” the JLARC report stated.
Even excluding the data center tax exemption, overall spending on incentives increased. JLARC also revised its methodology to give the exemption less weight in determining why data centers locate in Virginia, based on statistical analysis of tax exemptions for the industry across the country.
“Prior reports assumed between 90 to 100% of data center activity occurred because of the exemption,” Miller said. “This report uses a lower assumption, assuming only about 50% of the activity occurs because of the data center exemption.”
Amount invested by Virginia in economic development incentives in FY16-FY25. (Joint Legislative Audit and Review Commission)
The report found that grants often yielded the greatest returns  for the state in tax revenue and job creation. Those include the Semiconductor Manufacturing Grant Fund, the Space Flight Operations Facilitation Program, and the Pharmaceutical Manufacturing Grant Program.
The data center exemption’s estimated net impact on the state’s economy totaled 18,130 jobs over the last five years. The report also found that the data center industry created an average of 29 jobs per $1 million in investment from 2021 through 2025. 
 

The industry’s investments increased the state’s gross domestic product to by nearly $4 billion and had a net impact on personal income of about $2 billion. 
JLARC found that the data center tax incentive generated 22 cents in state revenue for every dollar spent. However, the report does not account for local investments and revenue in  localities that have welcomed data centers.
Loudoun County, home of the so-called Data Center Alley, reported $1.2 billion in real and personal property tax revenue, accounting for 39% of the county’s budget. JLARC’s 2024 report on data centers provides more details on local impacts.
JLARC officials suggested that the sales and use tax exemption’s influence on location decisions may continue to decrease amid rising public opposition to data centers.
“This is because power availability, availability of other infrastructure, and community acceptance have become large concerns to the extent that they become greater concerns and impact location decisions more than the exemption,” Miller said.
Earlier this year, lawmakers engaged in a prolonged debate over whether to continue the sales and use tax exemption. The final budget plan kept it in place while adding an energy consumption tax and other regulations for the facilities. Some legislators have promised to revisit the debate during the next legislative session, which begins in January.

name: Virginia Mercury
title: Commentary: The blue tsunami has a message for Virginia Democrats on data centers and campaign finance
description: Last Tuesday’s historic win for Democrats nationwide may not feel immediately applicable to state-level politics in Virginia, which holds its own elections on odd years rather than syncing them with federal elections. Democrats already enjoy a trifecta in the state, and last week Virginia voters handily endorsed the constitutional amendments the party put fo[...]
text:
The Virginia state Capitol in Richmond on Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Markus Schmidt/Virginia Mercury)Last Tuesday’s historic win for Democrats nationwide may not feel immediately applicable to state-level politics in Virginia, which holds its own elections on odd years rather than syncing them with federal elections. Democrats already enjoy a trifecta in the state, and last week Virginia voters handily endorsed the constitutional amendments the party put forward to secure reproductive rights, marriage equality and voting rights. 
So Virginia is bluer than ever – but that doesn’t mean next year’s state election will be a romp for Democrats. According to exit polls last week, 53% of voters have unfavorable views of the Democratic party. That’s better than the 59% unfavorable rating for Republicans, but it’s apparent that neither party has a well of good will to draw from. 
Democrats won elections across the country this month because voters are mad at Trump, his inflationary policies and his war. But they are also angry about data centers and money in politics. These are grassroots issues that Virginia’s leaders have not adequately addressed. If they want to win next year, they should take them seriously now.
Even a couple of years ago, the notion that data centers would play a major role in national elections would have been inconceivable. This year, data centers were on the ballot. Voters adopted data center bans or restrictions in at least 38 jurisdictions, while rejecting proposed limits in precisely one.
Opposition to data centers played a role in high-profile Democratic victories in states as diverse as Ohio, Texas, Georgia, Colorado and South Carolina – all states with significant data center activity. According to a Bloomberg analysis, 40% of planned data center capacity in the U.S. is occurring in states that may now hit pause. 
In Georgia, voters even flipped the public utilities commission to Democratic control, supporting candidates who campaigned on reining in monopoly utility Georgia Power. Like Dominion Energy, Georgia Power proposes a major buildout of gas plants to serve data centers. The incoming commissioners backed a data center construction freeze championed by Gov.-elect Keisha Lance Bottoms.
Virginia Democrats are out of step with the zeitgeist here. After years of making Virginia more welcoming for data centers, this spring the General Assembly passed only the weakest versions of a few laws demanding very little of developers. Nor would the new guardrails proposed by Gov. Abigail Spanberger’s “data center framework” do much to slow the buildout. 
Where our leaders see data centers as the key to economic growth, residents just want them to go away. Polling conducted this year revealed that 69% of Virginia voters would be “uncomfortable” with a data center near them, while 72% opposed Virginia’s sales tax exemption for data centers.  
Many data center opponents suspect the unrestrained spread of data centers has more to do with money in politics than economic policy. Certainly, a politician who accepts large campaign donations from a powerful industry, then acts in the interest of that industry, has an uphill job to persuade voters that the money wasn’t the reason.
A Pew Research Center poll conducted in May showed 74% of Americans considered money in politics a “very big problem for the country today.” A few weeks before the election, another poll showed voters were more concerned about corruption in government than any other issue. 
The concern isn’t limited to Trump-style grifting by individual politicians; a depressingly high percentage of people now think corruption is endemic to government.  
Americans support campaign finance reforms when they’re given the opportunity. Last week, in deep-red Montana, a ballot initiative to strip corporations of the ability to spend money on elections passed with fully 65% of the vote. The move follows a similar Hawaii law enacted in June. In Michigan, 82% of voters endorsed a set of campaign finance reforms, including a ban on utilities and large government contractors contributing to political candidates and their political action campaigns. 
Virginia legislators consider – and reject – these kinds of campaign finance reforms just about every year, and they have never allowed voters to consider them in a referendum. As I’ve previously noted, Virginia is one of just five states that allow unlimited corporate campaign contributions. Legislators claim they can keep money from affecting their judgement. Voters know better.
Even in the wake of the blue tsunami, some Virginia Democrats still act like nothing has changed. At an Energy Commission meeting on Nov. 5, two days after the election, two Democrats joined three Republican members to block the sending of a letter to the SCC encouraging additional scrutiny of the proposed merger between Dominion Energy and NextEra Energy. The merger, of course, is all about data centers and the profit to be had from supplying them with power.
Four of the five who voted against sending the letter – two Democrats and two Republicans – are sitting legislators. For each of them, Dominion is the largest contributor to their election campaigns, doling out from $145,000 to $507,000 apiece during the last election cycle. 
The spread of data centers and the role of money in politics are intertwined. Americans don’t like the influence of billionaires and big corporations on politicians under the best of circumstances. The tech oligarchs who sacrificed their don’t-be-evil  principles on the altar of Donald Trump fully earned the revulsion of the electorate. 
Give Elon Musk credit: if his $445 million effort to buy elections for Republicans failed spectacularly, at least he was upfront about what he was doing. That’s one rat who stayed on the sinking ship as the tsunami gained force. Other tech leaders might be wishing they hadn’t boarded in the first place. 
If Virginia Democrats take last week’s election results to heart, they will adopt the data center reforms constituents are demanding and enact the campaign finance laws needed to ensure that people, not corporate interests, call the shots in Richmond.

name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: Big corporations dodge taxes as Pennsylvania families pick up the tab
authors: Peter Hall, Marcus Baram, Captial & Main
description: The Keystone Research Center found that corporations’ share of Pennsylvania’s general fund tax revenue fell from 30% in 1972 to 12% in 2023-24, and that more than almost two-thirds of corporations operating in the state pay no corporate net income tax.
text:
The Keystone Research Center found that corporations’ share of Pennsylvania’s general fund tax revenue fell from 30% in 1972 to 12% in 2023-24, and that more than almost two-thirds of corporations operating in the state pay no corporate net income tax. (Photo by Jessica Kourkounis for the Pennsylvania Capital-Star)From the steps of the Pennsylvania Capitol, looking out toward the Susquehanna River, North Street runs off to the right — quieter than the avenues that feed the statehouse, more suburb than seat of power.
That is where Andrea Grove built Elementary Coffee, the shop she opened at Harrisburg’s Broad Street Market in 2014, when she was 26.
Grove pays her taxes. What she doesn’t have is what the coffee giants have. “We don’t have accountants that will tell us about loopholes and these ways to get around these things,” she said. “The expectations for small businesses, particularly in coffee, is to live up to what these big corporations are producing but with way less resources — so you’re hustling harder than ever.”
Just a few miles from her counter are several Starbucks, with which she competes for customers — but Starbucks has a huge advantage since its multinational parent company takes advantage of the so-called Delaware loophole, which allows it to avoid paying Pennsylvania income taxes by having its parent company in Delaware and shifting its profits to overseas subsidiaries.
Within walking distance of Grove’s counter, lawmakers have spent more than two decades deciding whether to close the mechanism that lets those corporations do exactly that. So far, lawmakers have balked.
The Voluntary Victim State
The Delaware loophole works like this: A multistate corporation sets up a subsidiary — often one that exists on paper only — in Delaware, which does not tax royalty income. The Pennsylvania operation pays that subsidiary a royalty for use of its own trademark and deducts it as an expense. Profits earned in Harrisburg or York are logged in Delaware, untaxed. Most states have closed the loophole through “combined reporting,” which taxes a company and its subsidiaries as the single business they present to shareholders. Pennsylvania is one of 18 states that still have the loophole, costing taxpayers in those states $2.85 billion annually in total lost revenue, according to the Institute on Taxation and Economic Policy.
Don Griswold spent nearly 40 years on the other side. He built a 600-person state tax minimization group at accounting giant KPMG — “We weren’t hiding what we’re doing,” he told Capital & Main. “It’s all legal loopholes” — and finished his corporate career as Warren Buffett’s executive tax counsel before joining the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities. At KPMG, he said, states that were easy to shift profits out of were called “voluntary victim states.” The company referred to Pennsylvania, Griswold said, as “the Rip Van Winkle of states in terms of tax policy.”
The strategies he designed, he said, “pulled hundreds and hundreds of millions of dollars out of state coffers.”
“Think about the food stamps that were cut by the One Big Beautiful Bill. Think about school lunches,” Griswold said. “How many kids did without their only meal of the day at school because of stuff I was doing?”
The Keystone Research Center found that corporations’ share of Pennsylvania’s general fund tax revenue fell from 30% in 1972 to 12% in 2023-24, and that almost two-thirds of corporations operating in the state pay no corporate net income tax. (The percentage paying up increased slightly in 2025-2026, a bump attributed by fiscal watchdogs largely to surging corporate profits and federal tariff refunds.) The Pennsylvania Policy Center estimated that the state collects $2.21 billion to $2.99 billion less each year in corporate income tax than it would have, had it kept pace with national collections — with no evidence the cuts delivered stronger economic growth.
Worldwide combined reporting — treating a company and all of its global subsidiaries as one entity for tax purposes — would, the center and the Institute on Taxation and Economic Policy calculated, raise $1.537 billion in Pennsylvania corporate tax revenue annually.
Working families pay the difference. The nonpartisan tax policy organization ITEP ranks Pennsylvania’s tax structure the fourth most regressive in the nation: the lower a household’s income, the larger the share that goes to sales, property and income taxes.
“I think of the woman who has incredibly limited income and a little kid,” Griswold said. “That sales tax may be the difference between choosing food or diapers.”
The Bill in the Drawer
In June 2025, Rep. Elizabeth Fiedler, a Philadelphia Democrat, pushed HB 1610 — a combined reporting bill — through the state House, 104 to 99. It has now been sitting in the Republican-controlled Senate Finance Committee since September 2025. When Democrats tried to force a vote, said Felicity Williams, executive director of the Pennsylvania Policy Center, the Senate refused to take one.
“Right now the tax system in Pennsylvania is really upside down,” Fiedler told Capital & Main. “The people who are benefiting from that are billionaires, for-profit corporations, all sorts of people who are really not paying their fair share, and the people who are suffering as a result are working and middle class Pennsylvanians who are just doing their best to get by.”
She added: “It’s always been outrageous, but especially right now during this affordability crisis.”
“Year after year this idea pops up,” said Fiedler, who has served since 2019. “It’s been an intractable problem.”
The opposition to eliminating the loophole is well financed. The Pennsylvania Chamber of Business and Industry, which represents nearly 10,000 companies, warned House members in a memo that the bill would make the state less competitive, add complexity for employers and create revenue volatility. Republican senators echoed it.
“Combined reporting is double taxation,” state Sen. Greg Rothman, a Cumberland County Republican, told ABC affiliate WHTM. “It’s going to drive companies out of Pennsylvania, and it’s not fair.” Rothman did not return calls from Capital & Main for comment.
“If businesses weren’t paying their fair share, you’d have more businesses moving into Pennsylvania,” Rep. Aaron Bernstein, an Ellwood City Republican, told WHTM. “Instead, businesses have been challenged and have moved out of Pennsylvania because of our high tax structure, because of the complications with it. We need to make our tax structure more competitive. This bill does not do that.” Bernstein did not return calls from Capital & Main for comment.
Williams, the Pennsylvania Policy Center director, offered three reasons the loophole survives: a Senate majority ideologically opposed to revenue measures, a broader “misbelief” that lower corporate taxes generate growth and “the amount of corporate money in the political process.” The Chamber’s political arm, ChamberPAC, endorsed Rep. Scott Perry, a Hanover Republican, and steers its money primarily to the Senate and House Republican campaign committees — funds that push millions into competitive districts. “The system is kind of rigged in favor of the bigger corporate giants,” said Williams.
The Bill Comes Due
Perry’s district is where the two halves of the story meet. One of the state’s top congressional fundraisers this cycle, Perry voted for the One Big Beautiful Bill, which imposed what Feeding Pennsylvania CEO Julie Bancroft called “the deepest cuts to SNAP and Medicaid in history.” Perry told FOX43 in May 2025 that the cuts targeted waste: “Everybody that applies, whether they’re eligible or not, can get the benefit, and again, it becomes unaffordable.”
Perry’s spokesperson did not return calls for comment from Capital & Main.
In York, Jennifer Brillhart counts the cost. The York County Food Bank she leads — 13 staffers, more than 100 volunteers — served about 30,000 people a month two years ago. Now it’s up to 40,000, she noted. Its twice-monthly drive-throughs are drawing record numbers of people, many of them first-time visitors.
“We truly are serving the working families,” she said. Federal shipments come sporadically — “Every other month we hear about another cancellation of loads” — and a box that once held two weeks’ worth of groceries now holds less. “Our goal is to never turn anyone away,” Brillhart said, “but in terms of the quantity of food that we’re providing, we have had to decrease that.”
The state sent emergency money, she said, but the Pennsylvania Agricultural Surplus System, the State Food Purchase Program and the Fresh Food Financing Initiative were flat-funded this year. “Effectively a cut with rising costs,” Williams said. The state balanced its budget “on paper,” she said, by moving bills that will still come due, and it remains $3.3 billion short of adequately funding its public schools, and some groups speak of an adequacy gap of  $4.8 billion.
Closing the Delaware loophole alone, estimated to be worth hundreds of millions of dollars, “won’t even cover” the new SNAP costs the state is about to absorb, Williams said. “Money is fungible, so it has to come from somewhere.”
In Hanover, in Perry’s district, it comes from parents. The South Western School District tentatively approved a roughly $3.4 million budget increase requiring a nearly 5% tax hike — and still halted a long-planned renovation of Park Hills Elementary, last renovated in 2001. “The [heating and air conditioning]  is going down. Electrical is not great. The intercom system is back and forth,” said Erin Keefer, whose third grader attends the school. “They don’t have the money to do it.”
Nearby, York City and West York cut full-time classroom aides to part-time hours; West York also raised taxes 4.6%. “All of a sudden, we’ve turned into this,” Keefer told Capital & Main. “We’re out of money, and we’re deep in debt. And how did this happen?”
Griswold has an answer. Pennsylvania law, he said, “discriminates against its own small business community and in favor of these abusive global giants” — small corporations don’t have shell companies in Singapore or the Cayman Islands, or the million-dollar fees to set them up. When people learn the system is rigged against them and their government does nothing, he said, “citizen confidence in this democracy goes down.”
On North Street in Harrisburg, confidence is in short supply.
“After year 12 of running a business, you should feel somewhat settled — have a little bit of stability,” said Grove, the coffee shop owner. Instead she is running on far less profit, unable to raise prices as fast as costs climb.
“People and the average consumer don’t know or understand that is what’s going on,” she said. “I wish people would be a little bit more conscious if they learned that Starbucks is doing this. But at the end of the day, people are still gonna stop at Starbucks, because they have all the locations.”

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Election 2026 by the numbers in Nebraska: a 93-county breakdown
description: As a blue wave washed over much of the nation, Nebraska’s 3rd Congressional District saw a smaller splash than the eastern, more urban areas.
text:
Lincoln residents line up to vote on Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026 at the Sandhills Publishing Building. in Lincoln, Nebraska. (Photo by Fisher Madsen/Nebraska News Service)LINCOLN — As a blue wave washed over much of the nation, Nebraska’s 3rd Congressional District held firm and saw a smaller splash than the state’s eastern, more urban areas.
In two statewide races this year — U.S. Senate and governor — the Republican candidates lost two of Nebraska’s three congressional districts. The sprawling 3rd District, one of the country’s most conservative districts, which is sometimes referred to as a “firewall, carried Republicans to victory.
Trump carried Nebraska by 20.6 percentage points in 2024 and 19.2 percentage points in 2020. Still, other states Trump won by larger margins saw more wins for Democrats on Election Day 2026 than in Nebraska.
A blue wave?
Nebraska did ride part of the national wave with wins for Democratic candidates for sheriff and county attorney in Douglas and Lancaster counties and the breaking of a GOP supermajority in the officially nonpartisan Nebraska Legislature.
Statewide, one of the clearest indicators of the blue wave was the race for Nebraska governor, where Republican Gov. Jim Pillen of Columbus won by a smaller margin in 89 of 93 counties than four years ago but still safely won a second and final four-year term.
It was the closest Nebraska gubernatorial race since 1990. Pillen won by 8 percentage points this year, or about 60,000 votes as of Friday.


In all but six of Nebraska’s 93 counties, former Democratic state Sen. Lynne Walz of Fremont earned a greater share of votes than then-Democratic state Sen. Carol Blood of Bellevue when she faced Pillen in 2022. At the time, Pillen was an elected regent for the University of Nebraska. 
Walz’s improvement was greatest in northeast Nebraska, in Dakota and Thurston counties (where the Omaha Tribe of Nebraska and Winnebago Tribe are located) and her home of Dodge County. Walz slightly underperformed Blood in Brown, Greeley, Harlan, Hooker, McPherson and Wheeler counties. Pillen expanded his winning margin in Hooker, Keya Paha, McPherson and Wheeler counties.
The overperformance meant Walz won two of three congressional districts, likely a first for any Democrat, even symbolically, since 2006. Pillen narrowly won the Omaha-area district in 2022, in part because Blood did not campaign as much in 2022 as Walz did this year. 
Walz raised more than $6 million by late October, the most for a Democratic gubernatorial candidate in state history. She had support from the Democratic Governors Association, too.
In 1990, Republican Gov. Kay Orr lost reelection by about 0.6%, or 4,030 votes to Democrat Ben Nelson. Nelson would go on to safely win reelection in 1994, and he was elected to the U.S. Senate in 2000.
The red ‘firewall’
Nebraska had already experienced a splash, of sorts, in 2024 when registered nonpartisan Dan Osborn outperformed in his bid to unseat Republican Sen. Deb Fischer, who won by 6.7 points. Osborn returned to challenge Sen. Pete Ricketts, R-Neb., but did worse in 91 of 93 counties, and Ricketts won by more than 6 points, just slightly less than Fischer did.
In the two counties where Osborn improved his performance, Boyd and Red Willow counties, Democrat Preston Love, who faced Ricketts in 2024, did better compared to either of Osborn’s runs for office. Osborn made up some ground this time in those two counties.
Ricketts performed worse in every county than his landslide victory in 2024 over Love. Yet in 39 counties, he still earned a greater share of votes than Fischer when she faced Osborn. Two of those include Hall County, home to Grand Island, and Lincoln County, home to North Platte, where Trump and Vice President JD Vance, respectively, stumped for Ricketts and Pillen.


Nebraska has not elected a Democrat, or non-Republican, to any statewide post since 2006. At that time, Nelson won reelection over Ricketts. Ricketts would go on to win the governorship in 2014 and 2018, and Pillen appointed Ricketts to the U.S. Senate in 2023. He won a two-year term in 2024 and won a six-year term this time.
Ricketts handily won all three of Nebraska’s congressional districts in his 2024 race.
U.S. House races
For Nebraska’s three U.S. House seats, results indicate a leftward shift of nearly 17 percentage points for the 1st Congressional District and almost 18 percentage points in the 2nd Congressional District. The shift in the 3rd District was about 9.7 percentage points.
Republican Rep. Mike Flood, who won by 20.2 points in 2024 for Nebraska’s 1st Congressional District, won this time by about 3.5 points against Democrat Chris Backemeyer. 
In the Omaha-based 2nd Congressional District, outgoing Rep. Don Bacon, who won by 1.9 points in 2024, will be succeeded by Democrat Denise Powell. She won by nearly 16 points over Republican Brinker Harding. She’s the first Democrat to win the seat since 2014.
Out west, Republican Rep. Adrian Smith won reelection by 51.1 percentage points, a shift of 9.7 points compared to 2024. His margin shrank in every county, but some by as few as 3 or 4 percentage points.


County-by-county breakdown
Ballot measures from the past three election cycles are also included in the county-by-county breakdown below. The measures and the years they went before voters are as follows:

Initiative Measure 432, in 2022, to require voter ID (approved).
Initiative Measure 433, in 2022, to raise the minimum wage to $15 and provide for annual increases after (approved).
Initiative Measure 434, in 2024, to prohibit most abortions after the first trimester (approved).
Initiative Measure 439, in 2024, to create a right to abortion up to fetal viability (rejected).
Referendum Measure 435, in 2024, to repeal a state law using taxpayer dollars to offset some costs of attendance at private K-12 schools (approved, law repealed).
Initiative Measure 436, in 2024, to require most employers to offer paid sick leave for workers (approved).
Initiative Measure 437, in 2024, to legalize medical cannabis (approved).
Initiative Measure 438, in 2024, to create the Nebraska Medical Cannabis Commission to regulate medical cannabis (approved).
Initiative Measure 440, in 2026, to legalize online sports betting (rejected).
Initiative Measure 441, in 2026, to regulate online sports betting (rejected).
Initiative Measure 442, in 2026, to require sex-separate K-12 and collegiate sports according to students’ sex at birth (approved).
Proposed Amendment 1, in 2026, to allow state lawmakers to serve up to three consecutive four-year terms, instead of two (rejected).

name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: DOJ sues Penn State over tuition policy for undocumented students
description: Penn State's policy says that undocumented students can be eligible for in-state tuition if they meet the university's residency requirements. That includes going to a Pennsylvania high school for at least four years.
text:
Old Main is Penn State's administrative building on the University Park campus. (Emily Reddy/WPSU)This story was originally published by WPSU. It is not available for republishing.
Penn State is the target of a U.S. Department of Justice lawsuit for its tuition policy on undocumented residents, becoming the 27th institution or state the DOJ has filed suit against.
Penn State’s policy says that undocumented students can be eligible for in-state tuition if they meet the university’s residency requirements. That includes going to a Pennsylvania high school for at least four years.
But the U.S. Department of Justice is challenging that. In a news release about the suit, the DOJ says the policy “unconstitutionally discriminates against U.S. citizens” who don’t get the same reduced rate and that universities cannot give reduced tuition that’s not available to all Americans.
A Penn State spokesman said the university is reviewing the complaint.
Three organizations — TheDream.US, MALDEF (the Mexican American Legal Defense and Educational Fund) and the Presidents’ Alliance on Higher Education and Immigration recently issued a report on what they say are the negative effects of the Department of Justice lawsuits.
Speaking during a recent news conference, Gaby Pacheco, president and CEO of TheDream.US, said the the students they work with arrive in the United States at a median age of 4 years old.
“We’re talking about toddlers. That means that these students have grown up here, studied here, succeeded from kindergarten to 12th grade. They have graduated and have earned admission to these colleges and universities,” said Pacheco. TheDream.US gives undocumented students scholarships and assistance.
The organizations say the in-state tuition policies expand access to higher education and support state and local economies.
According to TheDream.US, Penn State is the second institution facing a DOJ lawsuit, along with 24 states and Washington, D.C. that have faced similar lawsuits over the past two years.
As a result of the legal challenges, in-state tuition policies for undocumented students have ended in six states, according to the Presidents’ Alliance on Higher Education and Immigration, which tracks the cases. However, Illinois enacted a new law restoring access starting in 2027.
