name: National
title: Democratic wins create abortion rights opportunities in states with strict laws
description: Sweeping Democratic election wins could advance abortion access in states with tight restrictions, especially in Georgia, Iowa and Texas, where Democrats seized the governor’s office for the first time in decades. All three states will have Democratic attorneys general, and in Georgia and Texas, Democrats will control the state House while Republicans retain[...]
text:
Georgia Democratic Gov.-elect Keisha Lance Bottoms spoke last week at the state Capitol about her transition into office. In Georgia, Iowa and Texas, sweeping Democratic election wins could advance abortion access. (Photo by Ross Williams/Georgia Recorder)Sweeping Democratic election wins could advance abortion access in states with tight restrictions, especially in Georgia, Iowa and Texas, where Democrats seized the governor’s office for the first time in decades.
All three states will have Democratic attorneys general, and in Georgia and Texas, Democrats will control the state House while Republicans retain the state Senate. Texas has a strict abortion ban, while Iowa and Georgia only allow it up to about six weeks of pregnancy.
Meanwhile, in Arizona, Michigan, Minnesota, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin, Democrats have won new “trifectas” — control of the governor’s office and both legislative chambers — creating new opportunities to expand abortion rights. Both Pennsylvania Democratic Gov. Josh Shapiro and Wisconsin Democratic Gov.-elect David Crowley have already pledged to codify abortion rights through state law or constitutional amendment.
Abortion rights supporters also won victories in three of the four states — Missouri, Nevada and Virginia — where abortion-related measures were on the ballot. The lone exception was Idaho, where voters preserved their state’s strict abortion ban.
State consequences are already on display in Texas, where Democratic Attorney General-elect Nathan Johnson has promised to stop suing telehealth abortion providers in other states. Johnson’s proclamation is a stark reversal of the policy of his Republican predecessor, Ken Paxton, who failed in his bid to become a U.S. senator.
“My hope in humanity has been restored a little bit, and I don’t think I even realized how much that was wearing on me behind the scenes for the last two years,” said Kaitlyn Kash, who left Texas in 2021 to obtain an abortion in Kansas after fatal fetal complications threatened her pregnancy and potentially her own health.
Kash was among several plaintiffs who joined the 2023 Zurawski v. Texas lawsuit seeking to clarify the state’s medical emergency exceptions to its abortion ban. In 2024, the Texas Supreme Court ruled 9-0 in favor of the state.
But future abortion cases could see different outcomes: Last week, Democrats won all four Texas Supreme Court seats that were up for election. That leaves the GOP with a narrow 5-4 advantage on the state Supreme Court.
“To not have a vindictive attorney general anymore is going to save lives,” Kash said, referring to actions Paxton has taken, including bringing legal actions against abortion providers inside and outside the state and petitioning the state Supreme Court to halt a court ruling allowing the termination of a nonviable pregnancy.
Less impact in Washington
Despite huge Democratic gains in Congress, the change at the federal level is likely to be less significant, at least in the short term. President Donald Trump won’t leave office until January 2029, and Democrats did not win a filibuster-proof 60 seats in the Senate, let alone the two-thirds majority in the House and Senate they would need to override a presidential veto.
“As long as Trump holds executive and veto powers, we have more work than celebrating to do,” said Brittany Fonteno, president and CEO of the National Abortion Federation in a written statement. “The next two years will be a critical time to prepare for the kind of governing power that will deliver real and lasting reproductive freedom.”
Nevertheless, national abortion rights leaders have signaled high expectations for candidates they helped send to Congress, and they want Democrats to fight to preserve telehealth abortion. If Dr. Heidi Overton, Trump’s controversial pick to oversee the U.S. Food and Drug Administration, is not confirmed during the upcoming lame duck session, abortion-rights advocates will look to the new Democratic-dominated Senate to block her nomination.
“The Senate just became the backstop,” said Gowri Buddiga, campaign director of Free & Just, an abortion rights advocacy group, in a written statement. “An FDA nominee who’s spent years calling medication abortion dangerous now has to get past a chamber that’s heard from the women these bans have hurt.”
Unlike the 2022 midterms, which were held just months after the U.S. Supreme Court struck down the federal right to an abortion, there is debate over just how important abortion was in this election. According to an exit poll conducted for The Associated Press, 39% of voters cited the economy as their top issue, 33% said it was the state of American democracy and 14% pointed to immigration. No other issue broke single digits and abortion was not among the top six.
But abortion law expert Mary Ziegler said that while abortion appears to have been less of a top-of-mind issue this year, that’s not because voters care less about it.
“It’s that there was nothing happening with abortion right now, and that isn’t just a fun coincidence,” said Ziegler, a professor at UC Davis School of Law. “That’s because the Trump administration has been trying really hard to kick down the road any litigation or federal restrictions that would have made it front of mind for voters again.”
Ziegler said there are certain avenues that congressional Democrats could explore to expand access to abortion federally. Even if those efforts fail, she said, they might benefit Democrats politically leading up to the next presidential election in 2028.
“While Republicans have successfully drawn attention away from abortion, they haven’t really actually made abortion a good issue for Republicans,” she said. “So I don’t see what the harm would be in passing a bill that would be popular and having Trump veto it and have J.D. Vance and Marco Rubio have to defend it, because it’s been very good for Republicans not to have to talk about this issue at all.”
For their part, anti-abortion organizations have blamed Republicans and Trump for not campaigning on the issue and ignoring an important voting base, pointing to the highly funded and victorious anti-abortion win in Idaho as evidence.
“Let’s be clear: the GOP didn’t run on abortion in 2026. It ran an ostrich campaign: a big elephant with its head buried in the sand,” wrote Students for Life of America President Kristan Hawkins in a subscriber email the day after Election Day.
Hawkins also noted that several prominent Republican congressional candidates who said they supported abortion rights, including U.S. Sen. Susan Collins of Maine, U.S. Rep. Mike Lawler of New York and U.S. Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick of Pennsylvania, lost their seats.
Storytelling strategy
Abortion rights advocates argue that many voters were moved by the personal stories they heard from candidates and their surrogates.
On the campaign trail in Texas, Democratic Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa talked about her own nonviable pregnancy and argued that women and families should be able to make their own reproductive health decisions. She has publicly supported ending Texas’ abortion ban and restoring abortion access, a steep challenge given that Republicans still control the state Senate.
In Georgia, Turiya Tomlin-Randall campaigned for Democratic Gov.-elect Keisha Lance Bottoms and Democratic U.S. Sen. Jon Ossoff, who was reelected.
Tomlin-Randall lives in Kansas City, Missouri, but her sister Candi Miller was living in Georgia in 2022 when she became pregnant. Miller and her husband had three kids and Miller had lupus, diabetes and hypertension, which made pregnancy dangerous. But she was terrified of getting into legal trouble after Georgia passed its new law. She ordered abortion pills online, but when she started experiencing a life-threatening infection, she was too scared to go to the hospital and died at home in November 2022.
Tomlin-Randall said she only learned two years later that her sister’s death was connected to the state’s abortion law, because of ProPublica’s reporting on deaths related to abortion bans in Georgia and Texas.
“This journey has taught me so much more about the effects of the ban,” said Tomlin-Randall, who is now raising two of the three children Miller left behind. “I’ve learned that most women who have abortions aren’t having abortions because they just don’t want to have a child. A lot of the women that I’ve encountered had to have abortions for their own safety.”
Tomlin-Randall said she’s hopeful Bottoms will be a vocal advocate for abortion rights. Georgia Democratic Attorney General-elect Tanya Miller also has opposed the state’s six-week abortion ban and promised to defend access to legal reproductive health care. Miller defeated a prominent anti-abortion lawmaker in her race.
Lauren Peterson, co-founder and CEO of Abortion in America, which organizes storytellers and advocates for abortion rights, called abortion the “unsung hero” of this election. She said abortion storytelling is an effective political strategy.
“Our work is not over,” Peterson said. “Even in states where we won, we are going to have to now do the important work of holding people accountable to the promises they made.”

name: Maryland Matters
title: Commentary: Maryland already pays for climate change; the question is whether polluters ever will
description: Marylanders are already paying for the effects of climate change, with their responses to flooding and other climate disasters, writes Jamie DeMarco, but it's time for the state to make fossil fuel companies pay for their share of the damage with the RENEW Act.
text:
A duck paddles down what had been a street on the Annapolis City Dock during flooding on Aug. 9, 2024. (File photo by Steve Crane/Maryland Matters)Mary D. Kane, president of the Maryland Chamber of Commerce, declared in her recent Maryland Matters commentary that “Maryland must confront the costs of climate change and prepare for future resilience needs.” 
So far, so good. Climate change is happening, she concedes, and it is costly. But then she throws up her hands by asking, “And who will ultimately bear the cost?” 
It’s a good question, and Marylanders already know the answer, because they’ve been paying for climate disasters for years and years.
But there’s a better way. A proposed “climate superfund” bill in Maryland would take its blueprint from the federal Superfund law, which since 1980 has made polluters pay to clean up the toxic sites they left behind. Maryland’s climate version, the RENEW Act, would ask the largest fossil fuel companies to help cover what extreme weather is costing the state, and lawmakers took the first step in 2025 by ordering a study of those costs, due this December. 
The state’s comptroller estimates that 85 extreme weather events since the 1980s have cost Maryland $10 billion to $20 billion, money that came out of county road budgets, school repair funds, family savings and small business bank accounts. A Johns Hopkins poll found that about 70% of Baltimore-area residents expect climate change to raise costs for homeowners and businesses in the next five years.




Your opinion matters
Maryland Matters welcomes guest commentary submissions at editor@marylandmatters.org.
We suggest a 750-word limit and reserve the right to edit or reject submissions. We do not accept columns that are endorsements of candidates, and no longer accept submissions from public officials, elected officials or political candidates.
Opinion pieces must be signed by at least one individual using their real name. We do not accept columns signed by an organization. Commentary writers must include a short bio and a photo for their bylines.
Views of writers are their own.




The Maryland Chamber of Commerce says it speaks for employers, so I’d invite its leadership to spend a morning at City Dock in Annapolis. The city declared two flood emergencies in 2024 alone, and Tropical Storm Debby’s flooding that August cost 19 downtown businesses and organizations an estimated $162,000. Some Dock Street shops have had to close well over 100 times because of flooding.
Annapolis is now spending roughly $90 million to raise and armor its waterfront, and right now it’s local taxpayers and shop owners covering those costs, not the companies that caused the problem. 
The best part is that the oil companies and their shareholders will be forced to pay for climate damages and they won’t be able to pass those costs onto consumers. That’s the finding of an in-depth economic analysis of the policy and its impacts in New York. Oil is priced on a global market. Nothing Maryland does could affect the price of international benchmarks like the cost of Brent Crude or the West Texas Intermediary. If you own a gas station in Maryland, you buy oil at the price of the West Texas Intermediary, then sell it at the highest price the market will bear. Unless that gas station owner reads about this policy in the newspaper, they won’t even know it exists. The cost of the RENEW Act will be paid for by the shareholders of international fossil fuel companies, no one else. 
Of course the richest industry on Earth will fight this in court, and it has plenty of help. The U.S. Chamber and the American Petroleum Institute sue the states that pass these laws, the Trump Justice Department has joined in, and Republicans in Congress want to wipe the laws out entirely.
ProPublica traced the related push for an oil industry “immunity waiver” to a coordinated campaign run through groups bankrolled by Leonard Leo, the activist who helped build today’s Supreme Court majority. An industry that needs that much help to dodge its financial obligation on climate change is telling you how big that obligation is, and three in four voters oppose giving oil companies immunity, including two-thirds of Republicans. 
What the chamber leaves out entirely is that Washington isn’t coming to help. When floods tore through Allegany and Garrett counties in May 2025, FEMA itself validated more than $33 million in damage, and the Trump administration still said no, twice. And just this week, FEMA’s administrator told state officials to build up their own reserves and expect to handle most disasters without federal help, with changes starting in as little as six months.
The next flood or heat wave is coming whether or not Annapolis passes a superfund, and Maryland will be paying for it largely on its own. 
So the choice for lawmakers is simple enough. Either Maryland families and small businesses keep covering these bills, or the massive oil companies – who knew for decades what their products would do – start paying their share. The U.S. Chamber’s own research found that every dollar spent on resilience saves $13 in damage and recovery, and we couldn’t agree more. Real leadership means standing up to that industry for the people stuck with its bill, which is passage of the RENEW Act would do.

text:
Republican Rep. Lauren Boebert, left, and Democrat Eileen Laubacher appear at a debate hosted by 9News on Oct. 12, 2026. (Photo by Sara Wilson/Colorado Newsline)Democrat Eileen Laubacher declared victory Monday over Republican U.S. Rep. Lauren Boebert in the race to represent Colorado’s 4th Congressional District. 
The Associated Press had yet to call the race Monday, when Laubacher had 48.8% of the vote over Boebert’s 47.9%. Libertarian candidate Douglas Mangeris had 3.3% of the vote. The AP estimated 98% of votes in the race were counted at the time.
“Over 17 months, I traveled 40,000 miles across all 21 counties. The message was clear: Coloradans are tired of political games, broken promises, and being ignored by Washington,” Laubacher said in a statement. “They want someone who will fight for them and deliver results.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Laubacher attended orientation for new members of Congress Monday.
Scott Gessler, an attorney for Boebert’s campaign who represented President Donald Trump during a lawsuit that sought to remove him from the ballot in 2024, said in a statement last week that the campaign will fight to ensure every “legal vote” is counted, and it was “investigating some very unusual voting patterns.” Boebert voted against certifying results from the 2020 election, which former President Joe Biden won.
Boebert’s campaign did not immediately respond to Newsline’s request for comment.
The 4th District, which includes most of Douglas County and the Eastern Plains, has in recent years been considered Colorado’s most conservative district. While the district was previously considered safely Republican, some analyses of the Boebert-Laubacher race recently put the district in the “leans Republican” category. 
National Democrats looking to flip the district named it a top priority this election. The last Democrat to represent the district was former U.S. Rep. Betsy Markey, who was elected in 2008. She served one term.
Laubacher, a first-time candidate, is a retired Navy rear admiral and former National Security Council official. She was a longtime Republican but switched her party affiliation, first to unaffiliated, and then to Democratic in 2024. She defended that action at a debate against Boebert by saying her belief in personal liberties is currently found in the Democratic Party and that the GOP she historically supported is “nearly unrecognizable.”
Boebert, of Windsor, was first elected to represent the 3rd District on the Western Slope, but she moved across the state after two terms when she nearly lost reelection in 2022. She is a longtime ally of President Donald Trump, but a rift arose earlier this year when Boebert campaigned alongside outgoing Kentucky U.S. Rep. Thomas Massie, whom the president targeted for leading efforts to force a vote on releasing the Epstein files last year. 
Two other congressional seats in Colorado previously held by Republicans flipped to Democrats in last week’s election as part of a “blue tsunami” that swept the state and the country. Republican Rep. Gabe Evans lost his race to Democrat Manny Rutinel in the 8th District, and Republican Rep. Jeff Crank lost his race to Democrat Jessica Killin in the 5th District. With Boebert’s loss, the state’s congressional delegation will favor Democrats 7-1.

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: Arkansas judge says lawsuit challenging state’s abortion ban can go forward
description: A Pulaski County judge ruled Friday that the lawsuit seeking to overturn Arkansas’ near-total abortion ban can continue. Circuit Judge Cara Connors granted motions to dismiss Republican Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders and the state of Arkansas as defendants in the case, but said that Republican Attorney General Tim Griffin, three state prosecutors and the Arkans[...]
text:
Attorneys Maria Victoria Abut (second from right) and Molly Duane (right) leave the Pulaski County Circuit Courthouse on Sept. 28, 2026 after a hearing over Arkansas' abortion ban. Abut and Duane represent seven plaintiffs, including Theresa Van (second from left), pictured with her daughter, Camille (left). (Photo by Tess Vrbin/Arkansas Advocate)A Pulaski County judge ruled Friday that the lawsuit seeking to overturn Arkansas’ near-total abortion ban can continue.
Circuit Judge Cara Connors granted motions to dismiss Republican Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders and the state of Arkansas as defendants in the case, but said that Republican Attorney General Tim Griffin, three state prosecutors and the Arkansas Medical Board will remain as defendants in the case. 
Connors has not ruled on the request to block the law from six women and an obstetrician-gynecologist who are challenging the ban. The judge said dismissing Sanders and the state as defendants doesn’t remove that as a possibility.

Waldorf-Order-Defendant-MTD 
“Dismissing the state does not diminish the relief available to plaintiffs,” she wrote. “Plaintiffs seek only prospective declaratory and injunctive relief against enforcement of the challenged laws. That relief remains available, if warranted, against the officer defendants charged with enforcing them.”
Arkansas has among the nation’s strictest abortion bans, and the challenge against it is the first filed by Amplify Legal. Amplify Legal is the litigation arm of Abortion in America, an abortion-rights advocacy group co-founded by the late Planned Parenthood President Cecile Richards.
The challenged law bans the procedure with a narrow exception to save the life of a pregnant person in an emergency. It does not include exceptions for rape or incest.
It went into effect in 2022 when the U.S. Supreme Court overturned the federal right to abortion, leaving the matter up to the states.
At a September hearing over the state’s motion to dismiss, Connors pushed back on Solicitor General Autumn Hamit Patterson’s assertion that the abortion ban is reasonable and not vague.
In Friday’s order, Connors sided with Patterson’s argument that the state has sovereign immunity, meaning it cannot be sued in its own courts. Connors cited this standard as her reason for dismissing the state and the governor as defendants.
Amplify Legal’s attorneys argue that the abortion ban not only is unconstitutionally vague but also infringes on Arkansans’ constitutional rights to life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness.
“We are confident in the strength of our clients’ claims and await the court’s decision on immediate relief,” Amplify Legal wrote in a Monday news release.
Griffin’s office will appeal Connors’ partial denial of the motion to dismiss “and will continue to vigorously defend Arkansas’ duly passed laws that protect innocent life,” spokesperson Jeff LeMaster said.
Arkansas law makes it a felony punishable by a maximum prison sentence of 10 years, a maximum fine of $100,000 or both for a medical professional who performs an abortion.
Since its filing in January, the lawsuit has drawn national attention.
Five of the six women challenging the ban had nonviable pregnancies between 2022 and 2026, and four traveled to Kansas or Illinois to receive abortions. The fifth continued her nonviable pregnancy for weeks after being denied an abortion, and she began planning her funeral in case she did not survive, according to court documents.
The sixth woman plaintiff ended her pregnancy because she did not want children, according to court documents.
Connors dismissed the case in April under a 2025 state law changing how circuit courts handle constitutional challenges. She revived the case in May after the state Supreme Court struck down those changes to such challenges.
Arkansas, Alabama and Louisiana sue states with shield laws protecting abortion-pill providers

The court has yet to set a date for the hearing on the plaintiffs’ request for a preliminary injunction.
Patterson argued at September’s hearing that the defendants, including Griffin, do not enforce Arkansas’ abortion ban. Two days after the hearing, Griffin joined the Alabama and Louisiana attorneys general in suing three Democratic-led states over laws that grant immunity to doctors who prescribe abortion-inducing medication to people in states where it is illegal.
Amplify Legal wrote a letter to Connors in October arguing that the defendants “cannot claim sovereign immunity from suit in one court only to turn around and assert sovereignty to enforce the same law in different courts.”
Patterson wrote in response that Griffin’s litigation over abortion shield laws “does nothing to help Plaintiffs show that the Attorney General has authority to enforce the Challenged Laws or that their Amended Complaint’s allegations overcome his sovereign immunity.”

name: Daily Montanan
title: Supreme Court says Attorney General exceed authority in Gallatin County
description: Montana Attorney General Austin Knudsen’s administrative seizure of the Gallatin County Attorney’s office is “unenforceable” and he exceeded his authority in attempting to do so, the Montana Supreme Court said in a unanimous opinion issued late last week. Knudsen and newly re-elected Gallatin County Attorney Audrey Cromwell have been in a 13-month legal batt[...]
text:
Gallatin County Courthouse in Bozeman. (Keila Szpaller/The Daily Montanan)Montana Attorney General Austin Knudsen’s administrative seizure of the Gallatin County Attorney’s office is “unenforceable” and he exceeded his authority in attempting to do so, the Montana Supreme Court said in a unanimous opinion issued late last week.
Knudsen and newly re-elected Gallatin County Attorney Audrey Cromwell have been in a 13-month legal battle about the status of  U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement as it operates in Montana and how it stands in state law – either as a “criminal justice agency” as it’s termed in state code, or an agency that also includes civil enforcement components. 
“I’m grateful for the court’s clarification of the law, and look forward to continuing my duties to the people of Gallatin County,” Cromwell said in a statement to the Daily Montanan.
The dispute centers on whether state law enforcement, including county attorneys offices, must turn over “confidential criminal justice data” to other agencies in civil matters. In some circumstances, immigration arrests are civil in nature. 
Knudsen took over the office on April 30. He has argued ICE is always a criminal justice agency under Montana law, and therefore can have access to any data it pleases.
Montana has strong privacy laws, and Cromwell has argued ICE is not a criminal justice agency in all contexts, and therefore should have to follow rules and processes that are dependent on how that information will be used by the federal agency.
While the state supreme court ruled that Knudsen exceeded his authority in an attempted administrative take-over of the Gallatin County Attorney’s Office, it did not decide where ICE sits in Montana law, instead asking both sides to answer two questions for further deliberation:

(1) Whether ICE is a “criminal justice agency” as defined by §§ 44-5-103(2), and -103(7)(b), MCA, and whether that determination can be made as a matter of law or requires a factual determination.
(2) Whether a “criminal justice agency” as defined by §§ 44-5-103(2), and -103(7)(b), MCA, is entitled to confidential criminal justice information solely by virtue of its status as a “criminal justice agency.”

 
The parties have until Dec. 7 to submit their respective briefs.
“The Attorney General does not supervise the county attorney in her representation of her local government, and cannot override the local government client’s direction of a lawsuit,” the Supreme Court opinion, written by Justice James Jeremiah Shea said. “If that were the case, the Attorney General could deprive a local government of due process by directing a county attorney to dismiss any civil suit against the State and prohibit a county attorney from representing a county on an issue.”
The state Department of Justice did not respond to questions about the case, or give a response to the high court’s ruling. 
It wasn’t the first time Knudsen’s office has attempted to use supervisory authority: He unsuccessfully lobbied the state Supreme Court in 2025 to use the court’s supervisory authority over Missoula District Court.

name: Daily Montanan
title: Fort Belknap tribal members allege Blaine County commission elections discriminatory
description: A new federal lawsuit alleges Blaine County dilutes the relative strength of Native American voters in elections for Board of Commissioners. In the complaint, three tribal members of the Fort Belknap Indian Community are suing the county, the commissioners, the clerk and recorder, and election manager alleging the three commission districts were unlawfully d[...]
text:
The Blaine County Courthouse in Chinook, Montana (Photo by Darrell Ehrlick of the Daily Montanan). A new federal lawsuit alleges Blaine County dilutes the relative strength of Native American voters in elections for Board of Commissioners.
In the complaint, three tribal members of the Fort Belknap Indian Community are suing the county, the commissioners, the clerk and recorder, and election manager alleging the three commission districts were unlawfully drawn. 
The plaintiffs want the U.S. District Court Billings Division to find Blaine County’s three commissioner districts don’t comply with the Fourteenth Amendment, which guarantees a “one person, one vote” doctrine, by creating districts of unequal population. 
They also want the court to implement a redistricting plan that equalizes the population between the three districts. 
In a statement provided by Upper Seven Law, one of two groups representing the plaintiffs, litigation director Molly Danahy said “the right to vote is the starting premise of our free society — it ensures that we, the people, can hold our government accountable to the rule of law.
“Districts that violate the basic principle that every vote should count the same are unconstitutional. Blaine County’s Commissioner map must distribute power equally among its voters.”
The UCLA Voting Rights Project is also representing the plaintiffs. 
The Blaine County Attorney did not immediately respond to questions sent on Monday afternoon. 
The complaint alleges that the three commission districts have an unequal distribution of voters, which ultimately diminishes the voting power of Native American residents. 
The county redistricted last in 2024, and the redistricting resolution stated that the county was required “to maintain commissioner districts having essentially the same population percentages” as in previous years. The three districts were described as being “majority American Indian,” “Majority Non-American Indian,” and “Mix District.”
While the districts were originally created in 2013 and remained the same through the 2024 redistricting resolution, “the court documented disproportionate population changes within the districts,” according to the suit. 
Using numbers cited by the county, the lawsuit shows that District 1, the majority Native American district, has a total population of 2,777; while District 2, the majority non-Native district, has a population of 2,098 — a discrepancy of 28.41%.
Current population breakdown of Blaine County commission districts. Chart from lawsuit
An ideal population split would have equal districts of around 2,390. 
The districts are “presumptively unconstitutional because its population deviation exceeds 10%,” the suit argues. 
It also argued the county did not provide a “good faith basis” for the excessive population deviations because of the racial makeup targets.
District 1 is around 95% American Indian, and attorneys for the plaintiffs argue that it takes “approximately 1.32 people voting in District 1, the most populous district, to have the same effect as 1 person voting in District 2, the least populous,” and most non-Native district. 
The county as a whole is roughly 51.4% Native American according to the 2020 census. 
“​​There is no legitimate justification for the commissioners’ failure to equalize population,” the complaint states. 
“The weight of a person’s vote should not depend on which side of a district line they live on,” said Sonni Waknin, senior voting rights counsel at the Voting Rights Project. “Blaine County’s map goes against the principles of our representative government. We are asking the Court to enforce the Constitution and require districts that give voters an equal voice in their county government.”

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Blumenthal confirms support for Schumer despite call for ‘new energy’
description: Questions swirled Monday about whether Sen. Richard Blumenthal would support Chuck Schumer as Senate majority leader. He confirmed he would.
text:
Questions swirled on Monday about whether U.S. Sen. Richard Blumenthal would support Chuck Schumer for Senate majority leader next year after the Connecticut Democrat said earlier in the day that his party needs “new energy and ideas.”
But when he arrived back in Washington for Senate votes on Monday evening, Blumenthal confirmed he still plans to support Schumer — as he said a week earlier in Hartford.
Blumenthal’s comments on Monday morning seemed to suggest he was open to new leadership when Democrats regain the majority in the Senate next year following major victories in the midterm elections. A week earlier, in a post-election press conference, Blumenthal said he’d be supporting Schumer for the top leadership role.
But Blumenthal, who’s gearing up to run for a fourth term in 2028, clarified what he meant after a day of confusion about where he stood on Schumer and the need for his party to consider new energy through the lens of Democratic leadership.
“I plan to support Chuck Schumer as Senate majority leader, just as I said last week,” Blumenthal told reporters on Monday night when asked to clarify his earlier remarks. “I’m also incredibly excited about the new ideas and energy that new members are going to be bringing to the Senate. We need them.”
“I agree with many of them who have said that the Senate has to operate differently,” he continued. “We need to get things done to meet the really crushing and urgent problems of everyday Americans. And the Senate has failed to operate in a way that meets them.”
Blumenthal’s comments come as Schumer faces some resistance within the party. Even though Democrats had major victories across the board that knocked off Republicans in some of the reddest states, there’s a vocal segment of the party inside and outside of Washington that wants fresh faces to represent them at all levels in Congress.
Schumer currently serves as minority leader, and the New York Democrat previously held the job of majority leader from 2021 to 2025 when the party was in the majority.
Debate over Schumer’s future in leadership emerged this week as lawmakers returned to Washington after a month-long recess to focus on campaigning. Democratic leaders in both chambers are facing questions from their caucuses about who will take the helm at a critical time for the party.
And it comes amid broader calls for generational change in Congress as Blumenthal, 80, signaled running for reelection in two years. The senator took note of that sentiment as he acknowledged that changes are needed in the Senate.
“I expect that Chuck Schumer will be reelected as leader because no one has come forth willing to take the position,” Blumenthal said Monday morning in Hartford before departing for Washington. “But we need to have a conversation about leadership … because we need new energy and ideas.”
“It is a very, very tough job, and my focus is going to be on action that meets the needs of everyday Americans,” he said. “I think we need to have a conversation about leadership, but it should not delay our acting to meet those needs of everyday Americans.”
But within hours of Blumenthal’s Monday morning press conference, news started circulating about U.S. Sen. Chris Van Hollen, a progressive from Maryland, and his potential interest in challenging Schumer.
Monday evening, Blumenthal said he’s sticking with Schumer when asked what he’d do if Van Hollen or someone else decides to jump into the race for majority leader.

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, of N.Y., center, is flanked by House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, of N.Y., second from right, as he speaks during an event with House and Senate Democrats to mark 100 days of President Donald Trump’s term on the steps of the Senate on Capitol Hill, Wednesday, April 30, 2025, in Washington. Credit: Mark Schiefelbein / AP

Blumenthal said he spoke last Wednesday with Schumer following the Democrats’ midterm rout.
“I’m supporting Chuck Schumer ,and I think he will be chosen again as leader,” the Connecticut senator said last Wednesday in Hartford.
Questions emerged about Blumenthal’s political future after longtime U.S. Rep. John Larson’s primary defeat in August amid calls for generational change from younger challengers. If Blumenthal runs again and wins reelection to a six-year term, he would be about a month shy of his 83rd birthday when elected. He has dismissed questions surrounding age, saying a couple of months ago that “age is always a state of mind.”
“I’m so proud to be your United States senator. Democracy is a fight. I am glad to be in this fight,” Blumenthal said last Tuesday at Connecticut Democrats’ election night watch party in Hartford. “I look forward to continuing to fight and work for the people of Connecticut to 2028 and beyond.”
The next day, speaking outside the state Capitol, Blumenthal said he didn’t have an announcement but echoed a similar sentiment.
“I’m more excited and energized than ever. And I look forward to fighting and working for the people of Connecticut in this term through 2028 and beyond,” he said. “I don’t have a formal announcement today, but I look forward to being on the ballot in 2028 and continuing to serve the people of Connecticut.”
He wasn’t on the ballot this year, but the senior senator from Connecticut has an unrelenting work ethic. After Connecticut’s primaries in August, he suggested he’s not slowing down.
And after sweeping victories across the country last week, Blumenthal and his Democratic colleagues will enter the Senate next year back in the majority, with the likelihood of leadership roles on a couple of his committees.
Blumenthal said he doesn’t want discussion over the future leadership of the party to distract from Democrats’ focus on addressing what voters wanted out of government. 
Earlier on Monday, Blumenthal reiterated that he plans to serve as chairman of two committees he sits on: the Senate Veterans’ Affairs Committee and the Homeland Security’s Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations. The latter is a role he held when Senate Democrats were last in the majority.
As the top Democrat of that panel, he’s already wielded some of his investigatory power, including a recent investigation into a cryptocurrency firm and a series of public forums on U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s practices. But as a chair in the majority party, he and other Democrats will regain their subpoena power.
Blumenthal already has a framework of what his committee work will look like — corruption investigations that aren’t just focused on the president but members of his administration and corporations that he believes may have benefitted. As the prospect of another impeachment looms next year, he argues that’s not the only form of accountability. And he hopes his work and hearings will start quickly in the new year.
“I think impeachment could potentially be a blind alley, futile and frustrating and also a diversion from the focus that we really need, which is on affordability and accountability,” Blumenthal said Monday morning in Hartford. “Accountability doesn’t necessarily mean impeachment. It means uncovering corruption that then can be addressed by prosecution in a future Department of Justice or by other action that the Congress could take, like impeachment.”
But before Democrats assume the majority, they will serve at the remaining four work weeks of the year in the minority. Blumenthal and others hope to make an 11th-hour push on policy priorities in the lame-duck session before the end of the year. That includes seeking passage of the Kids Online Safety Act. But they have a limited window and will also contend with must-pass legislation such as government funding and an annual defense policy bill.
“The test will be for Republicans — will they work with us in the next 60 days and then afterwards in the next session?” Blumenthal said Monday in Hartford. “We will have the majority then and all we need is a few Republicans to go along with us to meet the needs of healthcare and housing and AI, which needs to be reined in.”
Since the 2024 election, when Democrats suffered defeats that relegated them to the minority and out of the White House, U.S. Sen. Chris Murphy has been vocal at times when his own party needed to do more. He was pressed earlier this year about whether Schumer should be replaced as leader. He didn’t weigh in on it at the time and said in March of this year that the caucus was united.
Murphy was recently discharged from the hospital after experiencing a stroke and will miss several weeks of votes while he recovers at a rehabilitation center.
It’s unclear if Schumer will get a challenger and even with some skepticism, he still appears on track to become majority leader again.
“Chuck Schumer was the quarterback of a team effort led by Senate Democrats and incredible candidates who ran all across the country,” House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries said at his press conference on Monday. The New York Democrat is looking to become the first Black speaker of the House next year and similarly faces some pushback to his own leadership bid.

name: Florida Phoenix
title: Hurricane Isaias claims keep climbing
description: Total estimated insured losses for Hurricane Isaias had climbed to more than $735.5 million as of Friday, data posted by the Florida Office of Insurance Regulation show. The total number of claims filed with insurance companies following landfall of the Category 2 Hurricane in Destin grew to 68,071. OIR data indicate 58.2% of the claims […]
text:
A resident of a storm-damaged apartment complex unloads his shovel on a pile of trash while cleaning out his apartment  in Pensacola Beach several days after the landfall of Hurricane Isaias on Oct. 11, 2026.  (Photo by Dan Anderson for Alabama Reflector)Total estimated insured losses for Hurricane Isaias had climbed to more than $735.5 million as of Friday, data posted by the Florida Office of Insurance Regulation show.
The total number of claims filed with insurance companies following landfall of the Category 2 Hurricane in Destin grew to 68,071. OIR data indicate 58.2% of the claims have been closed.
More than 81% of the total claims are for residential property coverage.
Private passenger automobile damage accounted for 7,825 claims, making it the second largest claim category behind residential property. There were 163 claims for commercial auto losses.
Of the 68,071 total claims that have been filed with insurance companies following Hurricane Iasias, 25,211 were closed with some form of payment. The data the OIR reports don’t include an average payment amount or details about payments made.
Another 14,402 claims have been closed with no payment.
Many of the closed, no-payment claims (6,835) involved instances in which the amount of insured damage claimed was less than the required deductible. Those account for the most claims closed with no payment.
That’s followed by claims closed for administrative reasons, of which there were 5,374. This category is broad and captures duplicate claims or those opened in error, claims with incorrect dates of loss, claims in which the policyholder didn’t communicate with the insurance company, and claims withdrawn by the policyholder or filed only as inquiries.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The OIR data show that three claims were closed with no payment due to suspicion of fraud. All three of those claims were submitted for private passenger automobile policies.
Isaias-related claims are open and no payment has been made to the policyholder in 20,482 instances.
The OIR website lists some of the “common reasons” claims can be closed without payment, including instances when the total damage reported in the claim does not exceed the policy deductible, and claims involving flood damage that “falls outside standard homeowner’s coverage.”
Another 20,482 claims are open and no payment has been made to the policyholder.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: WV lawmakers again question Flock reps as they gather information for potential bills
description: West Virginia lawmakers on Monday took another crack at getting answers to their questions from Flock Safety, a manufacturer of artificial intelligence-driven police surveillance devices, as they work to introduce legislation to rein in the technology during the 2027 legislative session.
text:
Dan Haley (left), chief legal officer for Flock Safety, and Matt Fanto (right), director of product security and privacy for the company, appeared before the Joint Standing Committee on Government Organization via video Monday, Nov. 9, 2026 in Charleston, West Virginia. (Photo by Will Price/West Virginia Legislative Photography)West Virginia lawmakers on Monday took another crack at getting answers to their questions from Flock Safety, a manufacturer of artificial intelligence-driven police surveillance devices, as they work to introduce legislation to rein in the technology during the 2027 legislative session.
Dan Haley, chief legal officer for Flock Safety, and Matt Fanto, director of product security and privacy for the company, appeared before the Joint Standing Committee on Government Organization via video conference to answer questions.
Municipalities in West Virginia have moved forward with contracts with the company, which has been the subject of privacy and constitutional concerns nationally. 
Committee members have gone back and forth with the company in a series of four letters with questions raised by testimony from Kevin Kane, the company’s director of government affairs, during August legislative interim meetings. Lawmakers have been generally dissatisfied with answers the company has given to their 19 written questions on topics ranging from security incidents and unauthorized access to data governance and infrastructure. 
In a letter dated Oct. 12, lawmakers requested that a representative from the company appear before the committee during November interim meetings. 
Haley said a rescheduled speaking commitment prevented him from traveling to West Virginia to appear in person. 
He defended Lane’s presentation in his remarks Monday, saying that all Flock employees are expected to speak “honestly and forthrightly, and with the intention of answering the questions posed. And I’m confident that my colleague did so.”
Haley said the company recognizes the concerns that automatic license plate readers raise, and he encouraged lawmakers to pass legislation that addresses those concerns. 
“Matt and I are here appearing before you today as my colleagues have appeared before dozens of legislative bodies and hundreds of city and town councils across the country, because we believe that the issues surrounding these technologies deserve to be fully aired and openly debated, and because we believe that these powerful tools should be subject to appropriate regulation,” Haley said.
“This is why we’re urging you, as we have urged your peers in states across the country, to pass a bill that establishes commonsense privacy protections and usage guardrails, while ensuring that law enforcement agencies have the ability to use this technology to keep the communities you represent safe,” he said. 
Lawmakers asked Haley questions for about an hour and a half. Del. Tristin Leavitt, R-Kanawha, started with the nearly 20 questions the company and lawmakers had exchanged letters about. 
Leavitt told reporters after the meeting he was “not particularly” satisfied with the company’s latest responses to his inquiries, but he noted that the company did provide some new information and clarified parts of Kane’s testimony.
Leavitt raised specific concerns with an incident in Dunwoody, Georgia, where live feeds of a children’s gymnastic class were reportedly accessed by Flock employees making a sales pitch about the devices. Leavitt said reporting of the incident indicated that the live feed was viewed for several hours.
Haley told lawmakers the city of Dunwoody was a development partner with the company, and granted permission for the company to use its data for the purposes of demonstrating it to prospective customers.  
Haley speculated Monday that if the incident happened, it’s likely that the gym’s live feed was left in an open browser.
“That would be pure speculation,” Haley said. “There would be no reason for a sales rep or anyone else to sit on an open feed for four hours.”
Leavitt told reporters Monday he still has concerns about the level of access to data that Flock employees, and the company should have more of a sense of how much of that is able to happen, he said. 
“Maybe it is the case that someone left their computer open,” Leavitt said. “But to have hours and hours of video streaming is a concern for anyone, certainly for a parent. And it’s just not clear to me that any municipality actually signed up for that.”
Leavitt said he and other lawmakers are working on legislation that would address issues including corporate practice questions, along with law enforcement use and abuse.
“The reality for any legislation is that you’re going to put together 100 members in one body, and a third of that in another body, and everyone needs to get together and talk about it,” he said. “So, although we’ve been gathering lots of data for legislation, the most important thing will be really to sit down and see where the will of those different bodies is, and then hash out the details.”
Del. Ryan Browning, R-Wayne, told reporters after the meeting his worry with the technology is the potential abuse of the system. 
“My biggest concern at this point is pattern of life searches when crimes have not been committed, and whether it be targeting gun owners or the LGBTQ community or whatever civil rights violation you want to throw out there,” Browning said. “Whenever you start talking about searching for those types of or having those types of searches, then you start infringing on people’s rights, and I have a serious problem about that. That’s been my concern from the beginning.”
Browning said lawmakers are considering portions of model legislation called the PEEPS Act, which aims to limit law-enforcement misuse of the technology, along with parts of another lawmaker’s proposal. 
“We want to get a general consensus with our colleagues on what is palatable as far as a solution goes on a bill,” Browning said. “The goal at this point is to have something ready to go day one, so we can get it in the system, and then start the fun part of debating it, and making changes if needed.”
The 2027 legislative session begins Jan. 13, 2027.

name: Source New Mexico
title: US Senate advances New Mexico US Sen. Heinrich’s controversial permit reform bill
description: New Mexico U.S. Sen. Martin Heinrich’s permitting reform bill is one step closer to becoming law after clearing a key U.S. Senate procedural vote Monday evening.
text:
The U.S. Senate on Nov. 9, 2026, advanced a controversial permitting reform bill championed by U.S. Sen. Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.). Above: Protesters decry the bill outside Heinrich’s downtown Albuquerque office Oct. 27, 2026. (Photo by Patrick Lohmann/Source NM)New Mexico U.S. Sen. Martin Heinrich’s permitting reform bill is one step closer to becoming law after clearing a key U.S. Senate procedural vote Monday evening. 
The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, which Heinrich, a Democrat, has championed alongside a bipartisan group of senators, aims to hasten federal environmental reviews of energy projects. The legislation  has received widespread criticism, including from fellow members of New Mexico’s congressional delegation, over provisions they will weaken environmental protections and exclude tribes from meaningful impact.
The U.S. Senate voted 73-25 to end debate on the bill, which requires 60 “yes” votes. The bill now heads to the Senate floor, where senators can add additional amendments, before a final floor vote expected in the coming days.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Members of the All Pueblo Council of Governors, which represent New Mexico Pueblos, flew to Washington, D.C. on Monday to urge senators to vote against the bill. They say the bill, even an amended version Heinrich and cosponsors released Saturday, makes harmful developments on sacred sites more likely. New Mexico Gov.-elect Deb Haaland also opposed the amended bill, as did state Attorney General Raúl Torrez in a letter to US Senate leaders signed by several other state’s attorneys general.
U.S. Sen. Ben Ray Luján (D-N.M.) cast one of the “no” votes. He said in a statement Monday that while he supports facilitating the faster development of clean energy and infrastructure projects, he shares the concerns expressed by tribal leaders and environmentalists.
“After spending the last month listening to these concerns, I cannot support advancing the bill in its current form,” he said. “I remain committed to working with my colleagues to address these concerns, make meaningful improvements, and get this right.”  
Other members of Congress said they oppose the bill out of concern they cannot trust President Donald Trump’s administration to make good on its commitments to help renewable energy projects receive permits along with fossil fuel projects like pipelines. 
While senators were casting votes Monday, Trump held a news conference in which he announced that he fully supported the permitting reform bill, but also that he would not approve any new wind turbines, which the bill seeks to encourage. 
New Mexico US Sen. Heinrich urges Senate passage of permitting reform bill amid ongoing opposition 

“The bill hasn’t been fully negotiated,” he told reporters, according to The Hill. “I will not approve wind turbines because wind turbines are a major loser.”
The vote comes after Heinrich and cosponsor U.S. Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse (D-R.I.) held a news conference Monday morning urging their fellow senators to support the bill. Heinrich said the bill, if passed, would reduce energy costs at a time when many Americans are frustrated with rising prices, as well as hold data centers financially liable for new costs they impose on energy grids. 
The vote to advance the bill prompted swift rebuke from the Western Environmental Law Center. Erik Schlenker-Goodrich, the center’s executive director, said in a statement Monday that the U.S. Senate and U.S. House of Representatives should wait to consider the bill until January, when a new Democratic majority would have a “constructive conversation” about build out renewable energy infrastructure. 
“The false urgency imposed on senators by the bill’s sponsors exists for only one reason—to minimize scrutiny and prevent lawmakers and Americans from understanding the enormity of BAAJA’s power transfer away from the people and to the oligarch class,” he said. 
If the bill passes the U.S. Senate, it would then head to the U.S. House.

name: Utah News Dispatch
title: Facing calls to resign, Sen. Kathleen Riebe says discrimination report is ‘distorted’
description: Nearly a week after Utah Senate Democrats called on Sen. Kathleen Riebe to resign, she’s making a case that a discrimination inquiry against her was based more on politics than proof and “rests on a distorted record.” Riebe’s attorney alleged in a Monday email to Utah News Dispatch and other news outlets that the investigator […]
text:
Sen. Kathleen Riebe's attorney said a complaint against her came days after she said she would run to lead the Senate Democratic caucus. Nearly a week after Utah Senate Democrats called on Sen. Kathleen Riebe to resign, she’s making a case that a discrimination inquiry against her was based more on politics than proof and “rests on a distorted record.”
Riebe’s attorney alleged in a Monday email to Utah News Dispatch and other news outlets that the investigator who conducted the outside review “blindly adopted the view of those politically opposed to Senator Riebe.” 
In a letter to Senate President-elect Evan Vickers dated Nov. 8, attorney Ryan McConnell said the complaint against his client, filed by a Senate employee, came days after Riebe announced she planned to run to lead the Senate Democratic caucus. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“Senator (Luz) Escamilla holds that post, and Senator Riebe’s challenge put it in jeopardy,” McConnell wrote to Vickers, saying most of the witnesses interviewed for the report had a stake in keeping Escamilla in the role, to which she was reelected last week. But he said nothing in the report shows the investigator accounted for those ties. 
Escamilla declined to comment on the matter through a Senate spokesperson, who cited confidentiality reasons. 
Also on Monday, newly released invoices shed light on the cost of the investigation. The law firm Parsons Behle & Latimer billed the Legislature $14,435, according to invoices provided to Utah News Dispatch in response to a public records request. 
The Senate last week made public a thoroughly redacted version of the report that concluded there’s a likelihood Riebe’s treatment of the Senate staffer was motivated at least in part by race, national origin or ethnicity and interfered with the employee’s ability to do her job. 
Riebe believed the employee’s complaint was an attempt at retribution after Riebe alleged the employee was working on another senator’s campaign, the report states, while witnesses said no formal campaign had been established. The redacted report does not show who the other senator is.
The review said Riebe acknowledged previously telling staffers that she did not want gay interns “who were coming out of the closet.” Her attorney argues in his letter to Vickers that in reality, the comment was based on concern but her accusers “recast them as bigotry.” 
Outside review details discrimination complaint against a Utah Democrat  

He said “in a long, confidential conversation with caucus staff, Senator Riebe explained that the Capitol can be a hard place for a young person who has just come out. She worried about their mental health. She wanted to protect them. Those who wanted her out stripped that private expression of concern of its context and turned it against her.” 
Through her attorney, Riebe is asking Vickers not to impose any of the discipline handed down by his predecessor, outgoing Senate President Stuart Adams, until she has an opportunity to weigh in on the final report. Details of the four corrective actions were also redacted. 
Although she was interviewed as part of the inquiry, Riebe said she hadn’t seen the findings until her colleagues voted to expel her from the caucus last week and publicly urged her to step down less than an hour before polls closed on Election Day.
Riebe says the report’s findings should have stayed confidential under the Legislature’s administrative policy. 
Her attorney reiterated statements Riebe made Friday, saying she “has spent her career fighting for underrepresented groups.” He noted she has carried measures freeing up funds to better pay and retain teachers in “high-need” schools and strengthening requirements for police interrogations of minors, among others.
Riebe, an educator and former member of the Utah State Board of Education, has served in the Senate since 2018. She ran to represent the 1st Congressional District earlier this year before dropping out to endorse Ben McAdams, who went on to win the seat in last week’s election. Riebe’s current Utah Senate term runs through Jan. 1, 2029.

name: Washington State Standard
title: WA state schools chief won’t seek re-election in 2028
description: Chris Reykdal, who has led Washington state’s public school system through a period of financial and political upheaval, and a pandemic, announced Monday that he will not seek re-election to a fourth term in 2028. “Public institutions are strengthened when leadership changes, new voices emerge, and those entrusted with public office understand that the posit[...]
text:
Superintendent of Public Instruction Chris Reykdal is sworn in on Wednesday, Jan. 15, 2025, at the Washington State Capitol in Olympia, Wash. Reykdal was first elected to the job in 2016. (Photo by Ryan Berry/Washington State Standard)Chris Reykdal, who has led Washington state’s public school system through a period of financial and political upheaval, and a pandemic, announced Monday that he will not seek re-election to a fourth term in 2028.
“Public institutions are strengthened when leadership changes, new voices emerge, and those entrusted with public office understand that the position belongs to the people, not to the person holding it,” he said in a statement. 
“While our state does not have term limits for statewide office, I believe we should impose those limits on ourselves to ensure new energy and new opportunities are always created,” said Reykdal, who was first elected superintendent of public instruction in 2016.
Reykdal, a Democrat and former state lawmaker, said he may run for another statewide position in 2028, seek a federal office, or “walk away from elective office altogether.”
Reykdal on Monday declined further comment on his future plans.
At this moment, if he were to run for another statewide or federal office, he would find himself facing an incumbent Democrat.
“My wife Kim and I will continue to weigh each of those paths, and I will be transparent about that decision along the way,” he said.
Until then, he said, there are needs to address in the next two years, starting with securing additional dollars for cash-strapped districts.
“There is important work ahead, particularly around sustainable and equitable school funding, student well-being, academic achievement, holding other elected officials accountable to public education, and ensuring every young person has meaningful opportunities after high school,” he said.
Reykdal, 54, was narrowly elected to the nonpartisan post in 2016, beating Erin Jones by a single percentage point. He had an easier re-election in 2020, defeating Maia Espinoza by nearly 10 points. Two years ago, Reykdal defeated David Olson by a similar margin.
A trio of major events continue to shape his tenure. 
In his first term, lawmakers and Gov. Jay Inslee dialed up a major increase in state funding for public schools. That brought the state into compliance with the state Supreme Court’s landmark ruling in the McCleary case that found Washington was not providing adequate financial support for local schools.
Since then, the state hasn’t kept up with its commitment in spite of annual urgings from Reykdal. Now, school districts are contemplating suing again.
In Reykdal’s second term, the COVID-19 pandemic upended the delivery of education in the public school system.  The aftereffects will linger for years. 
Learning loss was broad and deep. Social and emotional challenges among students were widespread, and manifested in disruptive behavior, a surge in chronic absenteeism and a youth mental health crisis. Closing campuses incited an exodus from public schools.
In his current term, districts continue to wrestle with financial challenges and pandemic-related effects. Reykdal is also coping with the hostile administration of President Donald Trump, who has directed U.S. Secretary of Education Linda McMahon to dismantle the federal agency. 
The Office of Superintendent of Public Instruction channels funding to schools, implements state education laws and sets curriculum standards. Like all state agencies, the office can request legislation, but cannot pass laws.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: University of Alaska reports $86.2M in frozen federal grants restored
description: Officials with the University of Alaska report more than $86 million in federal grants that were frozen or delayed by the Trump administration have been restored. The update was provided to the University of Alaska Board of Regents at their quarterly board meeting on Friday by Shelby Beck, assistant director of federal relations for the […]
text:
A sign, seen July 24, 2026, celebrates the University of Alaska Fairbanks' status as a leader in Arctic research. Behind the sign are buildings that house UAF's  Geophysical Insititute and International Arctic Research Center. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)Officials with the University of Alaska report more than $86 million in federal grants that were frozen or delayed by the Trump administration have been restored.
The update was provided to the University of Alaska Board of Regents at their quarterly board meeting on Friday by Shelby Beck, assistant director of federal relations for the university. The funds restored spanned 29 federal grants, totaling $86.2 million.  
“Our office is pleased to formally report to the board that the University of Alaska system no longer has any frozen or delayed federal grants,” Beck said.
But another 32 federal grants with remaining balances of $16.7 million have been terminated since 2025, she said. 
“We recognize the pain these terminations have caused, and while the odds are not great, we will continue to look for opportunities to restore terminated grants,” Beck added. 
At the meeting, regents and university officials did not directly address the Trump administration’s move to cut or freeze an estimated $177 billion in federal funding to universities and research divisions nationwide. But Beck acknowledged the UA funds were restored through support from Alaska’s U.S. Republican Sens. Dan Sullivan and Lisa Murkowski.
“They have helped us address numerous administrative delays and other challenges in ensuring federal grants are released and awarded as Congress intended, we are deeply grateful to them,” she said. “Without their support, we would be in a very different situation.” 
Federal grant funding restored
The 29 restored grants include funding through the U.S. Departments of Homeland Security, Energy and Agriculture, across all three university systems, according to information provided by the university on Monday. 
At the University of Alaska Anchorage, that included five federal grants totaling $42.1 million.
Over $40 million was restored to the Department of Homeland Security’s Arctic Domain Awareness Center, which conducts research and education initiatives which supports the U.S. Coast Guard and a variety of academic and industry partners in the U.S. and Canada. 
At the University of Alaska Fairbanks, 21 federal grants were restored totaling $43.2 million. That included $13 million through the Department of Agriculture for a project to strengthen agricultural systems and workforce training, called the Diverse Next Gen Food Policy Leaders program. 
Grant funding of $9 million through the Department of Defense was restored for an entrepreneurship program called RISE-UP. Funding of $9 million for an energy research and development initiative called Galena Alaska Microgrid Riverine Hydrokinetics was restored, as well as $7.5 million for critical minerals mapping called the Northwest Region CORE-CM Project through the Department of Energy. 
At the University of Alaska Southeast, three federal grants were restored totaling $857,408, including $470,000 in funding from the Department of Agriculture for developing an educational pathway for geocultural sciences for rural and Alaska Native students of Southeast Alaska. 
Federal grant funding terminated
Of the 32 federal grants terminated since 2025, the university reported 16 grants were terminated at UAA totaling $3.77 million, 16 grants canceled at UAF totaling $12.9 million and no grants were terminated at UAS. 
At UAF, that included $8.8 million terminated through the U.S. Department of Education as part of grant funding for minority-serving institutions, including Alaska Native and Native Hawaiian-serving programs and support services. When the cuts were announced last year, university officials said it affected programs at the Bristol Bay campus in Dillingham and in Fairbanks at the Community and Technical College focused on career training and workforce development, as well as student services. 
Nationwide, the Department of Education announced it would redirect $350 million in congressionally-allocated funding for minority-serving institutions elsewhere, part of the Trump administration’s initiative to eliminate programs that focus on diversity, equity and inclusion. 
In Alaska, Jonathan Taylor, UA director of public affairs, said by email Monday the reasons given by the Trump administration for terminating funding varied by project and grant program and was not immediately available, “but it was broadly due to a shift in federal priorities,” he said. 
Taylor said some grant managers were given explicit reasons, including “DEI-related reasons” while other funds were reallocated to other priorities.

name: VTDigger
title: Measles cases found in Orleans County, health officials warn
description:
“The risk presented to most Vermonters by the current situation is low,” the Vermont Health Department said, but it is asking providers to be on alert.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Measles cases found in Orleans County, health officials warn.
text:
Measles, mumps and rubella virus vaccine at Union Community Care clinic in Lancaster, Pa., on Thursday, Oct. 8, 2026. Photo by Jessie Wardarski/AP

The Vermont Department of Health has confirmed a “small number” of connected measles cases in Orleans County, it said Monday. An investigation and response are ongoing, according to a release.
The department is asking healthcare providers to maintain a heightened awareness and report suspected cases immediately, even if there is not yet laboratory confirmation of infection.  
“The risk presented to most Vermonters by the current situation is low,” department spokesperson Kyle Casteel wrote in an email. He said the department’s epidemiologists are in the field responding to the situation but will be able to provide further detail soon. The Health Department released a health advisory to providers Monday followed by formal confirmation of the disease later in the day.
“We are providing testing, offering vaccination and guidance and communicating with the people who have symptoms, working with local hospitals and healthcare providers to coordinate our response, and continuing to monitor the situation and communicate with the public,” Casteel wrote in an email to VTDigger. North Country Hospital in Newport and Copley Hospital in Morrisville are the closest hospitals for most of Orleans County. 
“I do know they don’t make this report lightly,” said Dr. Tracy Tyson, a pediatrician in St. Albans, referring to the advisory before the cases were confirmed. Tyson, who is president of the Vermont chapter of the American Academy of Pediatrics, said she takes the department’s advisory “much more seriously” than previous situations where cases were suspected.
Vermont had one reported case earlier in 2026, two in 2025 and a total of two in the 10 years prior, according to the Health Department. Casteel did not provide additional information on the number of cases confirmed Monday, citing patient privacy.
The virus is one of the most contagious known pathogens, with infection occurring in about nine of every 10 people exposed without appropriate vaccination, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
There is no antiviral treatment for the illness, which presents with a fever and rash that typically starts on the face and moves down the body. 
The measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine is known to reduce infection and illness. The Health Department’s advisory urged providers to ensure their patients are up to date on the vaccine. 
However, uptake of the vaccine has waned across the country in recent years, as questions of vaccine efficacy have become increasingly politicized and as federal Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and the president have sought to erode existing immunization recommendations. For the 2025-2026 school year, 92.4% of kindergartners nationwide received the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine, compared with 95.2% in the 2019-2020 school year, CDC data shows.   
In Vermont, Health Department data shows that 94% of children in independent and public schools have been fully vaccinated against measles before starting kindergarten. The data, however, does not include homeschooled children or those who have yet to begin school. 
According to Health Department data, more than 90% of students in most Orleans Central Supervisory Union schools have full compliance with their MMR vaccines, though the Albany Community School and Orleans Elementary School dip below that at 86% and 88% compliance respectively.
Herd immunity — the level at which enough people are resistant to the disease to prevent its transmission — requires 95% immunization, the department notes.
The cases in Vermont come just as experts forecast that the U.S. is on track to lose its measles elimination status.
“I think this has been coming for quite some time,” Tyson said. Losing elimination status, she said, is a benchmark of just how prevalent the disease already is, and it’s already widespread through the U.S.
On Friday, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention said the U.S. has seen 5,182 cases of measles this year. It’s the most the country has seen since 1991, according to a CDC database. The curbing of the multiyear outbreak in the early 1990s coincided with the timing of a CDC vaccine panel and American Academy of Pediatrics recommendation of two-dose MMR vaccine.
In 2025, the U.S. had 2,289 cases of measles, while 2024 saw only 285.
Just last week, a child in upstate New York’s Lewis County died amid an ongoing outbreak there. Across the U.S., the CDC reports a total of four deaths so far this year.
Tyson encouraged Vermonters to check with their doctor to ensure they are up to date on their MMR vaccines, and she reminded parents with children under the age of 1 that they could consider an early measles vaccine. Though the Health Department has not changed its official guidance to recommend earlier vaccination, Tyson said that it is still scientifically sound and more likely to be recommended if there is an outbreak. 
She also encouraged parents who may have been hesitant to vaccinate their children to revisit a conversation with their provider. 
“The risk of the vaccine may have felt higher to them,” she said. “This might change the risk calculation to them.” 
If parents still choose not to vaccinate their children, she recommended having a plan for exposure — about how to detect early symptoms, where to get care and how to keep from spreading the illness to others.
