description: TOPEKA — Details of an agreement to end a lawsuit affecting the Kansas City Chiefs stadium development were revealed Monday.   The agreement between the Unified Government of Wyandotte and Kansas City and the state of Kansas outlines boundaries of the STAR bond district, determines the local sales tax pledge area and allows for the appointment […]
text:
A banner on Dec. 22, 2025, outside the Docking State Office Building in Topeka signals the Chiefs are coming to Kansas but details of how the state will pay for the stadium development are still being considered. On Nov. 5, 2026, the Unified Government of Wyandotte and Kansas City agreed to a deal that resolves issues in a lawsuit the government entity filed to change the stadium development. (Photo by Morgan Chilson/Kansas Reflector)TOPEKA — Details of an agreement to end a lawsuit affecting the Kansas City Chiefs stadium development were revealed Monday.  
The agreement between the Unified Government of Wyandotte and Kansas City and the state of Kansas outlines boundaries of the STAR bond district, determines the local sales tax pledge area and allows for the appointment of Christal Watson, Kansas City, Kansas, mayor, to the Kansas Sports Facilities Authority that will govern the development. 
“Settling these outstanding items is a decisive step forward for all involved,” said Gov. Laura Kelly in a news release announcing the deal. “Every detail is critical when you’re working on a $4 billion deal — and our strong, committed partnerships paved the way for a shared path forward for all of us.”
The unified government commission voted unanimously Thursday to pledge its portion of sales tax revenue and a portion of its transient guest tax revenue collected in the Sales Tax and Revenue Bonds district limited to the stadium and areas surrounding it, the news release said. 
The commission also agreed to drop the lawsuit it filed over concerns the stadium deal and the Kansas Sports Facilities Authority interfered with their ability to make decisions locally to tax, zone and plan, as well as collect fees and provide utility service through its publicly owned utility. 
The state agreed to remove the Quindaro Ruins area, north of Kansas City along the Missouri River, from the STAR bond district, excluding future development there from being included in revenue requirements of the Chiefs stadium, the news release said. 
Watson said in the news release the agreement allays the concerns of the local community and is a “win” for all parties. She will have a voting seat on the sports facility board and on the Community Impact Committee that will be set up as part of the Chiefs STAR bond agreement. 
The agreement must be signed by the sports authority chair, and a meeting of the 11-member board is expected in the next two weeks, the release said.

title: New Mexico lawmakers review proposals to modernize state’s criminal justice system
description: New Mexico lawmakers on Friday previewed legislation for next year’s session that would significantly expand the New Mexico Sentencing Commission’s responsibilities as part of a 10-year effort to modernize the state’s criminal justice system. Commission leaders, however, oppose the bill in its current form.
text:
A New Mexico Department of Corrections official walks toward the front entrance of the Western New Mexico Correctional Facility in Grants in November 2021. A proposed bill for the 2027 legislative session would embark on a 10-year push to modernize the state’s criminal justice system. (Source NM file photo)New Mexico lawmakers on Friday previewed legislation for next year’s session that would significantly expand the New Mexico Sentencing Commission’s responsibilities as part of a 10-year effort to modernize the state’s criminal justice system. Commission leaders, however, oppose the bill in its current form.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Rep. Tara Lujan (D-Santa Fe) presented a legislative proposal to the interim Courts, Corrections and Justice Committee to significantly expand the responsibilities for the New Mexico Sentencing Commission, a University of New Mexico policy analysis commission that’s existed since the early 2000s, to modernize the state’s criminal justice system.
The proposed bill builds upon a memorial passed in this year’s legislative session that directed the Legislature to create a task force responsible for drafting a 10-year plan to address “systemic problems,” such as exceedingly high levels of crime and recidivism.
The draft bill would expand the Sentencing Commission into the New Mexico Criminal Justice Institute and charge it with creating five new standing committees focused on data; system capacity; workforce; funding and accountability; and juvenile justice. Under the proposal, the five committees would be responsible for rolling out the 10-year plan across four phases.
The fourth and final phase under the proposal would include the rollout of a data dashboard that focuses on metrics from eight categories: crimes categorized by offense type; arrests categorized by offense type; pre-trial detention; use and success of deflection and diversion; sentences; dismissals; probation and parole outcomes; and recidivism.
“The legislation that we are proposing is based on the input and ideas of hundreds of citizens and justice system professionals and dozens of legislative hearings,” Lujan said at Friday’s hearing.
However, Sentencing Commission Executive Director Douglas Carver, who spoke alongside Lujan during the hearing, said the commission opposes the bill “at this point,” largely because he said the commission wasn’t involved with its early drafting.
When Committee Chair Rep. Christine Chandler (D-Los Alamos) asked him where the commission stands on the proposal, he said he and his colleagues would happily work alongside lawmakers to improve it before the legislative session begins in January.
“Recognizing this is still in early stages, we’re more than happy to work with the representative,” Carver said. “The big objection that the executive committee has is that the commission wasn’t brought on board…it’s the kind of bill that would ideally be brought to the commission in early changes.”
Chandler told Lujan that it is “probably smart to be talking in detail” with Sentencing Commission leaders as the proposed legislation would directly affect them.
State Sen. Linda Trujillo (D-Santa Fe) raised concerns about ambiguity in the draft bill’s language, which she said made it difficult to ascertain whether the state or UNM would be on the hook for paying, hiring and managing staff at the expanded commission.
“You need to be really cautious about the things that you direct UNM to do,” she said.
Lujan thanked her fellow state lawmakers for their feedback and said that her proposals are “an endeavor.”
Lujan’s other proposed bill, which prompted little discussion at Friday’s hearing, would institute a “deflection” program, in which police officers and sheriffs’ deputies could offer low-level offenders a chance to participate in a social service program rather than be arrested and detained. 
“That’s why we’re having this conversation — to really flesh through how we’re going to get this,” she said.

name: Rhode Island Current
title: Hegseth attacks civilian-led education in Naval War College speech
description: As calls for his resignation and impeachment grow in Washington, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth came to the U.S. Naval War College in Newport Monday to announce a sweeping effort to strip military education of what he called its overly civilian influences. “This morning we strip away the comfortable veneer of academic tradition,” he told an […]
text:
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth speaks at the U.S. Naval War College in Newport on Monday, Nov. 9, 2026. (Photo by Mass Communication Specialist 2nd Class Connor Burns/U.S. Naval War College)As calls for his resignation and impeachment grow in Washington, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth came to the U.S. Naval War College in Newport Monday to announce a sweeping effort to strip military education of what he called its overly civilian influences.
“This morning we strip away the comfortable veneer of academic tradition,” he told an audience of 672 military personnel, students, faculty and civilian instructors inside Spruance Hall. “The fundamental duty of the armed forces of the United States is to ensure victory in war — full stop.”
Hegseth set the curriculum overhaul in motion in March, ordering a 90-day review of the Pentagon’s six senior service colleges, including the war colleges for the Army, Navy, Air Force and Marines and the National Defense University and National War College. The Pentagon established a task force to scrutinize their faculty and curriculum to ensure the schools were producing warfighters rather than “social justice warriors.”
The result: an eight-page memo dated Monday containing 33 directives Hegseth said would rid the colleges of “relics of 19th century academia” and better prepare officers for modern warfare.
“In the profession of arms, nostalgia is fatal,” he said. “When our war college graduates walk across the stage and take command, their minds cannot be anchored on the strategic consensus of a vanished world.”
Hegseth presented an outline on some of the new guidelines during his 30-minute speech at the after which he promptly left the auditorium. He allowed no time for questions and answers with faculty and students and did not take questions from local media. 
Under the new guidelines, the Pentagon will judge military education programs by a single standard: whether they produce leaders capable of winning wars. 
The directives would make newly hired civilian faculty ineligible for lifetime tenure and emeritus status, instead putting them on renewable three-year contracts tied to teaching performance and national security research. They also call for new “warfighter chair” positions at senior service colleges, filled by high-performing colonels and lieutenant colonels who have held operational commands within the previous two years.
“Peace through strength is not achieved by comfortable consensus and business as usual approaches,” Hegseth said. “It is achieved by preparing our minds and our forces to wage war with such devastating speed, precision, and lethality that no adversary dares test American resolve — that’s deterrence.”
Hegseth’s central critique against America’s military colleges is that they have become too much like civilian universities, importing what he called the “worst pathologies” of higher education at the expense of their focus on victory in the battlefield.
He pointed to the Naval War College’s 12-year partnership with Brown University as an example, saying he directed the Pentagon to end the relationship last month.
“The only place more strikingly ideological in one direction — more than Columbia or Harvard — is Brown,” Hegseth, a graduate of Princeton and Harvard, said. “It was long past due to end that relationship.”
The partnership between the two schools dates to June 2014, when then-Naval War College President Rear Adm. Walter E. “Ted” Carter Jr. and Brown President Christina Paxson signed a research and education agreement with the university’s Watson Institute for International Studies. The agreement was intended to promote joint research and teaching, including programs in science-related fields tied to long-term national defense needs.
A spokesperson for Brown University did not immediately respond to request for comment on Hegseth’s statements.



Quotation







Peace through strength is not achieved by comfortable consensus and business as usual approaches. It is achieved by preparing our minds and our forces to wage war with such devastating speed, precision, and lethality that no adversary dares test American resolve — that's deterrence.


– Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth in Naval War College speech


Hegseth praised several other military colleges for moving ahead with changes he wants to see across the system. He singled out the Marine Corps War College in Quantico, Virginia; Army War College in Carlisle, Pennsylvania; and Eisenhower School at the National Defense University in Washington, D.C., for dismantling diversity, equity and inclusion offices and removing what he called “ideological jargon” from their curricula.
He also criticized what he described as “frivolous research” into gender identity and climate change, and raised concerns about civilian university partnerships in specialized military education programs.
Hegseth reserved some of his sharpest criticism for the Naval War College itself. The Pentagon’s review, he said, identified a “stubborn undercurrent of passive-aggressive institutional resistance” there.
About 70% of the Naval War College’s faculty are civilians. Lt. Cmdr. Seth Koenig, the college’s public affairs officer, said its president and provost would review the 33 directives against the existing curriculum before determining what changes might be necessary. 
“A few things that (Hegseth) mentioned specifically on stage are not in direct conflict with anything we’re currently doing,” Koenig said.
The college’s academic programs include strategy and policy, national security affairs, theater security decision-making and joint military operations, Koenig said.
“Rhode Island Unwelcomes Hegseth, Again” protest organizer Kristen Lancaster leads a chant at the Pell Bridge off-ramp Monday morning, Nov. 9, 2026, as the secretary of defense visits the U.S. Naval War College in Newport. (Photo by David Hansen/Rhode Island Current)
Calls for impeachment 
Roughly three hours after Hegseth’s speech, U.S. Rep. Thomas Massie, a Kentucky Republican, reintroduced articles of impeachment against the defense secretary over the war against Iran and other military operations in Yemen and Venezuela. Massie previously did so in September before the chamber adjourned. 
A chorus of calls for Hegseth’s impeachment echoed along Hegseth’s route to the Naval War College as a group of about 30 to 40 protestors stood in the drizzly air near the Newport Pell Bridge off-ramp holding signs calling the secretary a “war criminal.” A group held up individual  block letters to spell RESIGN.
“We know what he’s doing is not legal,” said Kristen Lancaster, 51, co-founder of the Lil’ Rhody Visibility Brigade and a retired federal worker who served six years in the Army. “There’s no oversight.”
Lancaster cited as examples the War in Iran, the renaming of the Department of Defense to the Department of War and double tap strikes in the Caribbean targeting survivors clinging to the wreckage of suspected drug boats. “As a veteran and former civil servant, I find it revolting,” she said.



Quotation







We know what he’s doing is not legal. There’s no oversight.


– Kristen Lancaster, protester and a retired federal worker who served six years in the Army


Hegseth made no direct mention of Iran during his speech. He referred twice to Operation Epic Fury, the Pentagon’s name for the U.S. military campaign against Iran, as an example of modern warfare and the kind of operational experience he wants military colleges to prepare officers for.
“When joint headquarters in the Middle East faced intense combat operations during Operation Epic Fury, students were pulled directly from the war seminar rooms and deployed into the fight,” Hegseth said. “These officers stepped immediately into operational roles performing with devastating effectiveness and outperforming peers who had spent their academic year writing essays.”
Speaking to national outlets outside the Department of Defense’s plane at the Quonset State airport, he planned to hold a press conference Tuesday — his first since May 5 — on the impeachment calls.
Janine L. Weisman contributed to this report.

title: Delaware employers’ workers’ comp cut is nearly triple original proposal
description: Loss costs fall 3.99% Dec. 1 for a 10th straight year after regulators and the ratepayer advocate reviewed a 1.40% filing; safety discounts of up to 12% are also being restored DOVER, Del. — Delaware employers will get a larger workers’ compensation cost reduction than initially proposed when new rates take effect Dec. 1, extending a decade-long streak of de[...]
text:
Image created on 11/9 using AI.
Loss costs fall 3.99% Dec. 1 for a 10th straight year after regulators and the ratepayer advocate reviewed a 1.40% filing; safety discounts of up to 12% are also being restored
DOVER, Del. — Delaware employers will get a larger workers’ compensation cost reduction than initially proposed when new rates take effect Dec. 1, extending a decade-long streak of decreases.
The Delaware Compensation Rating Bureau originally proposed a 1.40% average reduction in voluntary-market loss costs and a 1.53% reduction in residual-market rates.
After review by the Delaware Department of Insurance, an independent actuarial firm and the state’s Ratepayer Advocate, the approved filing instead reduces voluntary-market loss costs by an average of 3.99% and residual-market rates by 4.11%.
That makes the voluntary-market reduction about 2.85 times the decrease originally proposed.
Insurance Commissioner Trinidad Navarro approved the amended filing Oct. 12 for new and renewal policies effective Dec. 1. Insurance carriers must submit filings reflecting the new values by Dec. 11.
The rating bureau said the final numbers followed discussions and a settlement involving the bureau, the Department of Insurance and the Ratepayer Advocate, which retained a second independent actuary.
The bureau cautioned that the amended figures represent a “negotiated outcome” and do not necessarily mean all parties agreed on what the appropriate rate level should be.
“I am pleased to announce that for a decade, we have been able to approve rate decreases which help attract new companies and jobs to Delaware,” Navarro said in an Oct. 20 statement. “Delaware’s businesses used to pay some of the highest workers’ compensation premiums in the country.”
Actual savings will vary from employer to employer. Loss costs are the estimates of future claim costs that insurers use as a foundation for setting workers’ compensation prices. An employer’s final premium can also depend on factors including payroll, industry classification, claims history and the insurer’s pricing.
Lower insurance costs do not reduce benefits paid to workers injured on the job, according to the Department of Insurance.
Safety discount restored
Employers may eventually have another opportunity to reduce their workers’ compensation bills through changes to Delaware’s Workplace Safety Program.
The program provides premium credits to eligible employers that undergo safety inspections and address recommended improvements.
A 2024 law, Senate Bill 306, expanded eligibility, but changes associated with a new experience-rating plan unintentionally reduced the maximum Workplace Safety Program discount available to some businesses.
Senate Bill 248, enacted June 10, changes the formula used to calculate the workplace safety credit from 20% times one minus an employer’s credibility factor to 40% times one minus the credibility factor.
The change restores a maximum credit of 12%. Credit determinations using the new formula may be communicated beginning Dec. 1, 2026, and apply to workers’ compensation policies effective Aug. 1, 2027, or later.
“This legislation provides Delaware business owners the opportunity to save money by maintaining a good workplace safety program,” said state Rep. Ed Osienski, who co-sponsored the legislation with lead sponsor Sen. Nicole Poore.
“This legislation invests in safe workplaces, rewards responsible business practices, and strengthens our commitment to protect every Delaware worker,” Poore said.
As of the end of 2025, 853 Delaware employers had saved an estimated $3.6 million through the Workplace Safety Program, according to the Department of Insurance. Eligible businesses are notified seven months before renewal, and failing to qualify for the program cannot be used as a reason to increase an employer’s premium.
The department’s revised guidance also reminds insurers that carrier-run workplace inspection procedures must be recertified twice a year. The department said the reminder was prompted by instances in which carriers had not kept those procedures properly certified.
What it means for Delaware businesses
The larger-than-proposed rate reduction matters most to businesses with significant payrolls or jobs carrying higher workers’ compensation costs, including construction, manufacturing, retail, restaurants and other labor-intensive industries.
The 3.99% figure, however, should not be interpreted as a guaranteed 3.99% reduction in every employer’s final bill. Insurers begin with DCRB loss costs and then apply their own approved pricing factors along with the employer’s classification, payroll and claims experience.
The Workplace Safety Program creates a separate potential savings opportunity for employers willing to undergo inspections and maintain qualifying safety practices.
The Dec. 1 workers’ compensation decrease is Delaware’s 10th consecutive annual reduction. Last year, the state approved an 11.6% average reduction in voluntary-market loss costs.
Delaware Public Media reported Nov. 4 on the 3.99% and 4.11% reductions and the expansion of workplace safety discounts. DCRB’s filing documents provide additional context showing that the voluntary-market decrease initially proposed was 1.40% before the regulatory and actuarial review produced the larger reduction.

name: Utah News Dispatch
title: Commentary: Taking notes from Texas and Virginia’s data center slow down
description: The energy at the Capitol was electric. Standing shoulder to shoulder last month with others who recognize how data centers tie into the fight for climate justice is energizing. Across the country, this movement is gaining momentum, and Utah is no exception. In our state, a woman was thrown to the ground Oct. 21 by […]
text:
A sign pointing toward data center construction sites is pictures in Eagle Mountain on Sept. 23, 2026. (Katie McKellar/Utah News Dispatch)The energy at the Capitol was electric. Standing shoulder to shoulder last month with others who recognize how data centers tie into the fight for climate justice is energizing. Across the country, this movement is gaining momentum, and Utah is no exception. In our state, a woman was thrown to the ground Oct. 21 by a sheriff’s deputy for protesting data centers in Utah County. 
Anybody that values what makes Utah unique can understand why data centers are threatening. I have spent my entire life hiking the Rocky Mountains in the summers and skiing them in the winters. I grew up in Summit County where spending time with the land we lived on was an integral part of my everyday life. I love and respect this land. 
Thanks to all of the time I spent (and continue to spend) outdoors, I can’t separate anything I do from the deep responsibility I feel for how my actions impact the planet that I am living on. The problem is, I don’t see our legislators considering their actions in a similar way. What I see is that profit is being prioritized over people and the planet we call home.
Legislators are selling out our public lands for mining, data center development, and profit. Utah is among the top states nationwide for planned data centers. So are Texas and Virginia, which just put major restrictions on new data centers, but Utah hasn’t done that. 
I have seen the research, heard the news, and understand the serious impacts that widespread hyperscale data center development poses to our land, air, and water. Yet, companies, and some of our elected officials, are trying to rush these massive projects forward without proper environmental surveys, consideration of public opinion, or the time we truly need to make an informed decision about what is built in our state. 
Virginia has over 340 data center buildings, the most of any state in the United States. It has positioned itself as a data center hub. The result is serious impacts on their energy grid, water resources, and local communities. Alarmingly, their energy rates have increased in recent years and are only likely to continue — not to mention the strain on water supply, or the constant air and noise pollution constantly disturbing local communities. As a result, On Sept. 18 Virginia Gov. Abigail Spanberger announced Data Center Accountability Framework guardrails that keep communities safe and healthy. The framework even admits that the state “welcomed data center development without a clear or coordinated plan to address their impacts on Virginians.” Virginia’s reality is a glimpse into Utah’s future if we keep doing business as usual. 
Texas was on track to surpass Virginia in data center development. On Sept. 21, Texas Gov. Greg Abbott put a pause on all data center related permits until the Electrical Reliability Council of Texas completes an audit of the existing data center waitlist. This pause is following the moratorium Abbott put forward in August halting data center development in the state. This came at a significant time as midterms were quickly approaching and Abbott was up for reelection, which he lost. Texans are clear — they do not want more unchecked data centers. 
But Utah Gov. Spencer Cox wasn’t up for reelection this year. Looking at this in a glass-half-full type of way, that means he can still shape the legacy of his time in office — which up to now, hasn’t looked the best when we consider a dying Great Salt Lake, supporting President Donald Trump as he slashed 3 million acres of public lands in the state, and increasing industrial development that pollutes our already toxic air. 
We need a moratorium in place until we can implement guardrails on data center development. Those guardrails should include: 

Require data centers to pay full cost of service, with long-term contracts, exit fees, and no new gas plants or delayed coal retirements to serve them.
NO taxpayer funded financial incentives for data centers unless they are conditioned on clean energy, battery backup, and full protection for other ratepayers.
Require third-party, publicly available environmental studies for all data center permits, including cumulative air impacts from backup generators and impacts on local water supplies.
Require all data centers over 20MW to undergo a public review process with a minimum of three-week public comment period, and disclose all proposed data centers clearly on a public website and on social media. 
Ban nondisclosure agreements and other measures to keep data centers from the public.
Require community benefit agreements negotiated by non-government community groups, in addition to, not instead of, ratepayer and clean energy protections

We, the citizens of Utah, deserve a say on what happens in our state that impacts our quality of life.

name: Idaho Capital Sun
title: Idaho to receive $182.7M in second year of federal rural health transformation grant
description: Federal authorities said on Monday Idaho will receive about $182.7 million in the second year of a grant designed to improve rural healthcare, marking a reduction from Idaho’s first-year award.  The federal Rural Health Transformation grant was part of the 2025 One Big Beautiful Bill Act, in which Congress allocated $50 billion nationwide for the […]
text:
Idaho will receive about $183.7 million in federal Rural Health Transformation Program funds, meant to improve rural healthcare access and quality. This is a reduction from the state's first-year award for the five-year program. (Getty Images)Federal authorities said on Monday Idaho will receive about $182.7 million in the second year of a grant designed to improve rural healthcare, marking a reduction from Idaho’s first-year award. 
The federal Rural Health Transformation grant was part of the 2025 One Big Beautiful Bill Act, in which Congress allocated $50 billion nationwide for the five-year program. The massive tax-and-spending bill also cut spending on Medicaid by about $1 trillion over 10 years — these reductions will start to take effect on Jan. 1, 2027. 
Idaho was awarded nearly $186 million on Dec. 30, 2025, for the first year of the program. 
Idaho’s Republican Gov. Brad Little gives an interview to a reporter during a GOP election night watch party on Nov. 3, 2026, in Downtown Boise. Also pictured is Emily Callihan, the communications director for the governor. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun)
“Where you live should not determine whether you can access quality, affordable health care,” Idaho Gov. Brad Little said in a press release. “That is especially important for families in rural Idaho, where distance and limited resources can create real barriers. This investment will help close those gaps, support local providers, and bring more care within reach for Idahoans across our state.”
On Oct. 28, Idaho and federal authorities announced the state had awarded all of its first-year funds on projects such as infrastructure improvements at rural hospitals, emergency medical equipment, healthcare workforce development, mobile clinics and others. 
The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid had been slated to announce the second-year grants on Oct. 31, but federal leaders told states on Oct. 30 that the announcement was delayed, KFF Health News reported. 
“This next $10 billion will expand access to care, strengthen the rural health workforce, improve prevention, and help states build solutions that fit the needs of their own communities,” Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. said in a press release Monday. “We are giving rural America the resources and flexibility to build stronger health systems that deliver better care and better outcomes.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
 How are the rural health grant amounts decided? 

The federal funds were allocated in two parts. Half of the money is to be divided among states equally each year. The second half of the funds are awarded competitively, based on states’ proposed initiatives in their applications, rural population characteristics, healthcare facilities, policies that align with Trump administration priorities, and other requirements, according to CMS. 
For the second year, states’ progress reports submitted on Sept. 30 were evaluated to help determine their second-year grants. 
Idaho’s second-year award ranked at No. 40 compared to the rest of the state’s grant amounts. Texas received the most, at nearly $282 million. New Jersey received the least, at $142.3 million. 
Idaho Department of Health and Welfare Director Juliet Charron told the state’s program implementation task force in September that the Gem State’s low population density and low density of rural healthcare providers resulted in a lower score based on federal criteria for the first year of the program. 
Montana, which has a lower population than Idaho but shares many rural characteristics, received the third-highest award at $239.7 million. Alaska received the second-highest grant at $272.6 million.

name: Michigan Advance
title: Incoming House Speaker Puri: Diversity is the new Democratic caucus’ greatest strength
description: Democrats were elected last week to control both the state House and Senate, and with it will come a diversity of thought on big policy ideas and approaches to wielding power —  which could pose a challenge for the party’s incoming House Speaker-elect Ranjeev Puri of Canton. Puri was officially elected speaker late last week […]
text:
State Rep. Ranjeev Puri (D-Canton) speaks to supporters in Detroit after Democrats retook the majority on the Michigan House and retained control of the Senate. Puri is likely to be the next Speaker of the House. Nov. 4, 2026. (Photo by Ben Solis/Michigan Advance)Democrats were elected last week to control both the state House and Senate, and with it will come a diversity of thought on big policy ideas and approaches to wielding power —  which could pose a challenge for the party’s incoming House Speaker-elect Ranjeev Puri of Canton.
Puri was officially elected speaker late last week as new members of the House Democratic caucus met for the first time and selected its leaders for the 2027-28 legislative session. The Nov. 3 election saw the Democrats expand their majority in the state Senate, while Democrats took back control of the House from Republicans, led by outgoing Speaker Matt Hall (R-Richland Township).
In an interview with Michigan Advance, Puri said he welcomed the challenge to bring together the new coalition of recently elected lawmakers, and relished their unique perspectives. Puri added that he views the management of their competing interests as a party as more of an honor than a chore.
Puri elected House Speaker as Democrats prepare to take control of state government

“It doesn’t always have to be about me,” Puri said. “I’m going to foster an environment, especially over the next couple of months here, between now and the first day of session, to make sure we have the right dialogue and the right forums for people to express their perspectives and for us to kind of naturally and organically have those debates and deliberations internally.”
Puri said that those efforts would help his caucus reach “a robust agenda that’s going to meet the needs of our caucus and this moment.”
The moment, as it stands, has given the state’s Democrats — and the party nationwide — a mandate to bring forth real change after a disjointed eight years of President Donald Trump in the Oval Office, Republican control of Congress over the last few years and with the GOP leading the agenda in the state House.
Puri said he would be the type of leader that will listen to his caucus, and approach his members’ individual policy aims on level ground.
“I’m hoping there’s no one coming into these conversations thinking that everyone agrees with them,” Puri said. “This is just going to be the kind of healthy debate that is imperative to a functional democracy. That is going to be the work that we do internally.”
That doesn’t mean there isn’t room for big swings and home run shots in Puri’s new House majority — quite the contrary. The incoming speaker said his approach would be to dream large and tackle tough issues that could lead to transformational laws and regulations.
“If we do that correctly, it is going to transcend some of those divides within my own party, those that exist along partisan lines, and in terms of real systemic problems, challenges that are facing our state,” Puri said. “Our median household income is not growing and is falling behind our peer states. Our population growth is still not where it needs to be. The more time we can spend tackling those larger issues, the better our governance will be.”
That’s where the incoming Democratic caucus’s diversity will shine, Puri said, while reiterating that his “decision-making process doesn’t always have to be about me.” 
Michigan House Speaker-elect Ranjeev Puri (D-Canton) speaks to members of the news media on Thursday, Nov. 5, 2026, outside of the House chamber in Lansing, Mich. Puri donned a baseball cap with the word “Immigrant” on it during the press conference; he will be the first South Asian American to serve as the chamber’s speaker, as well as its first Sikh speaker of the House. (Photo by Ben Solis/Michigan Advance)
Part of that comes from his close ties to his district, and his family, and his focus on not being a creature of Lansing every day of the week.
“I don’t think that this maybe sets me apart, but I’m rooted as the father of four young kids, and doing what I can to chart our state on a path to achieve the most success that it can,” he said. “But at the end of the day, I’ve never spent a night in Lansing. I come home every day, and it’s a promise I made to my family — that I’m either going to be home for dinner or home for breakfast. When I come home, I’m not a representative or leader or speaker, or anything; I’m just Dad. That’s my north star and if I ever lose that north star, that would be when I know that my time has come.”
One big change that Puri hopes to implement immediately is a shift in decorum of how the speaker handles disputes within his caucus.
Hall was replaced last week as caucus leader, with the House GOP tapping state Rep. Tom Kunse (R-Clare) instead. Kunse promised to lead the caucus with a steady hand and with a commitment to nip disagreements with Puri in the bud behind closed doors, and not on social media or in  the public view. He also vowed to do the same for disagreements within his own caucus.
Gongwer News Service reported that much of the reason why Hall was not reelected as caucus leader had to do with how he wielded power as speaker. Gongwer noted that Hall had scuttled bills in committees if their respective chairs had somehow crossed him, threatened committee assignments for rank-and-file members and pushed easy win legislation to the negotiating table for larger caucus priorities — including as leverage during fraught budget battles. That made it difficult for Hall to maintain his grip on the caucus. 
Return of the trifecta: Michigan Democrats reclaim full control of state government

The current speaker was not the only one who faced some dysfunction as the House majority leader in recent years, however; former House Speaker Joe Tate (D-Detroit) lost control of his caucus during its lame duck session of 2024, which saw obstructionism from Hall’s incoming caucus but also some key defections in the Democratic majority, mainly in the form of state. Rep. Karen Whitsett (D-Detroit), that blunted its session-end priorities.
Each of those experiences have given Puri some pause over how he intends to run the speaker’s office for the next two years.
“I can’t speak to the former speakers or impugn their motives, or to what happened and didn’t happen behind the scenes,” he said. “What I can tell you about myself is that I generally tend to be a little more decentralized than most preceding me. It’s really important to me to make sure we are uplifting the perspectives of my membership. I have 26 new members, and a 63-member caucus, that are going to represent a vast array of perspectives that are far different than just what I see in my own House district. I take that very seriously.”
Another change that will mark Puri’s time as a speaker:  “shying away from the politicalness that has been used by House leadership over the last couple of years to kind of lead on every issue.
“If we can spend less time talking about who’s playing in what sport and more time about how we can improve the lives of every Michigander, in terms of household median income and job growth, I think that would be a successful use of these next two years,” Puri said.

name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: ICE releases detained Wisconsin State Trooper
description: Federal immigration authorities have released a 21-year-old Wisconsin State Patrol trooper from Onalaska who was detained at an airport last week. Carel Aaron Van Der Merwe, who was born in South Africa and works out of Tomah, was brought to the United States as a child legally. After arriving in the country, his parents waited […]
text:
Federal immigration officers were at the Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport on March 23, 2026 to help with airport security as a partial governemnt shutdown continued. (Photo by Ross Williams/Georgia Recorder)Federal immigration authorities have released a 21-year-old Wisconsin State Patrol trooper from Onalaska who was detained at an airport last week. Carel Aaron Van Der Merwe, who was born in South Africa and works out of Tomah, was brought to the United States as a child legally. After arriving in the country, his parents waited seven years for an asylum interview, according to a press release issued by the law firm Christopher & De Leon. The firm said that Van Der Merwe was included on his father’s asylum application and holds a federal work authorization which expires in 2030. 
Van Der Merwe was released after U.S. Rep. Derrick Van Orden contacted DHS and intervened on the state trooper’s behalf. A spokesperson for Van Orden told the Milwaukee Journal Sentinel that appropriate authorities will now work to resolve Van Der Merwe’s immigration paperwork and legal status. 
Attorney Marc Christopher said that while Van Der Merwe and his family are happy he was released, he should not have been detained and that it should not have required congressional intervention to resolve the matter. 
Christopher called on lawmakers to confront what he called “inhumane and wasteful detention practices and the failure of our immigration system,” by ICE under the Trump administration, the Milwaukee Journal Sentinel reported.
“Wisconsin trusted him to protect the public,” the law firm said in a statement after Van Der Merwe was arrested. “Now, ICE is holding him in immigration detention in Dodge County.”
Van Der Merwe joined the Wisconsin State Patrol because his pending immigration status prevented him from joining the military, according to his lawyers. The Wisconsin Department of Transportation, which oversees the State Patrol, confirmed in a statement to the Examiner that it was “aware of the situation” involving Van Der Merwe. He has worked with the department since July 2025. 
DOT did not comment on the circumstances of Van Der Merwe’s hiring, how his arrest affected his colleagues and community, or whether ICE or the Department of Homeland Security communicated with the State Patrol before or after arresting Van Der Merwe.
The statement from his attorneys said  that Van Der Merwe was detained as he prepared to board a domestic flight. He tried to explain that he had a valid work permit pending an asylum claim, but “according to Van Der Merwe the officers said they did not care, placed him in handcuffs and shackles, and transported him to immigration detention in Dodge County. ICE says it is going after people who break the law. Here, it has detained someone whose job it is to uphold it.”
Christopher said in a statement that ICE did not have to detain Van Der Merwe. “He is neither a threat nor a flight risk,” he said. “He has a home, a career, and a community he serves. How does putting him behind bars make Wisconsin safer?”
A DHS spokesperson confirmed that Van Der Merwe was taken into ICE custody on Nov. 5. Calling him “an illegal alien from South Africa,” the spokesperson said that the arrest was part of a targeted operation at the Dane County Regional Airport in Madison. Contrary to his attorneys’ statement, DHS said that Van Der Merwe “entered the country in March 2019 with legal permission to stay until September 2019.” 
The spokesperson added that, “in defiance of our nation’s laws, he overstayed his admission. This illegal alien will receive due process and remain in ICE custody pending removal proceedings.” DHS added that, “work authorization or a pending application do not confer legal status in the U.S.” The agency stated that  “DHS reversed the horrendous Biden-era policy that allowed aliens in our country illegally to jet around our country. Under President Trump, DHS will no longer tolerate this. This administration is working diligently to ensure that aliens in our country illegally can no longer fly unless it is out of our country to self-deport.” 
Christopher called the government’s claims “absurd and ridiculous,” asserting that Van Der Merwe and his family were here lawfully and waiting for immigration to process their asylum claim, the Milwaukee Journal Sentinel reported.

Van Der Merwe’s arrest came just weeks after an Oshkosh middle school teacher who was raised in Costa Rica was detained and deported by ICE. The teacher, Wendy Mendez,  was recognized in 2025 as an employee of the year by her school district. 
As a white South African, Van Der Merwe is part of a group that has received favorable treatment from the Trump administration.
In 2027, the Trump administration is limiting the number of refugees it admits to the United States to   17,500 people, most of whom will be white South Africans fleeing what they say is persecution under the Black majority government of their country. Even as his administration has targeted immigrants from Latin America for deportation, President Trump welcomed white South African farmers and falsely claimed that white South Africans — the descendants of Dutch and French colonialists known as Afrikaners  — were the victims of genocide. 
Van Der Merwe’s family arrived in the U.S. during Trump’s first term, when he was 14 years old. As they were awaiting processing of their asylum claim, Trump signed an executive order saying the U.S. would “promote the resettlement of Afrikaner refugees” based on the claim that they faced anti-white racial discrimination. 
Van Der Merwe graduated from the Wisconsin State Patrol academy in 2025, as Gov. Tony Evers looked on. 
More reports of immigration arrests at airports stem from increased collaboration between the Transportation Security Administration and ICE, according to CBS News. TSA has been identifying noncitizen travelers who are “easy targets” for federal agents seeking to meet high quotas for immigration arrests.

title: Meet Gov.-elect Byron Donalds’ transition team
description: Gov.-elect Byron Donald announced the members of his transition team Monday afternoon, but gave no details about whether additional people will help guide the transfer of power from Gov. Ron DeSantis. “Bryan and I campaigned and won on a clear agenda: make Florida more affordable, invest in Florida’s young people, and ensure that Florida continues […]
text:
Then-Florida Republican U.S. House member and gubernatorial candidate Byron Donalds addressing the Sunshine State Showdown in Davie on June 27, 2026. (Photo by Mitch Perry/Florida Phoenix)Gov.-elect Byron Donald announced the members of his transition team Monday afternoon, but gave no details about whether additional people will help guide the transfer of power from Gov. Ron DeSantis.
“Bryan and I campaigned and won on a clear agenda: make Florida more affordable, invest in Florida’s young people, and ensure that Florida continues to lead the nation with common-sense governance and economic opportunity,” Donalds said in a prepared statement, referencing his running mate, Lt. Gov.-elect Bryan Avila.
Manuel “Manny” Kadre (Photo via Republic Services)
Miami business executive Manuel “Manny” Kadre will chair the transition team. He is CEO of Kollective Auto Group, formerly known as MBB Auto Group. He chairs the University of Miami Board of Trustees, and serves on the University of Miami Health System Board of Directors.
Ryan Smith, a senior campaign director for the Donalds-Avila ticket, has been named executive director of the transition team.
Tarren Bragdon. (Photo via Tarren Bragdon)
Teresa Ressel, a member of the Businesswomen for Byron coalition, becomes senior adviser.  The Federal Home Loan Bank’s Office of Finance announced that Ressel had been elected to serve on its board of directors.
Tarren Bragdon becomes policy chair. He is a transplant from Maine, having moved his family to Florida in 2011. His website notes that he’s driven by “faith, family, freedom, free markets, and the power of work.”
Donalds made history last week when he edged Democratic opponent David Jolly to become the first Black person elected statewide in Florida and the nation’s first Black Republican governor.
“We are proud to announce this incredible team of leaders from across our great state, who are already working diligently to ensure that our administration arrives in Tallahassee fully primed to execute on our mission for the people of Florida,” Donald said.

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Ballot review set in southern Indiana county amid tight race for state Senate’s top Republican
description: Democrats are raising concerns about the vote count in southern Indiana’s Clark County, where the state Senate’s top Republican has a narrow lead in unofficial tallies.
text:
Republican state Sen. Chris Garten, left, and Democratic challenger Nick Marshall. (Photos by Leslie Bonilla Muñiz/Indiana Capital Chronicle and Marshall campaign's Facebook page)Democrats are raising concerns about the vote count in southern Indiana’s Clark County, where the state Senate’s top Republican has a narrow lead in unofficial tallies.
Questions about possible differences between the number of ballots cast and those counted could roil the tight race between Republican Sen. Chris Garten and Democratic challenger Nick Marshall.
Garten said Monday that he expected his lead to stand and referred to the ballot doubts as “politically motivated speculation.”
Preliminary results posted by the Indiana Election Division show Garten leading by 297 votes, or about ⅔ of a percentage point — with 21,817 to 21,520 for Marshall. Libertarian Larry Mahaney had 993 votes.
Garten is ahead with 49.2% of the vote — the closest of the 25 state Senate elections across the state.
The tight margin comes as Republican senators have picked Garten to become the chamber’s new president pro tem — and Democrats gained at least five seats in last week’s election to narrow the GOP Senate majority to an apparent 35-15 for next year’s legislative session.
Democrats question ‘discrepancies’ at polling sites
The Clark County Election Board is scheduled to meet Tuesday evening to “count the physical ballots cast” for four precincts that voted at Jeffersonville High School, according to the board’s meeting notice.
“The Board will count only the number of physical ballots,” the movie said. “No votes for any candidate, office, or public question will be counted or tallied.”
Clark County Democratic Chair Miguel Hampton said Monday he was seeking answers about reported problems with computer tablets used to check in voters, a ballot machine jamming and possible procedural mistakes at the high school and other voting locations on Election Day.
The high school polling site is among the county’s busiest and is in a typically strong Democratic area, Hampton said.
“I’m not trying to be an alarmist,” Hampton told the Indiana Capital Chronicle. “I don’t know whether this changes the trajectory of the actual voting population. I can’t tell you that, but what I can tell you is that at least three locations there were discrepancies, and we asked about them.”
Balloting troubles could also impact a tight county auditor race, Hampton said. The Republican candidate was leading by about 250 votes, according to preliminary tallies.
Republican official believes actions appropriate
Clark County Clerk Ryan Lynch did not immediately reply Monday to a phone message seeking comment. Lynch, a Republican, is a member of the county election board and was unopposed for reelection this fall.
Clark County Republican Chair Fannie Broxon said a ballot machine jammed at the high school voting site on Election Day and was replaced. She said the election board’s ballot count was intended to ensure a correct tally.
“I don’t think it’s going to make one vote difference whenever they do that,” Broxon said. “I feel that it was handled appropriately and that that will come out Tuesday evening.”
Garten, who is seeking his third term representing Senate District 45, said in a written statement that he had “confidence in our election officials, confidence in the integrity of the process.”
“Hoosier voters deserve transparency, accountability, and facts — not politically motivated speculation intended to cast doubt on an election without credible evidence,” Garten said.
Garten poised to take Senate’s top post
The Senate is expected to vote during its Nov. 17 Organization Day on formally electing Garten as president pro tem. He would replace Sen. Rodric Bray who decided to step down after drawing the wrath of President Donald Trump over his opposition to last year’s proposed congressional redistricting.
Garten’s tight race comes in the same election that saw Republican House Speaker Todd Huston unseated in his reelection bid.
Marshall received about 38% of the vote when he ran against Garten four years ago.
Marshall referred questions about the ballot issues to Democratic Party officials, telling the Capital Chronicle that “we are letting democracy and process take place.”
Candidates have until Nov. 17 to file recount petitions, with party officials facing a Nov. 20 deadline.
All of Clark County is in Senate District 45, along with a portion of Floyd County. Votes from Clark County make up 87% of those included in preliminary tallies for the district.

name: National
title: Voters approve housing bond measures but reject easing lot-size and environmental rules
description: Voters in California, Hawaii and Rhode Island gave the go-ahead last week for bond measures aimed at boosting the housing supply and homeownership. But a California measure to cut back on the state’s decades-old environmental law to spur housing development and a Massachusetts proposal to loosen minimum lot-size rules both failed. Massachusetts’ Question 7, [...]
text:
A room inside a 25-unit complex under construction in Central Falls, Rhode Island, in 2024. Rhode Island was one of four states with housing measures on the ballot last week. (Photo by Christopher Shea/Rhode Island Current)Voters in California, Hawaii and Rhode Island gave the go-ahead last week for bond measures aimed at boosting the housing supply and homeownership. But a California measure to cut back on the state’s decades-old environmental law to spur housing development and a Massachusetts proposal to loosen minimum lot-size rules both failed.
Massachusetts’ Question 7, a ballot measure that would have overridden local zoning rules and allowed single-family homes on smaller lots, suffered defeat at the ballot box by fewer than 33,000 votes or 1.2 percentage points. 
The proposal would have allowed single-family homes to be built on lots of 5,000 square feet or more if they had at least 50 feet of street frontage and access to public water and sewer services. Zoning policies for single-family homes currently are set by local governments, not the state, and many require lot sizes of 40,000 square feet or more.
In California, Proposition 45 to shorten and streamline the permitting and environmental review process for several types of projects, including housing, under the state’s 50-year-old environmental law fell with nearly 56% of voters in opposition.
But California voters approved two measures to allow the state to issue bonds intended to boost housing.
Voters to weigh different approaches to housing affordability in November

Proposition 1, to allow the state to sell $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds for housing, passed with roughly 61% of the vote. It will dedicate $10 billion for housing programs and $1.25 billion for veterans’ home loans. The Legislative Analyst’s Office says the bond would provide subsidies for up to 40,000 multifamily rental units.
Proposition 37, to authorize the state to issue up to $25 billion in bonds to create a down payment assistance program, passed with about 62% of the vote. Each loan would cover up to 17% of the home price. Qualified buyers are defined as those who have been a California resident for at least a year, plan to occupy the home, earn less than 200% of the area median income and can pay at least 3% down.
In Rhode Island, more than 61% of voters approved a $120 million bond to fund the construction and development of housing projects in the state. At least $25 million must go toward producing housing intended for homeownership, and up to $10 million may support public housing development.  
Hawaii voters by nearly 62% approved a new constitutional amendment allowing counties to use special bonds to pay for infrastructure such as roads, water and sewer systems in designated areas. Those bonds would be repaid through future growth in property tax revenue in those districts rather than through an increase in the property tax rate.

name: VTDigger
title: Stop strong-arming towns into signing off on regional plans
description:
Act 181’s year-end deadline gives towns weeks to weigh land use maps that will shape them for decades.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Stop strong-arming towns into signing off on regional plans.
text:
This commentary is by Colleen Geddis, founder of the Rural Vermont Rising Facebook group.
Imagine being handed a 408-page document that will shape how land in your town can be used for decades. You get about 30 days’ notice before the first hearing. Your town’s map was redrawn only this summer, after the law changed again in June. And if your region misses the Dec. 31 deadline, your town could lose state grants, housing exemptions and the help it counts on after a disaster.
That is exactly where Cabot found itself this fall. So did many other towns.
Act 181 requires nearly every regional planning commission to adopt a new plan, with a land use map and housing targets for each town, by the end of the year. In theory, towns do not have to agree. In practice, the Legislature enforces the mandate with money. If the state Land Use Review Board does not approve a region’s plan, its towns can lose Act 250 housing exemptions, designation benefits and eligibility for state grants.
Simply put, the message from Montpelier is: Sign it or lose your funding.
The Central Vermont Regional Planning Commission spent two years preparing its plan. Towns got the same short review window that applied when regional plans were a fraction of this length and far less consequential. The Cabot Selectboard said so in comments approved Oct. 13 and told its commissioners to vote no until the town could finish its review. Saying “approve this plan or lose your funding” is no way to get buy-in. The commission adopted the plan anyway on Oct. 20, by a vote of 21-1.
Cabot’s own zoning administrator sits on the regional commission. Her question is the right one: Why should a town have to choose between a fair review and protecting its residents?

READ MORE

Rural landowners have good reason to be cautious. Act 181 used state habitat maps to create Tier 3 and added a road rule. The Legislature repealed both this year, but only after rural Vermonters saw what the maps meant and pushed back. The rules that may eventually attach to rural designations like Rural Forestry and Agriculture still have not been written. Some will not arrive until 2028. Landowners deserve to know what a designation means before it is locked in.
And this is not just Central Vermont. In the Two Rivers-Ottauquechee region, people in 27 of 30 towns commented on the draft plan. In August, the Land Use Review Board itself questioned whether that plan’s mandatory rules infringe on property rights. In Granville and Hancock, two of the region’s poorer towns, the draft map would expand the most restrictive category, effectively banning future economic development.
That is not planning. That is a freeze.
There is a simple fix. The funding and housing benefits at stake depend mainly on growth areas: village centers, downtowns and the Tier 1A and 1B areas that qualify for Act 250 housing exemptions. Regions could map those now and refine everything else next year. As the selectboard wrote in its comments to the commission, “None of these elements affect the Act 250 housing exemptions or grant eligibility, so there is no need to rush them.”
It was all Cabot was asking for. Adopt the village growth areas and the state minimum now. Leave rural mapping and final housing targets for a 2027 review.
The planning commissions did not choose this timeline. The Legislature did, and then it changed the rules in June. It is up to the Legislature to fix it. Lawmakers should move the deadline to Dec. 31, 2027.
Until they do, every Vermonter should read their regional plan and speak up. The Two Rivers-Ottauquechee plan has not been submitted yet. Once a commission adopts its plan, residents who took part in the process have just 15 days to file an objection with the Land Use Review Board on the board’s form. Details are at act250.vermont.gov.
Good planning takes time. Vermonters deserve the chance to get it right.

text:
The U.S. Capitol on July 2, 2025. (Photo by Ashley Murray/States Newsroom)U.S. Rep. Greg Steube of Florida is asking his GOP colleagues to elect him as the next Republican conference chair, the No. 3 House leadership position, saying he represents a “genuine conservative option and a fresh approach to leadership.”
U.S. Rep. Greg Steube (official portrait)
Steube will vie for the position Tuesday against Michigan U.S. Rep. Lisa McClain (the sitting Republican conference chair) and Indiana U.S. Rep. Erin Houchin. Steube was easily re-elected last week to his Florida Congressional District 17th District seat representing Sarasota, Charlotte, and parts of Lee counties.
In his statement announcing his candidacy last week, Steube contended the GOP suffered major losses across the country in the midterm elections not “because they were too conservative,” but because they “failed to deliver on the promises we made.”
“I am tired of watching Washington conventional wisdom dictate our policies,” Steube said in his written statement. “We should not be afraid to govern conservatively or challenge our own leadership when it loses sight of the commitments we made. If we want voters to trust us again, they need to see that electing Republicans actually makes a difference.”
Steube had blasted Republican Senate and House leadership in the immediate aftermath of last week’s election.
“You have been embarrassingly weak and more afraid of governing conservatively than of disappointing the voters who put us in office,” he said on X, addressing “Republican Senate and House ‘leadership.’
“Instead of standing firm on our principles, you have governed out of fear, continually knelt to the moderates in our conference (who all got crushed last night anyway), and discarded conservatives like me who warned of last night’s results.”
Steube was first elected to the Florida House in 2010. He won election to the state Senate in 2016 and then moved on to Congress in 2018.
Meanwhile, Florida Republican Sen. Rick Scott told Fox News over the weekend that he won’t challenge Senate Minority Leader John Thune’s bid for re-election.
“I don’t want to run again. I’ve run twice,” he said. Scott lost to Mitch McConell in the race to lead Senate Republicans in 2022 and to Thune in 2024.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: PODCAST: Most CT towns decline to change housing voucher distribution, despite segregation concerns
description: WSHU’s Ebong Udoma spoke with CT Mirror’s Sasha Allen to discuss her article written with Ginny Monk, “Data shows little change in CT housing voucher segregation,” as part of the collaborative podcast Long Story Short.
text:
Despite attempts to reform housing vouchers, most Connecticut towns have neglected to change how vouchers are distributed, contributing to housing segregation.
WSHU’s Ebong Udoma spoke with CT Mirror’s Sasha Allen to discuss her article written with Ginny Monk, “Data shows little change in CT housing voucher segregation,” as part of the collaborative podcast Long Story Short. Read their story here.
WSHU: Hello, Sasha. You say your story was born out of a May report on housing segregation through housing choice vouchers, also known as Section Eight. What were the report’s findings, and why did they interest you?
SA: Yeah, so this was a report from Open Communities Alliance, and they were looking at how housing vouchers, Section Eight vouchers, are distributed throughout the state. And what they found is that a lot of these vouchers are concentrated in higher poverty areas, worse schools, you know, worse environmental issues, worse air quality. I just thought this was really interesting because in this report they talked a lot about ways to solve this issue and stuff like that, right? And it was some of these methods and solutions that we’ve already seen put into place in some places in the state. I thought that it would be interesting to look into how some of these methods and possible solutions that have been implemented have changed this level of segregation within housing vouchers in Connecticut, if at all.
WSHU: There’s a new rule that was put in place by the Obama administration, and that took effect in 2017. What did that rule do in trying to deal with segregation, and how was it implemented in Connecticut?
SA: Yeah, so that rule was implemented in metro areas across the country, and it basically just changed the way that these vouchers were calculated. So before this rule, all vouchers were calculated using a wider region that could encompass, like a lot of different areas that had, you know, a large diversity of income, and the issue with that is that it would put the housing voucher rate at something that’s lower than, you know, you can’t live in maybe a more affluent area within the region because this housing voucher is just valued too low. So, what this ruling did was create small area fair market rents, and it required some of these metro areas to use small area fair market rents, which is basically calculating housing voucher value based on zip code rather than region, which allows for more movement within the system because it has more granular pricing and values for these vouchers that are just more accurate to the areas that you’re going to use them in.
WSHU: So, you could have a situation where a city is next to a suburban area, and they’re all part of one larger region, and the rents are very different between the city and the suburb, and what will happen is that the average will be much lower than what you would be able to get for the rents in the suburbs. So it would segregate people into the cities, right?
SA: Yeah, exactly, and it would force them to use it in places, obviously with lower rents, which would probably be, you know, cities and higher poverty areas, and then again, like the same things we’re seeing in this report, which is places with lower-rated schools with worse air quality and stuff like that. So yeah, in 2017, Hartford was one of the metro areas that was required to use this, and the Hartford metro area encompasses a lot of different towns. So it’s Hartford and some surrounding towns, and what I found, at least, is that after this rule was implemented, the percentage of housing vouchers held in high-poverty areas changed.
WSHU: Okay, it happened in Hartford. Did any other cities or towns adopt this in Connecticut?
SA: Yeah, so no other ones were required to adopt it, but two others did just because they wanted to. Two local housing authorities, one in Fairfield and one in Stratford, and we spoke with a woman who works for the Housing Authority in Fairfield, and she said that this has made a world of difference for them because, obviously, Fairfield is right next to Bridgeport. You know, sometimes people couldn’t afford to live in Fairfield just because it was all lumped into the same region. Bridgeport was being taken into account for this region, and it was calculated using Bridgeport median income, but also Fairfield median income. So, for them, this was like a game changer, and you know, people were actually able to afford to live in Fairfield with these housing vouchers.
WSHU: That’s quite interesting. So now, if that’s the case, why don’t we have the state mandating that everyone should do the same?
SA: You know, we talked to some legislators, and you know, it definitely is in discussions. But they haven’t done anything to pass that yet, and it would have to be a mandated thing. Like no other housing authorities have, you know, opted in.
WSHU: A lot of the pushback, as far as mandates, state mandates were concerned, came from the Republicans. Now there are fewer Republicans in the General Assembly, so do you think that will help this get passed this time around?
SA: Yeah. So we spoke with Representative Tony Scott, a Republican, and he said that he would rather see mandates on the Department of Housing to use rental assistance in suburbs than mandates on towns. They did have a very large Democratic majority last year as well; I think we’ll just have to wait and see if that is a priority for them. But it is possible that it could play into this as well.
WSHU: Yeah. In the meantime, segregation in housing continues in Connecticut based on Section Eight vouchers.
SA: Yeah.
WSHU: Okay. Thank you very much, Sasha.

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: Outgoing lawmaker to vote by proxy in Tennessee Senate speaker race
description: A Tennessee Republican senator who captured a redrawn congressional seat will vote by proxy Tuesday in the Senate GOP Caucus election, helping select the state’s next lieutenant governor in a tight race for the leadership post. In a caucus poll, Republican senators decided 26-0 to allow an attorney for outgoing Sen. Brent Taylor to cast […]
text:
Republican U.S. Rep.-elect Brent Taylor, a Memphis Republican and current state Senator, is in Washington D.C. for orientation to the new U.S. Congress, but will be allowed to proxy vote in the Republican state Speaker race. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)A Tennessee Republican senator who captured a redrawn congressional seat will vote by proxy Tuesday in the Senate GOP Caucus election, helping select the state’s next lieutenant governor in a tight race for the leadership post.
In a caucus poll, Republican senators decided 26-0 to allow an attorney for outgoing Sen. Brent Taylor to cast a vote in his place, according to a caucus spokesperson. Taylor will be in Washington, D.C., Tuesday for congressional organizational meetings and will not be able to attend the caucus meeting. 
The proxy vote is believed to be a precedent-setting move for the caucus, which has been caught up in a Senate speaker race for nearly a year between Senate Majority Leader Jack Johnson of Franklin and Sen. Paul Bailey of Sparta. 
The Johnson-Bailey election is believed to be within one vote, with two uncommitted, in the 27-member caucus, and Johnson needs Taylor’s vote to ascend to the speaker’s post, which controls the Senate.
The caucus poll was anonymous, and caucus spokesperson Molly Crawford said they don’t know who didn’t participate.  
Fourteen votes will be needed to decide who will serve as speaker and also lieutenant governor, first in line to replace the governor in case of incapacitation or inability to hold office.
Running in the 9th Congressional District, which state lawmakers redrew this year to split a Memphis district and give a Republican a better chance to win, Taylor bested state Rep. Justin J. Pearson by 1.1 percentage point in last week’s election. Taylor also defeated Democrat David Weatherspoon by 3.8 percentage points in the Senate District 31 race, but because he will be heading to Congress, the seat will be vacant until a replacement is decided in a special election.
Caucus members said Taylor submitted a letter to the Senate Clerk’s office requesting to vote by proxy in the caucus election. An email survey from the clerk’s office went out to members, some of whom were still responding last Friday.
Sen. Richard Briggs of Knoxville, who recaptured his seat last Tuesday, said in advance he wouldn’t be surprised if Taylor votes by proxy because Senate leadership supports it. Briggs added that he believes the Senate Republican Caucus needs to change its rules to allow exceptions for proxy votes.
Lt. Gov. Randy McNally, who is leaving the legislature after nearly 50 years, is no longer a senator and will not participate in the Tuesday vote or preside over the meeting but will remain Senate speaker until Jan. 12 when the new General Assembly convenes, according to spokesman Adam Kleinheider.
McNally didn’t take part in the Taylor proxy vote, either, according to Kleinheider. McNally is being replaced as District 5 senator by Jimmy Matlock, a former Republican House member who defeated Democrat David Miller.
Sen. Dawn White of Murfreesboro is the only candidate for Senate majority leader. In the running for caucus chair are the current chairman, Sen. Ken Yager of Kingston, Sen. Becky Massey of Knoxville and Sen. Bill Powers of Clarksville.
Dem leadership stays same
Sen. Raumesh Akbari of Memphis will remain leader of the six-member Senate Democratic Caucus following a vote last week. Sen. London Lamar of Memphis will continue to chair the caucus after a tie vote for the post.
“Senate Democrats are already focused on the special election in Senate District 31, and Tuesday’s results showed this race is winnable,” Lamar said in a statement.

name: National
title: Feds award $10B to states in second year of rural health grants
description: Federal officials on Monday announced $10 billion in awards across all 50 states in the second year of the Rural Health Transformation Fund, grants created by Congress to bolster rural health in response to concerns about Medicaid cuts. Texas received the largest grant for the 2027 fiscal year — almost $282 million — followed by […]
text:
Federal officials announced rural health grants to states. (Photo by David DeWitt/Ohio Capital Journal)Federal officials on Monday announced $10 billion in awards across all 50 states in the second year of the Rural Health Transformation Fund, grants created by Congress to bolster rural health in response to concerns about Medicaid cuts.
Texas received the largest grant for the 2027 fiscal year — almost $282 million — followed by Alaska, Montana, California and Oklahoma.
The five-year fund is providing $50 billion in grants meant to address rural healthcare access and health improvement, with $10 billion available each year until 2030.
Congress created the program in response to concern from rural health care providers — as well as lawmakers on both sides of the aisle — about the effects of sweeping Medicaid cuts in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act that President Donald Trump signed last year. Rural areas are expected to lose about $137 billion, according to health research organization, KFF.
Half of the annual funding is distributed equally among states, with each receiving $100 million in “baseline” funds. The other half is calculated based on a state’s rural population and healthcare facilities, as well as specific initiatives detailed in the applications, among other factors.
States hope to use rural health money to keep doctors, combat chronic disease

States applied for and developed their own programs, using the money toward  focus areas ranging from maternal and behavioral health, preventive health and chronic disease management, access to care and the rural healthcare workforce, and tech and health equipment investments.
All 50 states submitted annual reports documenting their progress from the first year. The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services said it reviewed the reports as part of determining each state’s award for this year. 
“States have already put these resources to work bringing better care closer to home for their rural communities, and CMS looks forward to helping them build on that progress in the coming year,” agency Administrator Dr. Mehmet Oz said in a news release. 
States must use the grants to test out and grow approaches toward making programs sustainable after the fund’s five years have ended, the agency said.
Rural healthcare leaders have said the infusion of federal dollars is welcome but won’t be enough to offset Medicaid cuts. Democrats, who won the majority in both the U.S. House and Senate in this month’s midterm elections, are aiming to push for a repeal of the law, which would still need Trump’s signature.

Stateline reporter Nada Hassanein can be reached at nhassanein@stateline.org.
