name: Kentucky Lantern
title: Commentary: What do Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and Clay County’s Oneida Baptist Institute have in common?
description: It sounds like something out of a spy novel: a Taiwanese-American major tech mogul, head of one of the most successful companies in the world pushing for U.S. dominance in artificial intelligence, is being investigated for his relationship with a woman being described as a Chinese spy.  But amid this international intrigue is, as often […]
text:
In 2019, Lori and Jensen Huang were at Oneida Baptist Institute for the dedication of a new dorm and classroom building they funded. President Larry Gritton is on the right. (Photo courtesy Oneida Baptist Institute)It sounds like something out of a spy novel: a Taiwanese-American major tech mogul, head of one of the most successful companies in the world pushing for U.S. dominance in artificial intelligence, is being investigated for his relationship with a woman being described as a Chinese spy. 
But amid this international intrigue is, as often happens, the Kentucky connection. Before Nvidia, CEO Jensen Huang’s rise to fame and notoriety started in Clay County, where he was a young student scrubbing toilets at Oneida Bible Institute, and taught his 17-year-old roommate to read in exchange for learning how to benchpress. 
“I remember that part of my life more vividly than just about any other,” Huang told Wired Magazine in 2002.
According to various press reports, Huang and his brother, Jeff, grew up in Taiwan and Thailand. But as political unrest hit those areas in the early 1970s, his parents sent him and his brother to an uncle in Washington State. In 1972, the uncle, who spoke limited English, sent the brothers, then aged 9 and 10, to Oneida Baptist Institute, thinking it was a prestigious boarding school, instead of a religious reform facility for high school students. The boys were so young, they had to go to school at Oneida Elementary, the nearby public school. They were bullied terribly, and a story in the New Yorker recounts how the other students would try to throw Huang off the rickety swinging bridge Huang had to take to get to school. 
He learned to play table tennis from the guy who came to fill the vending machines, Wired reported, later becoming a nationally ranked player, and he learned to scrub toilets, as work requirements were an integral part of Oneida’s curriculum.
The current president of Oneida Baptist, Larry Gritton said he’s not surprised by Huang’s ascendancy. “It’s our school and ministry – part of what we do – we’ve always tried to teach our students the value of work,” he said.
Gritton’s parents were teachers at the school at the time; then-president, Dr. Barkley Moore, could have turned the boys away, but didn’t, even though they were so young.
“Dr. Moore had a huge heart and even bigger faith,” Gritton said. “I’m sure he thought, if I can help some kids even though we didn’t have a middle or elementary school, then I will. I’m sure it was a major culture shock for them.”
Two years later, Huang’s parents came to the United States, and the boys returned to live with them in Oregon, where Huang went to high school and Oregon State University.
But Huang apparently remembers Oneida fondly. In 2019, he donated $2 million to Oneida to build a new girls dorm and classroom building. He even returned to Oneida for the dedication of the Jen-Hsun Huang Hall. 
Today, Oneida has about 350 students, Gritton said, most of them from the local community. But there are still about 65 international students who come to Clay County from all over the world to attend boarding school there.
Don’t sleep on Kentucky. You just never know.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Johnny Moore shares his vision for Rust College’s next 100 years
description: Mississippi's oldest, private historically Black college is celebrating its 160th year. On Friday, the Rust community inaugurated Johnny Moore as the college’s 13th president.
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
Johnny M. Moore envisions a future where Rust College becomes the heart of Holly Springs. 
It’s one of several ambitions Moore has as president of the historically Black college, which is celebrating its 160th anniversary this month. The celebration also included Moore’s inauguration Friday as Rust’s 13th president. 
But realizing Moore’s vision will require revitalizing the small, private liberal arts college, which has experienced declining enrollment, rising tuition and leadership turnover in recent years. 
A decade ago, Rust enrolled more than 1,000 students. By the 2024-25 academic year, enrollment had fallen to 467 students. Tuition has increased from $9,900 in 2022-23 to more than $13,000 in 2023-24. And just 12% of students who entered Rust in 2018 graduated within six years.
Addressing those challenges will require adapting Rust’s academic programs and providing students with more support to earn a degree, Moore said. 
The McCoy Administration Building is located on Rust College’s campus in Holly Springs.  Credit: Rust College
One of Moore’s priorities is to expand career and workforce opportunities for Rust students, including those who may not need the traditional four-year college degree. 
One example of that effort is a partnership that was launched in 2025 with the Mississippi Center for Innovation and Technology and Cisco Systems to offer a workforce certificate program to prepare students and local residents for cybersecurity jobs. The initiative aims to provide students with more flexible paths to employment while strengthening the college’s academic offerings, Moore said. 
“It’s not enough just to get people here,” he said. “It’s not enough to just retain them and graduate. We have to make sure we get them a job.”
Addressing barriers to a degree
Supporting students through graduation is also another priority for Moore. As a first-generation college student from rural Arkansas, he said he understands the barriers students face when pursuing higher education. 
Black students make up 92% of the college’s enrollment. More than half of students come from outside Mississippi. Many also rely on the federal Pell grant to afford college, Moore said. 
The college offers a one-stop shop on campus where students can receive assistance with class registration, financial aid and other concerns. Other campus resources include a food pantry, career clothing closet, emergency financial assistance, scholarships and work-study opportunities. 
Aubree Dillon, a junior mass communications major, said Moore often walks the campus and talks with students about work opportunities, student life and dormitories. His presence has made a difference in her college experience. 
“A lot of people may not think that it’s a big deal for your college president to make an effort to ask you questions or try to get to know you personally,” Dillon said. “But, that’s the great thing about being at a small school. Your leadership and president care, and that matters.” 
Moore and the college’s leadership are also working with students, faculty, alumni and other stakeholders to develop a strategic plan, which he expects to release next fall. 
Rust College is Mississippi’s oldest historically Black college and second oldest private college in the state.  Credit: Rust College
The plan comes after several leadership transitions. Ivy Taylor, the institution’s first woman president, served from 2020 to 2023. Two interim presidents led the college before Moore was named in July 2025. 
Moore previously served as chancellor of Arkansas State University-Newport and president of Philander Smith University, a historically Black university in Arkansas. He also led Pierpont Community and Technical College in West Virginia. 
His experience attending and eventually leading an HBCU has shaped his approach to leading Rust. 
“I know the power of these institutions,” said Moore, who is also a Philander Smith alumnus. “So, it’s only fitting that I finish my career at an HBCU.” 
For alumni, the new leadership comes at a significant moment in the college’s history. 
Focusing on a legacy
The college was founded in 1866, just after the Civil War, and counts civil rights activist and journalist Ida B. Wells among its former students. It is one of Mississippi’s oldest private colleges and oldest historically Black one. 
“Our founders understood that freedom was not complete without education,” Moore said. “So we inherited this legacy to build upon it, so other generations can appreciate their worthiness of legacy.” 
Moore is working to preserve that legacy by addressing the college’s challenges. 
Credit: Courtesy of Rust College
He has regularly met with alumni chapter presidents since taking office to seek their input on enrollment, recruitment and ways to strengthen the college’s visibility, said MeShonya Wren-Coleman, president of the Rust College International Alumni Association. Some of that feedback has led to raising the college’s social media profile  and staffing changes, she said.
Wren-Coleman said she appreciates Moore’s willingness to listen to alumni and address longstanding institutional concerns. 
“He’s not putting a Band-Aid on things that need to be fixed,” Wren-Coleman said. Instead, she said, Moore is solving problems.
She also emphasized the importance of Moore’s alumni engagement and how it lends to the financial support and restoration of the future of the HBCU. 
“Our commitment to Rust College alums isn’t limited to financial contributions,” Wren-Coleman said. “We set the example for our students and future generations when we raise money for scholarships, recruit students because we show the transformative  power of education, community and leadership for the school.” 
Moore’s ambitions also extend beyond Rust’s campus to Holly Springs, a city of 6,400 residents about 35 miles southeast of Memphis. His vision for the college town includes more partnerships with local high schools, economic development and projects with local businesses. 
For Moore, strengthening Rust also means strengthening the surrounding community. 
“When Rust grows, our community grows with us,” Moore said. “That is what has sustained this institution for 160 years, and it is what will sustain it for generations to come.”

name: Florida Phoenix
title: Machine recounts set this week for one Florida congressional race and one state House contest
description: The election results are final in Florida, with the exception of one congressional race and one state House contest in which recounts will take place this week. In Florida’s 27th Congressional District in Miami-Dade County, Supervisor of Elections Alina Garcia has said a recount in the race between Republican U.S. Rep. Maria Salazar and Democratic […]
text:
Election workers counting vote-by-mail ballots at the Pinellas County Supervisor of Elections office in Largo on Oct. 25, 2022. (Photo by Mitch Perry)/Florida Phoenix)The election results are final in Florida, with the exception of one congressional race and one state House contest in which recounts will take place this week.
In Florida’s 27th Congressional District in Miami-Dade County, Supervisor of Elections Alina Garcia has said a recount in the race between Republican U.S. Rep. Maria Salazar and Democratic candidate Eliot Rodriguez would begin Monday at 10 a.m.
Salazar leads Rodriguez by 1,090 votes, or 0.44% over Rodriguez, 50.22%-49.78%. That’s inside the 0.5% margin that automatically triggers a machine recount.
Garcia, a Republican, is one of three members of the Miami-Dade County canvassing board, which will oversee the recount.
The Rodriguez campaign has filed a federal lawsuit calling on Garcia to recuse herself from the canvassing board, claiming she has several conflicts, including that her son-in-law, Robert Fernandez, represents Salazar in the recount. Garcia has said she will not recuse herself. A hearing related to that legal challenge took place earlier Monday, but a federal judge denied the motion to relieve Garcia, as reported by NBC 6 South Florida.
Meanwhile, a state House race also requires a recount. That’s the contest for the House District 33 seat in Brevard County, where Democratic challenger Daniel R. McDow holds a lead of 289 votes over Republican incumbent Monique Miller. McDow had 36,430 votes and Miller 36,141 votes. That’s a difference of just 0.4%, 50.2%-49.8%. That recount will take place Tuesday at 9 a.m. at the Brevard County Election Support Center in Melbourne.
If the machine recounts in either case results in a margin of 0.25% or less, a manual recount would be ordered.
Several other congressional elections in Florida last week were extremely close, but their margins were outside the 0.5% required for a machine recount.

In Florida’s 7th Congressional District, Republican Ryan Elijah defeated Democrat Bale Dalton by apparently just outside the 0.5% margin. The Division of Elections website lists Elijah with 49.71% to Dalton’s 49.21%.
In Florida’s 9th Congressional District, Democratic incumbent Darren Soto defeated Republican Dan Green by 0.52%, 50.26%-49.74%.
In Florida’s 26th Congressional District, Republican incumbent Mario Diaz-Balart defeated Democrat Nicole Larkin by 0.74%, 49.86%-49.12%.
And in Florida’s 13th Congressional District, Republican incumbent Anna Paulina Luna defeated Democrat Leela Gray by 0.8%, 49.48%-48.68%.

name: VTDigger
title: Every child deserves someone in their corner
description:
Vermont's volunteer Guardians ad Litem bring a child's voice and best interests into the courtroom
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Every child deserves someone in their corner.
text:
The Statewide GAL Conference held on October 23rd at Capitol Plaza in Montpelier
When a child becomes involved in Vermont’s juvenile court system, there are often many adults involved in the decisions that will affect that child’s life. Parents, attorneys, social workers, court professionals and others may all have important roles to play.
But in the middle of all of that, there is one perspective that can be difficult to fully understand from a courtroom: the child’s.
That is where Vermont’s volunteer Guardians ad Litem come in.
Guardians ad Litem, commonly known as GALs, are trained community volunteers who are appointed by the court to advocate for the best interests of children involved in juvenile proceedings. Their role is unique. They are not the child’s attorney, they do not represent the Department for Children and Families, and they are not there to take the place of a parent.
Instead, they get to know the child.
They listen. They ask questions. They learn about the child’s circumstances, relationships, needs and hopes. They talk with the adults and professionals involved in the child’s life and gather information that may otherwise be difficult for the court to see.
And then they bring that perspective back to the court.
A different kind of courtroom advocate
The work of a GAL rarely begins in a courtroom.
It begins with a conversation, a visit, a phone call or simply taking the time to listen.
A GAL might meet a child at home, at school or in another setting where the child feels comfortable. Over time, the volunteer develops an understanding of the child’s circumstances and the challenges the child is facing.
That relationship matters.
Children involved in court proceedings may be experiencing circumstances that are complicated, stressful and sometimes frightening. They may have experienced significant changes in their homes, schools or relationships. They may have difficulty understanding what is happening around them or finding the words to explain what they need.
A GAL provides another adult who is there specifically to pay attention to those things.
The volunteer’s responsibility is not necessarily to advocate for what the child wants. Rather, the GAL works to understand the child’s situation and advocate for what they believe is in the child’s best interests.
That distinction is important — and so is the independence that comes with it.
Volunteers from communities across Vermont
One of the strengths of Vermont’s GAL Program is that it is built around people who live in the communities they serve.
GAL volunteers come from different backgrounds, professions and stages of life. They bring different experiences and perspectives, but they share a willingness to make a commitment to a child who needs an advocate.
They do not need to be lawyers.
They do not need to have a background in social work.
What they do need is the willingness to learn, to listen and to remain engaged in what can sometimes be a difficult and complicated process.
Before serving, volunteers receive training designed to prepare them for the responsibilities of the role. They are also supported throughout their service so that they do not have to navigate the work alone.
That combination — a committed volunteer, meaningful training and ongoing support — is at the heart of the program.
Why the need matters
Vermont’s courts cannot hear a child’s voice if there is no one there to help make sure that voice is understood.
That is why having enough trained and supported GAL volunteers across the state is so important.
The Vermont GAL Program serves children in juvenile proceedings throughout the state, and ensuring that every court has an adequate pool of volunteers requires an ongoing commitment to recruitment, training and retention.
It is not simply a matter of filling volunteer positions.
It is about building a statewide community of people who are prepared to take on an important responsibility and remain there for children during some of the most challenging periods of their lives.
The future of the GAL Program
The Vermont GAL Program is working to strengthen that volunteer network and ensure that the program is accessible, responsive and prepared to meet the needs of Vermont’s children.
That means looking at how the program recruits new volunteers, how it trains and supports them, and how it can make volunteering as meaningful and manageable as possible.
It also means raising awareness about what GALs actually do.
For many Vermonters, the first time they hear the term “Guardian ad Litem” may be when they encounter the court system themselves. But the work of GALs is something that communities across Vermont can support.
Every community benefits when children have adults who are willing to stand beside them.
Someone in their corner
Being a GAL is not always easy.
The cases can be complicated. The circumstances can be difficult. And the outcomes are not always simple.
But the role is important precisely because someone is willing to step into that complexity.
A GAL can be the person who notices something others missed. The person who asks one more question. The person who takes the time to understand what a child is experiencing. And, ultimately, the person who makes sure the child’s best interests remain part of the conversation.
That is the value of the Vermont Guardian ad Litem Program.
At its heart, the program is not really about courtrooms, paperwork or proceedings.
It is about children.
And it is about making sure that, when a child’s future is being decided, there is someone in the room whose responsibility is to make sure that child’s best interests are not lost in the process.
Every child deserves someone in their corner. Vermont’s volunteer Guardians ad Litem are there to help make that possible.

Interested in becoming a Guardian ad Litem? Please email VermontGAL@vtcourts.gov for more information on upcoming trainings.

title: Maine joined a pledge to ditch the Electoral College. Dems’ national wins could make it reality.
description: Democratic wins across the country open a path to get rid of the Electoral College by way of a compact Maine signed onto two years ago.   Currently, votes in a presidential election don’t go to candidates but to a state’s electors. Each state gets a set number of electors equivalent to the size of its […]
text:
The Maine sign at the 2024 Democratic National Convention, which was held in Chicago. (Photo via Maine Democratic Party)Democratic wins across the country open a path to get rid of the Electoral College by way of a compact Maine signed onto two years ago.  
Currently, votes in a presidential election don’t go to candidates but to a state’s electors. Each state gets a set number of electors equivalent to the size of its congressional delegation. Every state has two U.S. senators but the number of U.S. House of Representatives members vary, based on population size. A candidate needs at least 270 electoral votes, a simple majority, to win the presidency. 
In 2024, the Maine Legislature adopted something called the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact, which Democratic Gov. Janet Mills allowed to become law without her signature. States that are part of the compact pledge their Electoral College votes to the presidential candidate with the most overall votes across the country. However, it would only take effect once states with a total of 270 Electoral College votes have joined. 
Including Maine, 18 states and the District of Columbia have ratified the agreement, giving the compact a total of 222 electoral votes. 
But Democrats took control of several more state governments during the midterm elections, opening up the possibility of securing the 48 more needed to reach the threshold. 
Overall, Democrats have been leading the charge on the compact, though as Mills’ hesitation and a recent unsuccessful attempt to remove Maine from the agreement show, the debate does not fall squarely along party lines. 
Some more votes could come from Arizona, Michigan, Nevada, Pennsylvania, and Wisconsin, which now have Democratic trifectas. Arizona, Michigan and Nevada previously advanced proposals that ultimately failed. In total, 61 electoral votes come from these states. 
Maine and Nebraska, where Democrats broke the GOP supermajority in the legislature on Tuesday, are the only states that split their electoral votes across candidates. Other states use a winner-take-all system where the candidate with the majority of the state’s popular vote gets all of the state’s electoral votes.

name: VTDigger
title: Losing ground: Vermont’s struggle against river erosion
description:
River erosion causes the vast majority of the state’s flood damage. The problem is getting worse. And many Vermonters remain in harm’s way.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Losing ground: Vermont’s struggle against river erosion.
text:
This story is part of The Coming Storm, a yearlong investigation by VTDigger, in partnership with FRONTLINE (PBS), into Vermont’s ability to help communities recover from natural disasters.


MARSHFIELD — Julie Rapczynski wasn’t worried that her home on the Nasmith Brook would flood. She couldn’t even see the quiet little river more than 300 feet away, hidden behind a wall of trees at the far edge of her property. 
Then, on July 10, 2023, torrential rain turned the river fast and swift. It cut into the hill above her home, causing landslides. It also tore a new path through her backyard. One year to the day later, another storm came. The river charged down the new path near her home, eating into the riverbank closest to her house. 
“The water started to erode,” she said. “We had like six feet from the deck to the water, and then we had no feet. It went under the deck. It was exposing wires. It was really scary.”
By August 2024, Green Mountain Power, her utility company, warned that it would soon shut the power off. The river had eroded so much of their land that it was approaching their electrical lines. 
Rapczynski and her husband, Ray, soon left their home of five years. 


The Nasmith Brook winds through Julie Rapczynski’s former property, near where her house – now demolished – once stood. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger


In July 2023, the Nasmith Brook cut into the hill above Julie Rapczynski’s home, causing landslides. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger


River erosion is the greatest naturally occurring threat to Vermonters. It’s responsible for the vast majority of the state’s flood damage, officials say, including most of the more than $800 million in destruction caused by the floods in 2023 and 2024. 
When rivers and streams are powered by heavy rainstorms, they can cut into the land around them, causing erosion. Most of Vermont’s rivers are unstable, scientific assessments show, meaning their riverbanks are more likely to collapse in storms, causing landslides, destroying roads and sending houses tumbling into the water.  
More than 21,000 buildings are located in Vermont’s river corridors, where erosion occurs, according to state officials. Tens of thousands of Vermonters live in those buildings.
Many homes in the state, including the Rapczynskis’, are not located within flood zones mapped by the Federal Emergency Management Agency. FEMA hasn’t mapped most of the small streams in Vermont, and the agency does not consider erosion risk in its maps.
As climate change increases the threat of flooding in Vermont, the thousands of property owners at greatest risk have few options.

Read more of The Coming Storm series in partnership with FRONTLINE (PBS)

The state has studied the problem and put in place policies to reduce future erosion risks – giving rivers more space to roam, reducing development in river corridors and moving some homes and businesses out of the path of rivers. 
But that will take decades, or even centuries to have an impact. 
In the meantime, the state has no plan to help people who are currently at risk from river erosion. 
This is “the toughest nut” to crack, said Julie Moore, who leads Vermont’s Agency of Natural Resources. 
“As state agencies, we have to be able to hold, at the same time, that larger reality that there isn’t a simple fix – that there will be enough money and things will be okay,” Moore said.

About The Coming Storm: For a year, VTDigger, with support from FRONTLINE’s Local Journalism Initiative, has reported on Vermont’s capacity to manage recovery from natural disasters. VTDigger obtained emails from state officials regarding assistance to flood survivors, reviewed state and federal disaster funding and risk-reduction plans, examined federal proposals to change the Federal Emergency Management Agency, and analyzed FEMA data on disaster aid, with assistance from Eric Sagara of Big Local News at Stanford University and Erin Petenko of VTDigger. VTDigger also interviewed flood survivors, frontline recovery workers, state and local officials, lawmakers, emergency management experts, scientists, and social services providers, among others, for this series.
Controlling the rivers
Vermont has more than 7,000 miles of rivers, around which many of the state’s cities and towns were built. Rivers once powered mills and factories, provided transportation, and gave farmers easy access to irrigation.
As Vermont cities and towns grew, decades of state policy focused on flood prevention through controlling rivers. Officials built dams, dredging and straightening rivers to keep them neatly alongside roads and underneath bridges. Those measures also helped prevent rivers from overflowing their banks.
But, in heavy rains, straight rivers that can’t access natural floodplains – areas of land next to rivers and streams that slow down rivers and soak up excess water – get stronger and cut deeper. 
“That’s the fire hose effect,” said Rob Evans, Rivers Program manager with the state Department of Environmental Conservation. 
Today, state surveys show that about 75% of Vermont’s rivers are disconnected from their floodplains.
Vermont’s mountainous terrain makes flooding — and erosion — more likely. During heavy storms, rain-swollen streams can run down steep mountainsides, causing landslides and dumping water into narrow river valleys.

In the late 1990s, the state shifted its flood prevention strategy to focus on large-scale floodplain restoration projects, which involved using large machinery to move rivers and create new floodplains, according to Mike Kline, a river ecologist who used to lead Vermont’s Rivers Program.
But many of those projects soon failed, because the rivers took a different path than the scientists expected, said Kline, who retired from the state in 2019.
Kline remembers sitting with his boss in northern Vermont, on the banks of the Trout River, which had just “blown apart” one of their projects. 
“The Trout River is going to sort this out for itself,” Kline recalled telling his boss. “And it was then we decided that our number one priority was river corridor protection as a program. We got out of the big yellow machine business.”
Now the state’s policies are centered around giving rivers space to move and revert back to their more natural, curving paths – wherever possible. 
By protecting river corridors, the area where a river is most likely to move and cause erosion, policymakers aim to restore rivers’ stability. 
“Rivers have a physical imperative,” Evans said. “The river is going to take that space. It’s just a matter of when.”
“No one was offering that”
But as rivers take more space, they could threaten the homes of thousands of Vermonters.
In Plainfield, erosion has been causing landslides for decades, according to multiple studies by town resident George Springston, a geologist and an assistant professor at Norwich University,  Floods in the 1980s washed away two houses.


George Springston, a geologist and an assistant professor at Norwich University, has been studying erosion in Plainfield for decades. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger 


“We knew that there were houses that, ideally, there should be buyouts for,” Springston said. “But there was no money to buy out all the houses. There just was not.” Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger


“We knew that there were houses that, ideally, there should be buyouts for,” Springston said in a recent interview. “But there was no money to buy out all the houses. There just was not. I have no idea where anyone would have said, ‘You got five houses that aren’t in good places? Here’s some money to buy them.’ No one was offering that.”
In 2021, Vermont officials created the Flood Resilient Communities Fund to launch a state buyout program. 
The fund would purchase homes at risk of flooding or erosion at their pre-storm value. The federal government provided most of the money – $20 million – with the state contributing an additional $5.8 million.
Experts say that buyouts, which are voluntary, have several benefits. They help flood survivors get back on their feet financially, often giving them the pre-storm value of their homes. They reduce risks in areas prone to flooding and erosion, potentially saving lives. They save taxpayer dollars because governments no longer pay to repair repeated flood damage in the same area. (Most buyout land is not redeveloped.) And over time, they can be less expensive than projects that protect homes from encroaching rivers, which can also make erosion worse over time.
Vermont used the money to buy 52 properties, including the Rapczynskis’ home. They applied to the state’s program in April 2024, and, within a year, they had purchased a new home a few towns over, in Danville. 
“I consider our situation a success because we were able to leave,” Julie Rapczynski said. 
In 2024, lawmakers set aside $3.5 million for a new, similar program, called the Community Resilience and Disaster Mitigation Grant Program to help 2023 flood survivors elevate their homes above floodplains. In the future, the fund could help with disaster mitigation including buyouts, but lawmakers don’t currently have plans to replenish it. 
Rep. Robin Scheu, D-Middlebury, the chair of the House Committee on Appropriations, said the state doesn’t have money for buyouts.
“When we were doing this budget, we were looking at food — more people are going hungry,” she said. “Housing, a perennial problem. Healthcare, especially primary care, and the cost of health insurance. There are a lot of competing priorities, and I think the way we all need to be looking at this is saying, ‘What are the highest priorities?’”

READ MORE

In recent elections, voters haven’t named a state buyout fund as a priority, Rep. Scheu said. “Unless it’s right in your face, it’s not top of mind for folks,” she said.
Last year, Vermont’s Agency of Natural Resources recommended that the state put a minimum of $5 million into the buyout fund on an ongoing basis, describing such an investment as a top priority to reduce erosion risks and recovery costs following major storms. But the report noted the need to find “sustainable, ongoing funding for the program” and said it should not come from an increase in taxes or fees.
If the fund is replenished, homeowners could apply for buyouts and the state’s scientists would have to decide which to prioritize. Thus far, they have mapped the river corridors, but state officials haven’t proactively identified “properties where, before the next flood hits, we could perhaps get those folks out of harm’s way,” Evans said.
“Yeah, that isn’t happening,” he said. “Just because, that’s easier said than done.”
Vermont typically gets funding after floods hit — which it uses for recovery and climate resilience planning. 
“Mitigation has largely been reactive,” Evans said. 
Moore, head of the state’s Agency of Natural Resources, says the state considers erosion an urgent issue. She pointed to Vermont’s 2024 Flood Safety Act, which will require a new state permit for any new construction in the state’s river corridors.
​​Julie Moore, secretary of the Agency of Natural Resources, speaks about flooding during a press conference on Dec. 18, 2023. Photo by Natalie Williams/VTDigger
When the legislation takes effect in two years, Moore said she hopes it will “reduce new investments being made in bad places.”
The new law is a necessary step, but doesn’t come close to solving the problem, said Kevin Geiger, chief planner for Two Rivers-Ottauquechee Regional Commission, which helps municipalities in eastern Vermont navigate disasters.
Rather, those regulations are acting to “stop stabbing the patient,” Geiger said.
Because the Rapczynskis’ home is not located in a FEMA flood zone, it’s harder for them to qualify for a federal buyout. Experts say that most of the country’s FEMA maps are outdated and don’t account for changing land use patterns and the increasing risk of flooding due to climate change.
FEMA declined interview requests for this series, instead answering questions by email. Asked whether its flood maps would be updated to better account for erosion risk in Vermont, an agency spokesperson responded that “FEMA is always reviewing its programs to seek efficiencies and improve their performance.”
“Fluvial [river] erosion does not necessarily disqualify a property from acquisition programs, which seek to mitigate losses and consider eligibility, technical feasibility and cost-effectiveness,” the spokesperson said.
State officials expect FEMA’s maps to be updated by 2030, and in some communities, by 2027. But they still won’t account for erosion risks, according to Ned Swanberg, the state’s flood hazard mapping coordinator.
FEMA officials know that the homes located in their mapped hazard areas face flood risks. But getting buyouts for homes outside of those areas is a more difficult process, according to state officials. 
“There needs to be a state buyout program, full stop, that’s wicked robust, that can deal with things that don’t qualify for FEMA buyouts,” said Pete Fellows, a certified floodplain manager with the Two Rivers-Ottauquechee Regional Commission.
Battling the elements
In the middle of a rainy night in late July of 2024, Leena Aly got a flash flood alert on her phone. Beyond the deck of her rental home in Lyndon, the visiting dental student normally saw gravel and a river a stone’s throw away. Now, she could see a torrent of water right outside her door. The small home shook. It dipped toward the river.
“I stepped with my right foot off of the tiny house, the steps, and I immediately was in the water,” Aly said in an interview after the storm. “I had no chance to stand. There was no standing.”
The current pulled her underwater, and she screamed when she surfaced. She tried to grab onto branches, but they were becoming completely unearthed from the riverbed.
When she finally grabbed a stable branch, she called 9-1-1 from her cell phone, which she had managed to hold onto in the raging waters. Rescuers searched for Aly, but couldn’t find her. The Hawkins Brook had erased most of the road.
“I thought I was going to die,” Aly said. “It was really just a moment of just battling with the elements. And I’ve never in my life thought I could be that close to death.”
River erosion can happen slowly, over years — or within hours, causing catastrophic damage during intense storms. 

Between midnight and 5 a.m. on July 30, 2024, nearly 8 inches of rain fell on a small area in northern Vermont, including Lyndon. Her rental and three other houses on Red Village Road were destroyed. One belonged to a family with three children who fled just before their house fell into the river. 
Another home was swept downstream with 98-year-old Dorothy “Pete” Blackadar and her niece, Paula, inside. Both survived “due to the help and heroics of a neighbor,” said Gov. Phil Scott, who knew Blackadar, during an event last year commemorating the floods.
The flooding and erosion in Lyndon reshaped the landscape overnight. Residents who saw clear skies before they went to sleep woke up to what looked “like a totally different place,” Rose Reynolds, Aly’s neighbor, said after the storm. “Like we were dropped out of the sky, and now we’re in a new town or something.”
A different flood had hit Lyndon weeks earlier, on July 10, when water rose slowly from the riverbanks and covered large portions of the town. Town Administrator Justin Smith said the second flood “was much more quick, a lot less warning, and obviously resulted in a great deal of damage.” Both floods destroyed homes. 
Vermont’s annual rainfall has increased by 7.3 inches since the early 1900s. Three weeks before the storm in Lyndon, the remnants of Hurricane Beryl dropped nearly 5 inches of rain in Plainfield, turning the Great Brook violent. Again, the river valley walls came down. Scientists have connected Hurricane Beryl, which was fueled by record-warm ocean temperatures, to climate change.

READ MORE

For over a century, the Great Brook had been contained in a channel. But on that July night, the stream claimed a new path that, as in Lyndon, changed the shape of the entire river valley. Now, the Great Brook spreads out in a wide curve where Brook Road used to be.
The flooding destroyed nearly 36 homes in Plainfield, displacing as many as 70 people in the town of around 1,200. The town isn’t sure yet whether it will rebuild the road. If it does, cost estimates range between $12 million to $21 million. The town’s annual budget in 2025 was $1.8 million.
If the town doesn’t rebuild the road, “extended travel times between residents and the Village, delayed response times for emergency service providers, and longer drives between Plainfield and Barre would persist,” according to a recent report that detailed replacement options. 
In his 2001 paper, Springston, the geologist at Norwich University, found that Brook Road took up much of the stream’s floodplain, increasing erosion along the riverbanks. 
Springston said the fact that no one died in Plainfield’s 2024 flood was “just luck.”
In Plainfield, a stairway is all that’s left of a home that was swept away in 2024 floods. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger
Temporary fixes 
Flooding in 2023 and 2024 in Middlesex washed out driveways and threatened homes, which sit along the edge of another river named Great Brook, and altered the landscape.
Trees now tilt at unnatural angles, their canopies colliding above the river, and small landslides dot the riverbanks. Another big storm could collapse the riverbanks and send the trees tumbling into the stream.
During the 2023 flood, Linda Helms, a physical therapist and ski patrol member whose house sits along the Great Brook, evacuated to her neighbors’ home across the street. From there, she monitored her porch light — if she could see it, she remembers thinking, her house must still be there.
Her home sustained almost no damage, she said, but the flood destroyed her gardens, washed away some of her land, and caused a landslide directly across from her house. One year later, in the 2024 flood, her house again stayed mostly dry, but she found in the morning that the river had moved much closer to the back of her house. 
“I lost land — lost a shit ton of land — to the stream,” she said.
The morning after a storm in July 2024, Linda Helms discovered that the Great Brook had moved much closer to the back of her house.  “I lost land — lost a shit ton of land — to the stream,” she said. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger
After the first round of flooding she scrambled to protect her home. She said she felt “powerless, out of control.” She did not want to go through a winter with her house unprotected. 
“I’ve always had a very strong respect for water,” she said. “I’ve always been in water, in water sports. I grew up by the ocean, body surfing my whole kid-hood.” 
But the floods changed that feeling. The water was “so loud for so long,” she said. She used to enjoy listening to the brook, which she can hear from her bedroom. 
“I don’t like the sound of the brook,” she said. “I do not like it.”
She received a grant from the U.S. Department of Agriculture’s Emergency Watershed Protection Program to secure the riverbank near her home with a wall of rocks, called riprap. 
While these projects may protect individual homes, experts say that they have downsides: They keep the river acting like a firehose, unable to spread out into its floodplain. And the riprap sometimes needs to be replaced soon after it’s installed.
“This can go next year in a thousand-year flood,” Helms said.
Kline, the retired river ecologist, studied those projects for the town of Middlesex. According to his research, at least 8% of the riprap that had been installed after the 2023 and 2024 floods was already failing by the spring of 2025.

 
Video by Riley Robinson and Ben Braun for VTDigger

The USDA acknowledges the watershed protection projects can fail soon after they’re built. The agency limits how often it will replace riprap to two times in 10 years. 
Helms says she’s staying put for now. 
“I’ve thought about selling this house. I wouldn’t find a house that I can afford, a mortgage that I could afford,” she said. “Maybe I would have to move out of Vermont.”
“What are we up against?” 
Like many rivers in Vermont, the Huntington River and its tributaries weave through farm fields and in between houses, under bridges, and through the heart of downtown Huntington.
The town flooded in 2019, then badly in 2024. Resident Amy Seoane said the river ripped through her neighborhood in the 2024 flood. When the floodwaters receded, the gravel in the riverbed had moved, changing the river’s path. It’s now pointed at homes in Huntington Acres, where she lives.
Amy Soane and her husband, Justin Houghton, are considering a FEMA buyout. They live near the Huntington River, and their neighborhood has flooded multiple times in the past decade. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger.
Seoane has organized a group of residents that has pleaded with town and state officials to help them remove some of the gravel to protect their homes. While state officials told her they could permit some of the work, the state wouldn’t pay for any of it, Seoane said.
Many flood survivors have argued that Vermont should dredge rivers to control flooding, as it has done in the past, but the state has moved away from the practice.
Vermont now requires anyone who wants to move a significant amount of material in a river’s channel to obtain a stream alteration permit. If the work is likely to make erosion worse, the state won’t approve it. Even if the state grants an alteration permit, it won’t pay for the work.
The policy is intended to prevent large-scale “hogging out the rivers, put the flood water back in the channel, make them deep and steep and get it off my land” types of projects, said Evans, of Vermont’s Rivers Program. In the long term, the policy could help rivers return to a more meandering, less dangerous state.
In the short term, it leaves residents with few options. 
At a meeting in January with state officials, leaders of several community recovery groups said flood survivors don’t know how they can protect their homes, according to a recording VTDigger obtained through a public records request. 
There is “a whole bucket” of flood survivors in north central Vermont who want to do streambank stabilization on their property, said Mike Dacey, who leads a recovery group in Waterbury. 
“Some of them have received permits and just got to the point where, if they had the money to pay for it, they would do it, but these are massively expensive projects,” he said, noting they often cost in the tens or hundreds of thousands of dollars. 
Moore said her agency sent river engineers to Huntington to see what it would take to “essentially dredge the Huntington River in a manner that would appreciably reduce the flood risk to those folks.”
“The price tag was enormous, well north of a million dollars, if not more,” she said. “But perhaps more challenging than the price tag is the fact that they believed all of that dredging would be undone in the next significant rainfall event.”
Town officials are considering some changes to the river. With FEMA funding, they have hired engineers to design two projects that would protect public infrastructure. Engineers are also considering whether any projects could benefit residential property, said Adam Argeropoulos, Huntington’s town administrator. 
Argeropoulos said the town often feels pulled in two directions when it comes to the debate about whether to touch the river.
“There’s the science saying it’s not a good idea,” he said. “And then there’s the other side, which is like, ‘Well, my great great grandfather did this, and his son did this, and then I did this, and now you’re telling me I can’t do it? And so what, you want me to give up my house?’”
“I see both sides very clearly, and I don’t think one is more right than the other,” he said.
Seoane said she’s attended public meetings in Huntington at which officials and river experts have raised the idea that houses should never have been built in the floodplain.
“We went to one of those meetings, and we all had to leave because our blood pressure was through the roof,” Seoane said. “We keep saying, we didn’t just build these houses, they were permitted 60 plus years ago.”
In 2024, Soane asked FEMA for a buyout, but she worried the agency would reject her application because her home is located just outside of the agency’s designated flood zones. Last month, she learned FEMA said it would approve buyouts for her and 10 other households in Huntington.
But Soane isn’t sure she will take the offer. Given Vermont’s housing shortage, she’s worried she won’t be able to afford another home in the state. 
“It’s not ideal to be relocating right now, and I don’t believe we could do it,” she said. “But then, if we stay and we turn down the buyout, what are we up against, with no work done on the river and storms getting worse?” 
This story was reported with support from FRONTLINE’s Local Journalism Initiative, which is funded by the John S. and James L. Knight Foundation.

The series continues. Our third and final story in The Coming Storm: Disaster recovery can be expensive and complicated, with enormous financial consequences for survivors. As federal agencies cut back on disaster assistance, is Vermont prepared to help them?

name: Washington State Standard
title: Washington schools prepare to sue the state for failing to fund public education
description: Three large Washington school districts are preparing to sue the state, alleging it is once again failing to fully fund basic education.  School boards for the Lake Washington, Tacoma and Yakima districts contend the state’s failure to meet its constitutional obligations is forcing them to rely on local levy dollars to pay day-to-day expenses, echoing […]
text:
(Photo by Dana DiFilippo | New Jersey Monitor)Three large Washington school districts are preparing to sue the state, alleging it is once again failing to fully fund basic education. 
School boards for the Lake Washington, Tacoma and Yakima districts contend the state’s failure to meet its constitutional obligations is forcing them to rely on local levy dollars to pay day-to-day expenses, echoing an argument made in the landmark McCleary ruling that forced the state to pump billions of additional dollars into education. 
The Lake Washington and Tacoma School Districts simultaneously passed resolutions on Oct. 22, directing staff to start assembling the pieces for a lawsuit. On Nov. 2, the Yakima School District followed their lead, effectively declaring participation in a future suit. 
The three districts, which serve more than 74,000 students, did not disclose when they plan to file — but their decision wasn’t made overnight. 
In March, Lake Washington Superintendent Jon Holmen explained to parents why the school was preparing to sue the state. 
“Year after year, our district must bridge significant funding gaps to provide legally required services for students, relying on local resources to make up for what is defined as the ‘paramount duty’ in our state constitution,” Holmen wrote. “Local levy support cannot replace the state’s constitutional obligation to fund basic education.”
Per its resolution, Lake Washington “plans to allege” that the state is violating a provision of the state constitution, “which imposes a mandatory, affirmative duty” to “fully fund a program of basic education for all children residing in this state.”
The argument mirrors one that’s already played out in the state’s Supreme Court. In the 2012 McCleary decision, the high court ruled that the state violated its “paramount duty” to provide ample funding for public education, and ordered it to do so. 
In 2014, the court ruled it hadn’t complied, issuing a contempt order and eventually, imposing an unprecedented $100,000 per day fine on the state. By 2018, the state came into compliance, the court ruled. 
In the years since, schools have been hit with rising transportation, utility and insurance costs. Local levies have failed for some districts that have come to rely on them. Student enrollment continues to decline. And, there are now 11 school districts, more than ever before, on binding conditions, or state financial oversight.
Superintendent of Public Instruction Chris Reykdal has warned for years that a McCleary-like case could soon arise. For years, his office has requested budgets that would have addressed funding shortfalls, said Katy Payne, chief strategy officer. 
Overall, Reykdal supports the districts’ efforts. 
“While litigation is never a first choice, OSPI and school districts have been sounding the alarm about underfunding for several years,” Payne said. “While the Legislature has made slight improvements, districts are still spending $800 million per year in local and federal funds in order to cover the state’s obligation.” 
The lack of funding has driven school districts to “layoff staff, increase class sizes, and some are even considering closing schools,” Payne added. “We urge the governor and Legislature to close this funding gap this legislative session.”

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Frustrated by ‘prolonged inaction,’ Spilka might backtrack on extending legislative deadline next term
description: Lawmakers still have dozens of major policy decisions to make in the eight remaining weeks of the term, all of which will happen in the lame-duck stretch after Election Day.
text:
NEW LEGISLATIVE RULES were supposed to ease the end-of-session pileup as lawmakers rushed to finish major bills in the summertime before downshifting to maintenance mode before and after Election Day. If negotiations could continue past the traditional July 31 deadline, the thinking went, the House and Senate could be more productive and their closing business could be less frantic than years past.
Now, a top Democrat who first suggested the change has issued a sharp rebuke of how the updated timeline actually unfolded.
In a statement provided exclusively to CommonWealth Beacon, Senate President Karen Spilka called the months-long lack of movement on the massive pile of unfinished legislation “unacceptable.” She also signaled that she might want to backtrack from the altered timeline in the next two-year term.
“Prolonged inaction on many of the major bills currently in conference as residents face rising energy bills and an ongoing housing crisis is unacceptable,” Spilka said. “Unless we see movement soon, I cannot support extending the time for conference negotiations again in our joint rules next session.”
The Senate, she said, “stands ready to reach a resolution on the many conference reports still pending.”
Spilka issued her statement in response to a CommonWealth Beacon inquiry about the state of play on Beacon Hill for the eight remaining weeks of the term. We asked how she plans to manage more than 40 discrete policy decisions that are still pending across a dozen conference committees, and if she views the current dynamic as an improvement on the chaotic past two terms.
 “If the recent midterms taught us anything, it’s that voters expect their elected officials to take meaningful action to reduce costs and improve lives. I agree,” Spilka said. “The Legislature must act with a sense of urgency to lower energy costs, make primary care more accessible, make schools cell phone free and increase transparency in government, among other things.”

Read more: Election season is done. Holiday season is approaching. And lawmakers still have dozens of big decisions to make.

It’s a public escalation of discontent, especially in contrast to the tone taken by the other end of the negotiating table. Asked the same question about the legislative outlook, House Speaker Ron Mariano instead offered plenty of praise for the new system.
“It’s important to understand that these are complex policy decisions that take time, and often many conversations and meetings to resolve,” he said in a statement Friday. “That being said, the new rules have allowed the Legislature more time to work diligently to reach the best possible policy outcomes — understanding that the content of the final product is far more important than reaching an agreement quickly solely for the sake of doing so.”
Mariano’s office did not immediately respond to a CommonWealth Beacon inquiry Monday morning about Spilka’s newly expressed dissatisfaction.
This is the first term in which lawmakers granted themselves codified authority to continue their talks over significant proposals this late in the cycle.
For more than 30 years, legislative rules held that no formal sessions could take place after July 31 in the second year of the two-year term, meaning the only bills that could be touched in those five-plus months were uncontroversial measures that had unanimous support.
But lawmakers are prone to procrastination, and even though Democrats dominate both chambers, the House and Senate often struggle to get on the same page. This time around, legislative leaders agreed to a new approach: As long as both chambers each approved their version of a bill by July 31, they can reconvene in a formal session to approve a final compromise any time before the term ends on January 5, 2027.
House and Senate Democrats both endorsed codifying the idea early last year after using an ad-hoc version of it in the 2023-2024 term. In fact, Spilka herself used her inaugural speech on the first day of the current term to float it, saying the Legislature should “allow conference committee votes to continue through the full two-year session.”
“The bills that emerge from conference committees contain provisions that have been vetted by one or both branches and have been reported upon — sometimes extensively,” she said.
When the final gavel rang out on July 31, a dozen conference committees were in place to negotiate the fate of packages dealing with energy affordability, economic development, cell phone use in K-12 schools, and more. Nearly three and a half months later, none of those panels have reached consensus, leaving every single matter that was pending on August 1 still unresolved heading into an eight-week lame-duck sprint after the election.
House and Senate Democrats might dig their heels in on policy differences if they feel the chambers are at odds. At times, tensions on one front — or at the top of the leadership hierarchy — have rippled out to complicate work on other conference committees.
In 2024, reporters asked Mariano about a Senate vote to authorize supervised drug injection sites days before the end of formal business. “It sort of tells me you’re not really serious about passing the bill to begin with,” he said.
The next day, when reporters pressed Spilka on a House-supported proposal to temporarily rebalance Boston’s property tax formula, she pulled out a crumpled piece of paper and read from it.
“It sort of tells you,” she said, repeating Mariano’s words, “that they’re not really serious about passing the bill to begin with.”

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Alaska voters on track to reject 2 Kenai judges in initial election results
description: Alaska voters in the Third Judicial District opted to reject two state judges standing for retention in the midterm election by wide margins in initial results on Tuesday. The vote comes after the non-partisan Alaska Judicial Council — charged with vetting and nominating judges, as well as conducting performance evaluations — issued a rare recommendation […]
text:
An empty judge's bench is seen in the Boney Courthouse in Anchorage on Jan 17, 2025. (Photo by Corinne Smith/Alaska Beacon)Alaska voters in the Third Judicial District opted to reject two state judges standing for retention in the midterm election by wide margins in initial results on Tuesday.     

Kenai Superior Court Judge Kelly Lawson was appointed in 2023. Voters opted not to retain her in the 2026 election, according to preliminary results. (Alaska Judicial Council photo)
Kenai District Court Judge Martin Fallon was appointed in 2019. Voters opted not to retain him in the 2026 election, according to preliminary results. (Alaska Judicial Council photo)
 

The vote comes after the non-partisan Alaska Judicial Council — charged with vetting and nominating judges, as well as conducting performance evaluations — issued a rare recommendation for voters not to retain the two judges in this election. They were the only two they recommended not be retained out of 21 judges standing for retention elections. For another Juneau judge, they issued no recommendation.
Voters opting to retain Kenai Superior Court Judge Kelly Lawson and District Court Judge Martin Fallon were outnumbered by “no” votes, according to initial results released by the Alaska Division of Elections. As of Wednesday, 58% of voters voted “no” to retain Lawson, and 41.8% voted “yes” — a 16 point margin, or 19,939 vote split. For Fallon, 59% of voters cast a “no” vote and 40.9% voted “yes,” — a roughly 18% margin, or 21,853 vote split. 
If the results hold, the two will step down from the bench at the end of February, 90 days after the election results are certified, according to state law. 
Judicial retention votes take place in even-number years to allow voters to decide whether judges should be allowed to stay on the bench. According to preliminary results on Wednesday, voters opted to retain 19 of the 21 judges up for retention. 
Lawson and Fallon did not respond to questions from the Alaska Beacon about the results and their opinions of the council’s recommendation not to retain them on Friday. 
Lawson was appointed to the bench in the Kenai Superior Court in 2023, and this was her first retention election. After a performance evaluation, the council found she did not meet performance standards for judicial temperament and integrity. 
This was the second retention election for Fallon, who was appointed to the Kenai District Court in 2019. The council found in its review that he did not meet performance standards related to integrity, diligence and administrative skills, including failing to resolve cases in a timely manner. 
The vacancies in the Kenai courts will be filled by retired judges, called pro tem judges, according to Rebecca Koford, a spokesperson for the Alaska Court System.
“We are grateful to the pro tem judges who step in to help in times of need,” Koford said by email on Friday. “We expect that pro tem judges will assist with helping to cover the caseloads for the two Kenai positions until they are filled but coverage details are still being worked out.”
The number of cases that Lawson and Fallon are currently presiding over was not immediately available on Friday, Koford said.  
Looking ahead, Susanne DiPietro, executive director of the council, said by email Friday that the council will interview and nominate applicants for the two judicial vacancies at its next meeting in May. The nominees will then advance to the new governor to make appointments for two new judges.

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: Meet the 10 Democrats who flipped Statehouse seats in SC
description: Most of the winners were Black, following a loss of Black representatives over the past two election cycles, and many were political newcomers.
text:
Ten Democrats flipped seats from Republicans to join the state House for the legislative session that starts in January 2027. (File photo by Travis Bell/STATEHOUSE CAROLINA/Special to the SC Daily Gazette)COLUMBIA — A former police officer under criminal investigation and a veteran who lost a special election earlier this year are among the state House’s 10 new Democrats.
In Tuesday’s midterm election, Democrats flipped 10 House seats, including six districts lost to Republican opponents over the past four years. The wins represented the best showing Democrats have had in recent memory and broke the House’s Republican supermajority.
Of the 10 winners, seven were Black and three were white, bolstering the numbers of the Legislative Black Caucus. GOP losses included the chamber’s only Black Republican, who two years ago defeated 20-year incumbent Rep. Joe Jefferson from rural Berkeley County.
He was among five Black Democrats in the House who lost over the last two election cycles in seats flipped back Tuesday by Black Democrats.
Many of Tuesday’s winners are newcomers to state politics. While four of the winners had run for Statehouse seats before, the rest had either never campaigned before or sought only local offices.
These are the 10 Democrats who flipped seats to join the 124-member chamber in January.
District 12
Jumelle Brooks ousted Rep. Daniel Gibson in the race to represent Greenwood and McCormick counties. Gibson lost by nearly 10 points, four years after defeating Anne Parks, a Black Democrat, from the seat she’d held for a quarter century.
Brooks, who lives in Greenwood, runs a home health care service for elderly adults in rural counties.
She ran for the same seat two years ago and lost by roughly 700 votes.
Her goals include bolstering renters’ rights by putting penalties on landlords that don’t clean up or repair properties, according to her campaign website. She also wants to work on closing gaps in how well students perform and improve working conditions for support staff in schools, such as bus drivers, custodians and substitute teachers.
And she hopes to introduce afterschool programs and job training programs in an effort to reduce violence among teenagers, according to her website.
“I truly hope the upcoming session does not get bogged down in unproductive hyper-partisan issues,” Brooks wrote on Facebook. “There are so many things, non-controversial items, that we can work on together so that all of South Carolina can benefit.”
District 57
Cynthia Ford defeated Lucas Atkinson in the district representing parts of Horry, Marion and Williamsburg counties. His ousting followed his decision to run as a Republican this year after a decade as a Democrat.
Ford is an Air Force veteran and former Marion County director for the Department of Juvenile Justice. She is a consultant, grant writer and author of multiple self-help books, according to her Facebook page.
Her priorities include creating jobs and housing in rural areas and improving access to rural health care, according to her campaign page.
“Throughout this campaign, I have listened to your concerns, heard your stories and witnessed firsthand the challenges and opportunities within our communities,” Ford wrote on her campaign page. “Those conversations will not end because the election is over. In many ways, our work is just beginning.”
District 64
In the district representing Clarendon and Sumter counties, Michele Demery defeated Rep. Fawn Pedalino by nearly 5 percentage points. Pedalino ousted then-Rep. Kimberly Johnson, a Black Democrat, in 2022.
Demery jumped into the race late. David Epperson, who initially filed to run against Pedalino, withdrew in April, less than a week after filing closed. The Democratic Party reopened filing for 48 hours, drawing three more candidates.
One was disqualified immediately. Demery, whose only foray into politics was an unsuccessful run for a county council seat earlier this year, easily won the primary with 66% of the vote.
Demery, a 51-year-old from Manning, teaches fifth grade in Berkeley County. This is her ninth year working in public schools. She’s taught various grade levels and special education classes, as well as worked as an instructional coach, a teacher mentor and an assistant principal, she told the SC Daily Gazette.
That experience means public education is a big priority for her, she said. She wants to take a closer look at the funding formula for public schools at a local level.
Rural areas like Clarendon County struggle to supplement state aid for public schools because they have few businesses paying property taxes, she said.
This school year, Clarendon County receives more than $10,200 per pupil in state funding, about $630 above the state average. But the county’s total revenue per pupil, when including local property taxes and federal aid, still falls about $3,500 below the average total for school districts statewide, according to data from the state Revenue and Fiscal Affairs Office.
“Our local community doesn’t have the ability to provide funding to our public schools like they need,” Demery said.
District 66
Heather Hart, a writer with a master’s degree in the Biblical New Testament, was the only Democrat to defeat a member of the ultra-conservative Freedom Caucus on Tuesday.
Hart, who lives in Fort Mill, ousted freshman Rep. Jackie Terribile, a marketing consultant.
Hart had never run for election before, but she decided to challenge Terribile after seeing what she called “cruel and unhelpful policies” passed at the Statehouse.
Specifically, Hart opposes school vouchers. which allow families to use taxpayer dollars on education expenses including private school tuition, as undermining public schools. And people in the York County district, where students consistently outperform the rest of the state, care deeply about supporting their local K-12 schools, she told the Daily Gazette.
She also pointed to Terribile’s lack of support for funding local projects, which fell in line with the Freedom Caucus’ general opposition to budget earmarks. Cities in York County could have used some funding for needs such as better fire trucks, Hart said.
“There were some key votes from her I felt did not reflect the values of our community,” Hart said.
The 47-year-old wants legislators to reconsider how tax dollars fund schools and what she sees as an unfair burden on small businesses to pay school operating costs, she said.
“We can bring some fairness so our local small businesses have a chance to succeed,” she said.
Fort Mill, an affluent suburb of Charlotte, North Carolina, is receiving about $8,700 in state aid per pupil this school year, or about $900 less than the state average, due to funding formulas that provide a greater share of aid to districts with less of a tax base, according to state fiscal data.
District 89
Joe Madge, an electrical engineer, had a narrow lead over newly minted House Majority Leader Micah Caskey, who has held the Lexington County seat for the past decade.
Because the vote tallies came within 1 percentage point, the race will go to an automatic recount. However, Caskey wrote on X he doesn’t expect the totals to change enough for him to claim victory.
Madge, who spent four years as chair of the Lexington County Democratic Party, plans to focus on lowering healthcare costs, strengthening public schools and “protecting personal freedom,” he said in a news release.
“The people of House District 89 have entrusted me with a great responsibility at a time of great change in South Carolina,” Madge said in the news release. “I am grateful for the opportunity to serve my neighbors in the West Columbia, Cayce and Springdale area.”
District 92
Byron Walters, a 52-year-old from Ladson, defeated two-term Rep. Brandon Cox in the Berkeley County district.
Walters, who runs Acme Lowcountry Kitchen on Isle of Palms, decided to run for office after getting a text message from Contest Every Race, a candidate recruitment group that seeks Democrats to challenge Republican incumbents, he told the Daily Gazette.
This was his first campaign. Along with better affordability for working class people, Walters wants to find ways to recruit more foster parents and help children who age out of the system.
Walters and his wife fostered 11 children between 2021 and 2024, all 5 years old or younger and all with complicated medical needs. They adopted two of those children, who are both in kindergarten now.
Because of that experience, Walters is aware of how difficult it is to find people willing to take on the challenge of helping children with medical needs and how many children turn 18 without finding a consistent foster family, sending them out into the world without much of a support network, he said.
“That is a real trauma situation for those kids,” Walters said.
Walters is also a Marine veteran and a retired member of the National Guard. Because of that, he wants to find ways to support veterans, he said.
District 98
Sonja Ogletree Satani of North Charleston lost to Rep. Greg Ford of Summerville by 21 votes in a special election in January to replace former Rep. Chris Murphy, a Republican, in the Dorchester County district.
Tuesday, Ogletree Satani defeated Ford by 9 percentage points.
Ogletree Satani is an Air Force veteran and a professor of business management at ECPI University, a private college in Lexington County. She also runs Corporate Cycle Consulting, a North Charleston-based business consulting firm.
Attracting new business to the area, funding public education and vocational training, and reducing homelessness and food insecurity were among Ogletree Satani’s biggest campaign priorities, according to her website.
“You trusted me with your vote, and I will never take that trust for granted,” Ogletree Satani wrote on Facebook. “I am ready to roll up my sleeves, get to work, listen to your concerns, and fight for the people of District 98.”
District 102
Montez Aiken, a former Summerville police officer, defeated Harriet Holman, a U.S. Army veteran, by nearly 15 points. She made history two years ago as the chamber’s first Black Republican female.
Aiken is under investigation by the Summerville Police Department and the State Law Enforcement Division over texts unearthed during the campaign. SLED confirmed the investigation in an email to the Daily Gazette but did not give any more information.
Text messages released by the Berkeley County and Dorchester County Republican parties show sexual messages sent during the 2023-24 school year to a then-18-year-old student at a high school where Aiken was a school resource officer. Aiken also worked with the Summerville Police Department for 23 years before retiring in 2025.
“The accusations against me are inflammatory and I take them seriously,” Aiken said in a statement Oct. 22. “I have consulted my attorney and have been advised to consider legal action if they continue.”
Aiken did not respond to a call or text message from the Daily Gazette requesting further comment.
Aiken’s campaign focused on affordability and support for public schools.
District 116
Clay Middleton ousted Rep. James Teeple, a Navy veteran who runs a childcare center, in the district that spans southern Charleston County, plus the town of Edisto Beach, which is in Colleton County.
Middleton, who is managing director at a public affairs firm and a lieutenant colonel with the Army National Guard, has run for mayor of Charleston and for a different Statehouse seat but never won.
His campaign focused on affordability and smart development in the fast-growing district, he told the Daily Gazette.
The 44-year-old plans to introduce legislation that would require developers to work with surrounding communities and make deals to pay the difference in property taxes for people on fixed incomes if property values start to rise.
His goal is to ensure the area has “smart growth, not reckless growth,” he said.
“We need to make sure the infrastructure is in place first before development begins,” he said.
Four years ago, Republican Matt Leber flipped the seat of rural, sea islands held by a Black Democrat since 1974. Teeple kept the seat red in an open contest two years ago, as Leber ran successfully for the state Senate.
District 122
Korey Williams, a Hampton County attorney, defeated Rep. Bill Hager, a retired engineer from Hampton, to represent parts of Hampton, Jasper, Colleton and Beaufort counties.
Hager flipped the seat in 2022 by defeating then-Rep. Shedron Williams, a Black Democrat who in 2018 ousted a white Democrat who’d held the seat for 20 years.
Williams’ top priorities included affordable healthcare, protecting vulnerable natural resources along the coast, and improving workforce training in public schools, according to his campaign website.
“We won this together and we will continue to work together to do what’s best for EVERYONE in the district,” Williams wrote on Facebook.
