name: Connecticut Mirror
title: CT officials say Madison woman tried to vote twice. She called it a test
description: The woman said she didn't intend to vote twice and was only testing the state system when she tried to obtain a second ballot at the polls.
text:
A Madison woman facing questions about her conduct in this week’s election said she never intended to vote twice and was only testing the state’s system when she took steps to obtain a second ballot at the polls.
At a press conference on Election Day, Deputy Secretary of the State Jennifer Barahona advised voters against trying to conduct independent tests of voting systems — a phenomenon she said was popping up on social media. Barahona provided few details, but pointed to a Nov. 1 incident that took place during the early voting period in Madison as an example.
“Attempting to test the system by voting twice is not a harmless experiment,” Barahona said. “Voting more than once is voter fraud and it is illegal.”
In Connecticut, voting more than once in the same election is a criminal offense and can result in a fine between $300 and $500, along with one to two years in prison and the loss of the right to vote.
Documents reviewed by Connecticut Public show the Madison incident involved voter Terri LaChance, a 65-year-old registered Democrat in the town.
Records show a town registrar contacted the Secretary of the State’s Office to raise concerns about LaChance’s actions at the polls.
A letter submitted by the registrar provides little information, but includes a brief statement attributed to LaChance. In it, LaChance says she wasn’t going to vote twice, but decided to “see if it was possible” and “how far would I get if I tried.”
LaChance later described what happened in an interview with Connecticut Public.
LaChance said that she had grown concerned about the security of the election system after seeing social media posts with claims of voting machines changing people’s votes.
Election experts and state officials have said such issues are usually caused by calibration problems or human error.
LaChance said after voting, she returned to her polling location on Nov. 1. and checked in to vote again.
LaChance said her license was scanned and a sticker printed out; she signed twice and was handed a ballot. LaChance said she then alerted an election worker that she had previously voted. She said she believes she would have been able to cast another vote if she hadn’t said something.
The Secretary of the State’s Office has referred the incident to the State Elections Enforcement Commission for review.
“We understand that people want to know that our elections are safe and secure, so do we,” Barahona said at the Tuesday press conference. “But protecting the integrity of our elections is our job.”
Responding to questions about the incident, Matthew Clyburn, assistant director of communications for the office, said in a statement that state systems are designed to prevent double voting.
“When a voter casts a ballot during early voting, election officials record that the voter has voted in the statewide voter registration system,” Clyburn said. “That prevents the voter from voting again during early voting, by absentee ballot, or on election day.”
Alexander Russell, director of the University of Connecticut Center for Voting Technology Research, said each town also has a printed list that it uses to keep track of registered voters.
“There is a physical poll book,” he said. “People are crossed off in the poll book as they vote, and that’s supposed to prevent someone from voting twice.”
The incident was one of at least two in Connecticut that raised concern about improper voting activity.
Records released by the Secretary of the State’s Office show in October, a woman who local officials said is believed to have short-term memory issues checked in to vote two days after successfully voting early at the same location.
“I don’t believe she understood that she was in line to vote again or even if she remembered voting,” reads a document written by an election official.
The election worker who checked the woman in did not see that the Connecticut Voter Registration System showed she had already been issued a ballot, according to public documents. An early voting label was printed, the woman signed, and another ballot was issued and subsequently put into the tabulator.
At the end of the day, the tabulator counted one more ballot than the amount recorded in the early voting ballot report. Poll workers found that while the woman had signed a label for that day, her name was not on the report. Additionally, her record in the electronic registration system showed she had been issued a ballot two days prior.
Unable to adjust the tabulator count, the early voting moderator asked state officials for help.
State officials also referred the case to the State Elections Enforcement Commission, which is meeting next on Nov. 18. A SEEC representative said it cannot comment on any matter unless the commission opens an investigation.
This story was first published Nov. 6, 2026 by Connecticut Public.

name: Missouri Independent
title: What two surprise Democratic victories reveal about Missouri’s blue wave
description: Suzanne Luther has already picked out this year’s Christmas card. It’s a campaign mailer, sent to Jefferson City voters by people who wanted to keep her out of the Missouri House. It used what appears to be an AI-generated photo and accused her of supporting data centers. Three other Democrats, she said, were targeted using […]
text:
Suzanne Luther speaks to a voter in Jefferson City (photo submitted). Suzanne Luther has already picked out this year’s Christmas card.
It’s a campaign mailer, sent to Jefferson City voters by people who wanted to keep her out of the Missouri House. It used what appears to be an AI-generated photo and accused her of supporting data centers. Three other Democrats, she said, were targeted using the same template.
A TV ad, she said, was worse.
It featured an unflattering photograph of her (this one was real) set against what she described as the “flames of hell.” Then an operating room, and a push to tie Luther to surgeries on transgender children.
Finally, the ad cut to her Republican opponent, Shane Kampeter, enjoying a park with his family.
Luther wasn’t particularly intimidated.
“It was irritating,” she told me Thursday. But with Election Day approaching, “I had a checklist of what I needed to do and wasn’t going to get distracted.”
Luther went on to defeat Kampeter by 189 votes in a district Republicans won by 25 points just two years earlier.
Her victory was among the more surprising results of an election that saw Democrats flip 16 Missouri House seats, shatter Republican legislative supermajorities and win in places where their party has struggled for decades.
Missouri Republicans suffer biggest electoral setback in a generation

Make no mistake, Missouri experienced a blue wave. The national backlash against President Donald Trump and the Republican Party was enormous, and unlike previous elections, it didn’t lose much strength when it reached Missouri.
But waves don’t automatically produce victories.
For years, Democrats struggled to recruit candidates who could compete in Republican territory. Some seats went uncontested. In others, nominees lacked the name recognition or community connections needed to persuade voters to cross party lines. Even when the political environment turned favorable, opportunities were squandered.
This year was different. Democrats fielded candidates in 158 of Missouri’s 163 House districts. And some of their most unexpected victories came from candidates whose strongest political asset wasn’t a clever message or an enormous campaign treasury.
It was that their neighbors already knew them.
Consider Staci Czar.
A lifelong Belton resident, Czar has spent decades raising her family and volunteering in the community. She’s served on the city’s park board and helped develop its charter.
Her campaign slogan was simple: “From here. For here.”
When she knocked on doors in Belton and Raymore, she talked about public schools.
Missouri lawmakers had fallen $190 million short of fully funding the state’s school formula, and Czar worried about what that meant for local districts already confronting rising costs.
Those schools, she reminded voters, weren’t just educating their children. They were among the communities’ largest employers.
“We may not always see eye to eye on every policy or everything we believe in,” she said. But most families want the same basic things: financial stability, a vacation now and then, the ability to take their kids to a ballgame.
Czar won with nearly 53% of the vote.
There were other factors. The incumbent Republican, Michael Davis, lost his August primary to Steve Baker. And Czar unquestionably benefited from the national political climate.
But an opportunity is worthless without someone capable of seizing it.
Luther’s path was remarkably similar.
She grew up in Jefferson City, attended its public schools, taught for years and eventually served on the school board. She didn’t need a television commercial to introduce herself to the community.
“I think they felt listened to,” she said of voters, adding that she knew many of them from childhood.
Both women emphasized public education. Both talked about affordability. And both had established reputations in communities where the Democratic label has long been a political liability.
That matters when campaigns spend enormous sums trying to convince voters that their neighbors are dangerous extremists.
Democrats flip 16 Missouri House seats, ending Republican supermajority 

Republicans spent much of this election cycle using anti-transgender messaging to attack Democrats, including in Luther’s race and the unsuccessful effort to restore Missouri’s abortion ban.
Those attacks didn’t deliver the intended victories. And attacks portraying a candidate as an extremist carry less weight when voters have known that person for decades.
None of this means Missouri has turned blue. Republicans still control the legislature and every statewide elected office.
One of the smartest things anyone told me last week is that Tuesday was an opportunity for Democrats, not a mandate. Voters rebuked Republicans. They didn’t necessarily embrace anyone else.
Luther and Czar didn’t prove Democrats can win everywhere. They demonstrated that some places considered unwinnable may simply require the right circumstances, the right message and, most importantly, the right candidate.
For a party that spent years writing off much of Missouri as hopelessly Republican, that’s no small lesson.

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: Families fear state Medicaid billing change means loss of programs for disabled adults
description: Disabled adults in New Jersey are losing access to certain programs as the state tightens scrutiny around Medicaid billing to protect federal funding.
text:
Randi Meltzer puts lip gloss on her daughter, Marni Tanenbaum, 10, in Marlboro on Nov. 7, 2026. Meltzer co-founded Project MAC, which hosts art, music, and social skills classes for disabled adults and other members of the public. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)Trish Thomason describes herself as a “soccer mom, all day, every day,” shuttling her 27-year-old autistic son Eric from their home in Mullica Hill to activities like art, music, and cardio karaoke.
For Eric, who needs one-on-one supervision and is prone to outbursts, a mix of short, specialized programs have fed his curiosity, connected him to other young adults with disabilities, and allowed him to live his “best life ever,” Thomason told the New Jersey Monitor.
“He actually went out for pizza with some of them. That was huge,” she said.
Thomason fears all this could change because of a billing dispute between program operators and officials with the state Medicaid program, the state and federally subsidized insurance that funds healthcare and support services for nearly 30,000 disabled adults in New Jersey.
Starting last summer, New Jersey officials began to more sharply scrutinize how Medicaid was paying some operators who work with disabled adults, prompting payment denials for programs that had been reimbursed in the past, sometimes for years.
Multiple program operators, parents, and disability advocates said the shift has left a growing number of disabled people without programs they have come to love. Eric has not yet been impacted, she said, but she worries what’s to come.
“It just snowballs into this effect on the community. All of these people will be at home with nothing to do,” Thomason said.
Camille Milo-Gordy, of Norwood, is in a similar situation. Her daughter Nicole Kleine, 27, has autism and has benefitted from cooking, gym, and financial literacy programs over the past five years. Milo-Gordy worries the change will “pull the carpet out from under” families like hers and that without access to these programs, Nicole will languish at home with little hope for the future.
“My daughter’s going to sit in her chair and play on her laptop until I die. And then I don’t know what is going to happen to her after that,” she said.
Officials at the state’s Department of Human Services, which oversees the system, said they are trying to protect vulnerable residents and comply with the rules under Medicaid, a publicly funded system now facing massive federal funding cuts under the Trump administration. There is no policy change around billing for disability services, just a stricter adherence to rules designed to protect taxpayer funds, they said.
“Accurate billing is essential to maintain Medicaid compliance and protect federal funding, particularly as states face increased federal scrutiny of Medicaid spending,” said department spokesman Tom Hester Jr.
The state is now working with these organizations to help them comply with the rules while protecting high-quality services, he said.
Services for disabled residents in New Jersey are funded through individual Medicaid budgets established by the department based on that person’s needs. Families work with program coordinators to select care and services from a list of approved organizations.
 ‘Doesn’t make any sense’
Organizations that provide specialized services for disabled individuals, including medical care, behavioral health, speech and physical therapy, and tailored support services specifically for people with disabilities, are licensed as Medicaid providers. Entities that provide add-on services designed to ease life for people with disabilities or run programs that add value, skills, or independence, but are not specifically for people with disabilities, are considered Medicaid vendors. These include the programs Eric and Nicole attend.
Payments to vendors, who bill through a category called goods and services, have grown significantly in recent years, prompting the state to take a closer look at how the money is being spent. Paid claims for goods and services have increased more than fivefold since 2020, state officials said, from $10.4 million to more than $54.2 million in last year’s budget.
Starting last summer, a growing number of vendors have had payment requests denied by state Medicaid officials, even though the same programs have been paid in the past, multiple operators said. Some were told the rates they charge are too high, while others learned their programs were not inclusive enough, meaning they didn’t have enough members of the broader public participating.
“It just doesn’t make any sense. Like we’re being punished for creating a space where they feel like they have somewhere to belong,” said Jennifer DelQuaglio, a gym teacher who founded Limitless Adaptive Fitness three years ago.
DelQuaglio coordinates group fitness programs for about 100 clients, renting gym space around Central Jersey where they can work out in small groups with individualized instruction — services she said would be impossible at a regular gym. At the end of each session they sit together and share positive affirmations, she said. The program is open to all, but most clients are disabled.
“What we do is so much more than just a fitness class. Like they’re able to build friendships. They gain confidence. They socialize and they look forward to it every week,” DelQuaglio told the New Jersey Monitor. “So much is limited to their family members, their day programs, their caregivers. They need friends just like everyone else needs friends.”
Gwen Orlowski, executive director of Disability Rights New Jersey, said the advocacy organization has heard from multiple people who have lost access to programs after payments were denied. Medicaid members should be informed of these changes in writing so they can challenge the decision, she said, something she said has not happened in at least one case.
“Anytime a Medicaid service is denied or terminated, people are supposed to be able to have due process and have a right to appeal,” she said.
In some cases, vendors have been told by the state that they should instead be operating and billing as licensed Medicaid providers, which are subject to rigorous training, criminal background checks, and other safety protocols that are not required for vendors.
“This is an important concern as we work to ensure the health, safety, and well-being of the individuals we serve,” Hester, the state spokesman, said.
DelQuaglio and others said the shift leaves families with fewer options.
“I feel like these individuals deserve to have a choice,” she said, adding, “And now it’s just being taken away.”
 Financially unsustainable
Randi Meltzer, who has a 10-year-old daughter with autism, said many Medicaid vendors would be happy to undergo background checks and additional safety training. She and her fiance, Marc Caponi, operate Project MAC, a vendor that hosts art, music, and social skills classes for disabled adults and other members of the public. She said they underwent that scrutiny when they first applied to become a provider, only to be told by the state they should be vendors instead.
“I don’t think they should let every Joe Schmo become a vendor. I don’t want to put anyone in a room with someone who isn’t qualified,” Meltzer told the New Jersey Monitor.
Orlowski said programs that are designed specifically for individuals with disabilities should be offered through providers subject to criminal background and other safety checks, as these protocols are important to protecting vulnerable residents. She said operators should not be able to “back-door” through a different billing category that doesn’t include the same protections and allows them to charge more than licensed providers would get paid under Medicaid.
While vendors set their own rates and bill the state or clients directly, Medicaid providers get paid according to a set fee schedule that lags the national average. Meltzer and others said these rates are financially unsustainable for small businesses like theirs.
Jaclyn Hunt of Woodbridge runs ASD Life Coaches, which provides life skills to about 30 adults with disabilities through virtual classes. It’s one thing for the state to “put these vendors out of business, but what gets me is these clients that have been depending on these services are getting left in the dark,” she told the New Jersey Monitor.
After years of being paid by the state for classes that she said have helped hundreds of people, Hunt said she started getting denial letters earlier this fall, leaving at least 20 clients without services. The state told her ASD’s rates were too high. Hunt said she charges $180 for a bundle of services that Medicaid would reimburse at $30.
“They’re lumping my coaching, my hyper-specialized team, with anyone who can throw a sign on their door,” Hunt said.
Suzanne Buchanan, executive director of advocacy organization Autism New Jersey, said they have heard from multiple families and program leaders about “very disruptive” shifts in reimbursements.
For operators running small, individualized programs with multiple, highly trained staff members, the costs are higher than for larger programs where people need less assistance, Buchanan said.
“I think the bigger picture is that it’s very difficult to provide safe opportunities with the current financial constraints,” she said.
Vendors are also frustrated with what they see as a lack of clear guidance from the state. The division held webinars in August and September seeking to clarify billing practices under the goods and services category, but Meltzer, Hunt, and others said they only learned about these after the fact. The first denials came as a surprise.
“They’re not talking to anybody, and these disabled adults in the state of New Jersey are losing programming all day, every day, which means they’re home, they have nowhere to go, they have nothing to do, and it is devastating,” Meltzer said.
While the official policy may not have changed, many attribute the enforcement shift to the Trump administration’s focus on Medicaid fraud and federal funding cuts to the program that could leave more than 300,000 New Jerseyans without insurance and reduce payments to hospitals, doctors and public health by some $6 billion annually in the years to come.
“I think we have to be mindful that what is driving this behind the scenes is probably what’s going on at the federal level,” Orlowski said.
“We don’t want New Jersey to have a clawback of Medicaid money that the federal government thinks was improperly spent on goods and services. That would be disastrous, so we don’t want that. But they still have to give people due process rights,” she said.

name: Maryland Matters
title: Open enrollment for ACA health plans again brings a sharp price hike for Marylanders
description: Thousands of Marylanders face another round of sticker shock while shopping for healthcare, after state officials approved a second year of steep premium increases in response to the expiration of federal tax credits that made those plans more affordable.
text:
Marylanders looking to buy private health insurance have until Dec. 31 to have coverage start in January. Those who miss that deadline have until Jan. 15 to sign up for coverage that starts in February. (Photo by Danielle J. Brown/Maryland Matters)Thousands of Marylanders face another round of sticker shock while shopping for individual healthcare plans after state officials approved a second year of steep premium increases in response to the expiration of federal tax credits that made those plans more affordable.
Marylanders purchasing health plans on the state’s insurance marketplace face an average 14.6% premium rate increase on plans offered by the Maryland Health Connection, on top of the 13.4% rate hike from last year.
Healthcare advocates hope that the incoming Democrat-controlled Congress will reinstate the popular tax credit program or issue a similar relief, but any restoration of that federal assistance could be months away — if it comes at all.
In the meantime, Marylanders have about two months to compare plans and find the one  that works best given their household’s finances. State officials say there are resources available to help families weigh those options.
Johanna Fabian-Marks, executive director for the Maryland Health Benefit Exchange, during a meeting of the Maryland Health Insurance Coverage Protection Commission. (Photo by Danielle J. Brown/Maryland Matters)
“We know getting or renewing health insurance can be confusing,” said Johanna Fabian-Marks, executive director for the Maryland Health Benefit Exchange, which operates Maryland’s insurance marketplace. “We’ve got folks standing by, trained experts who offer free help.”
The 2027 open enrollment period started Nov. 1 and runs through Jan. 15. Those who pick a plan by Dec. 31 will start their plan year on Jan. 1. Those who miss that deadline have until Jan. 15 to select a plan, which will delay the start of healthcare coverage until February.
The Maryland Health Connection, the state’s insurance marketplace part of the Obama-era Affordable Care Act, offers a variety of private health plans, with differing levels of coverage to those who do not get health insurance coverage through an employer. The exchange also offers subsidies that help bring down monthly costs for insurance plans for those who qualify.
As Marylanders shop for coverage, the exchange can provide support over the phone, online or in-person if they need help navigating their options. Through the exchange, Marylanders can connect with insurance brokers to help them at no cost.
“Our navigators are on the ground, in-person community assisters, and they’re hosting pop-up enrollment events around the state. That information is also on our website,” Fabian-Marks said. “In addition, we’re providing virtual enrollment sessions on our website so that people who are looking for help can log into a webinar environment that we’re hosting.”
Thousands of Marylanders downgraded health plans on ACA marketplace amid rising premiums

Those resources and more can help Marylanders with questions they have while selecting insurance for the 2027 plan year, especially those who previously benefited from the enhanced federal tax credits that expired in December 2025 after Congress failed to renew them.
In 2025, state lawmakers approved Maryland Premium Assistance, funding to help replace some of the lost benefits for 2026 plans and 2027 plans that Marylanders are shopping for now.
The exact amount of assistance varies by the financial need of the household. Residents with household incomes of up to 400% of the federal poverty level could qualify for Maryland Premium Assistance, replacing some or all of the savings that would have been available if the federal tax credit did not lapse last year.
Those who make more than 400% of the federal poverty level do not qualify for the state subsidy and face steep premium rate increases approved for next plan year. Many households will opt to pay for more expensive plans in the coming plan year, while others may find those options to be unaffordable and drop coverage entirely.
“We know rates have gone up for a lot of people, and it’s unfortunate … and it’s really sad,” said Vincent DeMarco, president of the Maryland Healthcare for All coalition.
Even with the new state subsidy in place, Fabian-Marks said Marylanders still struggled to afford coverage in the 2026 plan year.
Initially, state officials reported record high enrollment in the 2026 plan year as 255,600 people selected individual health plans at the start of the year, despite expectations that the average 13.4% premium rate increase would lead to a drop in enrollment. But many later had to downgrade their plans in order to afford coverage at all, taking on significantly higher deductibles to maintain less-comprehensive health coverage. So while more people were enrolled in a plan, many opted to take on higher risk coverage for lower monthly premiums.
Vincent DeMarco, president of the Maryland Health Care for All Coalition, during a meeting of the Maryland Health Insurance Coverage Protection Commission. (Photo by Danielle J. Brown/Maryland Matters)
And as the year went on, thousands found even those plans unaffordable for their household finances and dropped coverage.
Fabian-Marks reports that enrollment in August was 12% lower than August last year. Now, about 211,890 Marylanders are covered by health insurance on the exchange. A majority of the enrollment loss is due to new federal restrictions that prohibited certain legally-present non-citizens from accessing federal assistance for low-income households.
The state’s premium assistance program was designed as a temporary mitigation effort, and Maryland’s tight fiscal outlook means that the subsidy will end after next year, unless new funding is found.
It’s why advocates like DeMarco are pushing for state leaders to find new revenue sources to help support the state subsidy. Meanwhile, he hopes that incoming Congressional leaders prioritize restoring those federal tax credits next year, after the midterm elections resulted in Democratic control of the U.S. House of Representatives and Senate.
“When you mess with people’s healthcare, you lose,” DeMarco said. “Many people saw their premiums skyrocket – people thrown off healthcare. They saw a lot of problems caused by H.R.1 and the failure to continue those tax credits … Hopefully that will convince the president and the Republicans in the Senate, who could block things, not to do so.”
The cost of healthcare is hitting America where it hurts: The wallet

Fabian-Marks said Maryland health officials would “certainly be happy to see a restoration of the tax credits,” noting that the exchange would be able to implement those changes quickly after Congress takes action.
“They [enhanced tax credits] really made coverage more affordable and put it in reach for a lot of Marylanders,” she said. “For multiple reasons, from a financial standpoint, for our enrollees and for the state, we would certainly welcome reinstatement of those enhanced tax credits.”
But in the meantime, she notes that despite the rising premium costs in the state, healthcare costs are more affordable in Maryland compared to other states, even if it doesn’t feel like it.
“I know healthcare doesn’t feel affordable, and it is still a financial challenge for a lot of people,” she said. “We are fortunate in Maryland to have the investments the state has made … There are changes coming next year during open enrollment, but this open enrollment is operating as people are used to and it should look familiar.”

title: $323M plan for Omaha’s old auditorium site back on track
description: OMAHA — After months of legal wrangling with city officials, a planned $323 million campus of housing, retail and entertainment venues appears back on track at the former home of Omaha’s storied Civic Auditorium.  The roughly eight acres of prime downtown real estate had been cleared for development a decade ago, and ideas had come […]
text:
Night perspective at Civic Square, former Civic Auditorium in downtown Omaha.  (Courtesy of White Lotus Group and RDG) OMAHA — After months of legal wrangling with city officials, a planned $323 million campus of housing, retail and entertainment venues appears back on track at the former home of Omaha’s storied Civic Auditorium. 
The roughly eight acres of prime downtown real estate had been cleared for development a decade ago, and ideas had come and gone before the city officially sold the land in 2023 to Civic Corner LLC, owned by private developer White Lotus Group.
An apartment structure with street-level commercial and retail space is one component of the planned redevelopment of Omaha Civic Auditorium and arena property in downtown Omaha. (Courtesy of Holland Basham Architects)
The six-phase mixed-use project stalled somewhat in September 2025 after Omaha city officials issued a notice of default and tried to reclaim the property, saying that construction had not progressed according to terms. The developer disagreed and took the matter to court this past January. 
Though the city initially filed counterclaims, it retreated from those efforts with a judge’s stamp of approval in August.
Most recently, on Wednesday, Civic Corner representatives appeared before the Omaha Planning Board  — which voted 6-0 to green-light their request for $34 million in public tax-increment financing to help cover costs. That financing is integral to the project, and the request now heads to the City Council for final approval.
TIF — a legislatively created public financing mechanism aimed at spurring economic development — allows the new property tax revenue on a TIF site to be diverted for up to 20 years to help pay a developer’s eligible project costs. 
Old Shrine Circus days
Planning Board member David Rosacker spoke favorably about the redevelopment plan he called “well-conceived” with elements that “feed on each other.” 
He reflected back to his youthful years going to the auditorium to see the Shrine Circus, though Rosacker also noted the lengthy wait for something to fill the tract historically known for hosting decades of school graduations, concerts, political rallies, sports and other events. White Lotus and the city entered into an initial agreement in late 2021, but the developer has owned the land for three years, having paid the city about $1.4 million for it.
A site plan for the former public auditorium site in downtown Omaha. Civic Corner LLC, tied to private developer White Lotus Group, is called Civic Square and also is nicknamed The Nest, a nod to its proximity and intended attraction to Creighton University Bluejays. (Courtesy of Holland Basham Architects)
Poised to sprout on the four city blocks are about 380 apartments, 30 for-sale condos, 120 hotel rooms, 125,000 square feet of offices and 150,000 square feet of retailers, including a fitness center and a grocery store. The latest plan submitted to the city  estimated creation of 80 new jobs. 
“I’m excited about this whole concept,” Rosacker said.
Board Chair Michael Pate sought answers about the timetable. “Obviously we don’t want that property to be sitting there … and not having much activity on it.”
Pate complimented the overall vision, however, which focuses on drawing young talent and Creighton University Bluejays to the site called Civic Square but also nicknamed “The Nest” by student groups.
“We hope you succeed,” said Pate. “It’s a good project.” 
The developer’s tax-increment financing request has also been endorsed by a city TIF committee and the Planning Department staff, though an exchange between Pate and Deputy City Attorney Jennifer Taylor showed that not all is resolved in the legal battle with the city.
Arun Agarwal, founder and CEO of developer White Lotus Group. (Courtesy of White Lotus Group)
Pate, noting that a TIF review committee last September had denied the same TIF request, wanted to know: “What changed?” 
Taylor said the default notice was at play in last year’s denial. The city has since withdrawn that, she said, removing a cloud on the title and allowing the developer to proceed “as they see fit.” She told board members that litigation remains ongoing between the city and developer and she was limited on what she could say. She declined to talk about the project to the Examiner, citing the litigation.
Civic Corner attorney George Achola said that as the case stands now, the only “viable claims” yet to be decided are damages the city owes to the developer.
‘Don’t take that lightly’
White Lotus founder Arun Agarwal told the board that he recognizes the site’s importance to the urban core of the state’s most populated city, adding: “We don’t take that lightly.”
His company also served as lead developer for the recently completed first phase of Lincoln’s transformation of the former Pershing Center auditorium site into a mixed-use community hub.
Battle fires up over future of Omaha’s old Civic Auditorium site

On the more wide-ranging and costly Omaha redevelopment, Agarwal said his team intends to “restart” infrastructure work next spring or summer and afterward would “go vertical” with first-phase buildings. 
Agarwal said his team is substantially invested and it is in the developer’s best interest to get moving. The first phase on the southeast quadrant is 120 apartments, some to be offered at rents targeting low- to moderate-income tenants and others at market rates in a mixed-use building as high as five stories. Street-level retail and commercial space would help activate the area.
The plan, which the developer said has evolved, anticipates completion of all phases in about 2032. What previously was said to be a $200 million-plus initiative now carries a projected cost of $323 million, according to the latest city documents. 
“This is, in our opinion, the highest and best use for the site,” said Agarwal, noting an eventual addition to property tax rolls. The estimated value is projected at nearly $210 million. 
Agarwal declined to discuss legal proceedings; however, his “highest and best use” remark was an apparent reference to an alternate proposal he said the city was entertaining from a tax-exempt nonprofit. 
Fitness club angle at Civic Square project site. (Courtesy of White Lotus Group and RDG)
Court records revealed more details about the alleged behind-the-scenes dealings that involved the highest offices of city government. In one 56-page filing, Civic Corner lawyers argued that the record “establishes that the city was privately courting a substitute developer — one whose designs and renderings had progressed well beyond the concept stage …”
The developer’s legal team compared the scenario to that of a marriage where one of the partners (in this case the city) was “enticed” by a suitor with a tempting package (in this case an indoor athletic complex) and sought a way out of its existing, contractual relationship. 
“This case is about which party kept the promises it made at the altar, and which party spent (time) planning and looking for grounds to walk away,” wrote the lawyers.
‘Pumped’ to restart
Then-Mayor Jean Stothert brought up the mystery competitor during a mayoral debate in April 2025 where she publicly expressed concern over White Lotus’ progress at the former public auditorium site. She stated that a different developer was interested in taking over the property. She didn’t name the other, but Civic Corner in later court filings identified the competing project as one initiated by Omaha Public Schools and supported by Sherwood Foundation.
Civic Square site in September 2025 when city officials were issuing a notice of default against the developer, contending construction had not progressed accordingly. The city has since withdrawn that notice. The public auditorium stood on the land for six decades before demolition in 2016-17. (Cindy Gonzalez/Nebraska Examiner)
John Ewing Jr. won the election and was mayor at the time the now-withdrawn notice of default was issued against the developer. Civic Corner lawyers argued that the default complaint was based on a “windshield inspection” and that the city’s deputy chief of staff involved in the process had not reviewed key work permits and did not know the city’s public works engineer assigned to the project.
“That confirms in the most  concrete way possible, the absence of any operational or engineering diligence behind the default decision,” wrote the developer’s Achola-led legal team.
The developer and the city operated under a shared understanding that TIF would be the anchoring financing mechanism for the project. Civic Corner submitted its initial TIF application in July 2025, and a city committee that reviews requests delayed action.
On Sept. 8, 2025, the City Legal Department issued the notices of default and right to repurchase based on what it said was the developer’s failure to meet construction deadlines. About 10 days later, the TIF committee voted to recommend denial based on a dispute of ownership. 
That’s when the developer, in a move it said was to protect its investment, filed the lawsuit arguing that the city interfered with the developer’s ability to perform and violated the “implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing.”
Agarwal told the Examiner he was excited for what’s ahead at Civic Square.
He sees growth in surrounding downtown areas — such as the Builders District, Millworks Commons and the year-round public market planned near The Riverfront — as a plus for the redeveloped auditorium site. 
“We’re pumped to be able to restart, so to speak,” said Agarwal. 
Bird’s eye view of proposed redevelopment of the former Omaha civic auditorium site near 19th and Capitol Streets in downtown Omaha. A plan by Civic Corner LLC, a limited liability company of private developer White Lotus Group, calls for a mixed-use campus. The project site is called Civic Square and Creighton University Bluejay students have nicknamed it “The Nest,” a nod to its proximity and intended draw for area students. (Courtesy of Holland Basham Architects)

name: Idaho Capital Sun
title: The nation saw a blue wave this election. Idaho saw a ripple.
description: In Idaho, a Republican stronghold, the closest Democrat in this year’s election to securing a seat in Congress or statewide office was 11 points behind. The candidate, Ellie Gilbreath, was trying to stop Republican U.S. Rep. Mike Simpson’s bid for reelection to a 15th term. Across the country last week, Democrats secured control of both […]
text:
Voters cast their ballots in the general election on Nov. 3, 2026, at the Calvary Baptist Church in Boise. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun)In Idaho, a Republican stronghold, the closest Democrat in this year’s election to securing a seat in Congress or statewide office was 11 points behind.
The candidate, Ellie Gilbreath, was trying to stop Republican U.S. Rep. Mike Simpson’s bid for reelection to a 15th term.
Across the country last week, Democrats secured control of both chambers of Congress, won governorships in most states and made headway in state legislatures. 
Amid national blue wave, Idaho Democrats gain six legislative seats — flipping competitive districts

But by the time the national blue wave — or tsunami, as some are calling it — hit Idaho, the tide had turned it into a ripple.
Idaho Democrats made modest gains. They swept full control of three legislative districts, gaining six more legislative seats, a shift that does little to chip away at Republicans’ supermajority control of the Legislature. 
And a closer look at election results shows that across the board, Democrats captured slightly more votes against Republican incumbents in statewide office and congress, who easily won reelection. But in all of those races, Democratic victory was still far off. No Democrat has won a statewide office in the state since 2002, and the last Democratic congressman in Idaho served in 2010.
If Democrats want to upset decades of Idaho political history by winning a top of the ticket race, they have a long way to go.
On average, Democrats gained 6 points of the vote share in federal and state races compared to the last time those offices were up for election. Still, Idaho Democrats this year were an average of 27 points behind Republicans, according to an analysis of election results by the Idaho Capital Sun. 
Boise State University political scientist Jaclyn Kettler wasn’t surprised that the blue wave didn’t carry Democrats through in Idaho.
“Idaho is a solidly Republican state. We don’t tend to see too many competitive races” in the general election for statewide races, she said in an interview. “ … It’s just solid enough Republican that it’s hard for even a blue wave in other areas of the country to have too much influence, especially for those statewide races.”
The Idaho Democratic Party also boasted another gain: Democrats got more of the vote in 67 legislative races than they did in 2024.
This year’s election results are unofficial until they are certified by the State Board of Canvassers, which meets Nov. 24.
 Idaho Democratic Party leader says the state saw a blue wave. Republican leader says state fended it off.

Idaho Democratic Party Chair Lauren Necochea said the state did indeed see a blue wave.
In this file photo, then-Assistant House Minority Leader Rep. Lauren Necochea, D- Boise, at the State Capitol building on Jan. 8, 2024. (Otto Kitsinger for Idaho Capital Sun)
“We’re a red state, where it looks different,” she said, adding that many conservatives had moved into the state in recent years.
Democrats, she said, reached out to many voters and it shows. 
“We were able to be specific about what we wanted to do as we campaigned. And I think voters are getting tired of the culture war rhetoric that Republicans rely on, and they’re looking for more common sense solutions to their everyday challenges. That’s where we were. We met voters where they were,” Necochea said.
Idaho Republican Party chairwoman Dorothy Moon gives a speech on Jan. 12, 2026, at the State Capitol Building in Boise. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun)
Idaho Republican Party Chairwoman Dorothy Moon said she saw minimal signs of the blue wave in Idaho. Turnout in some Democratic leaning parts of the state, she said, was up. But Republicans in higher office were reelected, and voters rejected Proposition 1, a ballot initiative that would’ve repealed the state’s near-total abortion ban, by a nearly 56% no vote. 
“I think we had a great night,” Moon said. “We fended off the blue wave.”
And she noted that Republicans maintained control of a North Idaho legislative district, District 6 that includes Moscow. Democrats ran for every legislative seat there.
Necochea said high Republican turnout for Prop 1 was a problem for Democrats. 
“Our hypothesis is that conservative churches galvanized conservative voters to go to the polls to vote against Prop 1,” Necochea said. “And absent Prop 1, there would not have been as much money and there wouldn’t have been electioneering from the pulpit driving voters to the polls.”
State data on who turned out to vote this year isn’t available yet. Nearly 99% of voters who cast ballots voted on the ballot initiative, state data shows.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
 How did Democrats perform in Idaho elections this year? 

Ellie Gilbreath (Photo courtesy of Ellie Gilbreath)
The closest a Democrat got in Idaho to unseating a Republican was in the race against incumbent Simpson, a longtime congressman. Gilbreath, a Democrat, was only about 11 points behind Simpson, with 40.3% of the vote compared to his 51.7%. She outperformed Simpson’s last two Democratic challengers. (Two independents and a libertarian took 8% of the vote in the race this year.)
Necochea said that Gilbreath ran a “fantastic campaign focused on issues that Idaho voters care about: Making life affordable, protecting public lands, personal liberties.”
And, she said, Gilbreath ran in a congressional district that didn’t see as many conservatives moving in than the state’s other congressional district. 
“I think we have in her district more longtime Idahoans who lean conservative perhaps but are looking for common sense and common ground, and are willing to consider voting for a Democrat,” Necochea said. 
Gilbreath couldn’t be immediately reached for comment. 
In the race for the state’s attorney general, Democrat Lori Hickman had the smallest gains compared to recent Democratic challengers for the office. She picked up about 2.8 more points than the last Democratic challenger in 2022, Tom Arkoosh. 
And even though GOP incumbent Raúl Labrador had a commanding lead, the gap between him and Hickman, of 19.7 points, was smaller than many other challenges. But Hickman still outperformed Democratic challengers in the race for that office for the past three election cycles, back to 2014, eight years before Labrador was elected.
In some races, Democrats this year didn’t even have the best performance that Democratic candidates have put up in runs for that office in recent years. 
Democratic gubernatorial candidate Terri Pickens speaks to a crowd at Boise’s third No Kings protest on Saturday, March 28, 2026. (Kyle Pfannenstiel/Idaho Capital Sun)
In the governor’s race, Democrat Terri Pickens had the biggest swing — gaining 12 points against incumbent Republican Gov. Brad Little compared to 2022 Democratic challenger Stephen Heidt. But Pickens performance, with 32% of the vote, was still behind Democrat Paulette Jordan’s 2018 run against Little when the seat was open. Jordan got 38% of the vote. 
In the race for Idaho’s first congressional district, Democratic challenger Kaylee Peterson performed about 3 points better than in her last run against incumbent Republican Rep. Russ Fulcher in 2024, and more than 2 points better than her first run against him in 2022. But she faced the biggest point gap: She was 35.5 points behind Fulcher. Peterson clinching nearly 28.8% of the vote this year was still shy of Democrat Christina McNeil’s 2018 run against Fulcher, where she got 30.8% of the vote.
In Idaho’s U.S. Senate race this year, the Democrat, David Roth, dropped out after pressure from supporters of independent candidate Todd Achilles; leaders of Ada County Democrats also asked Roth to withdraw. Achilles, a former Democratic state legislator, only performed slightly better than the last Democrat to challenge Risch in 2020, Jordan, who had also ran for governor. 
Achilles received about 33.5% of the vote, compared to Jordan’s 33.2%. In 2014, Democratic U.S. Senate challenger Nels Mitchell got more of the vote, 34.7%. 
Independent candidate for U.S. Senate Todd Achilles speaks with supporters at an election night watch party on Nov. 3, 2026, at Iconic Bistro and Bar in Garden City. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun)
Two Democratic candidates whose campaigns raised $0 — secretary of state hopeful Shawn Keenan, and state treasurer challenger Kevin A. Jones — outperformed the last Democratic run for those offices. (Keenan ran against Republican Phil McGrane in 2022, when the office had no incumbent.) 
“It tells me that even when voters weren’t sure about the details of the person on the ballot,” Necochea said, “and let’s face it, we sometimes have a four-page ballot, and you don’t always research every single candidate. Most people don’t have time to do that, but they were using that Democratic label as a clue that that was someone who wasn’t part of the Republican grift machine, was someone who’s going to be looking out for regular Idahoans, and so they used that clue to vote for them.”
Moon, head of the Idaho Republican Party, doesn’t see the state becoming politically competitive anytime soon.
“We’re gonna work very hard to maintain our Republican base, increase the numbers, broaden our base as well, and make sure the issues that are important to everybody here in Idaho, that we keep Idaho Idaho and keep it conservative,” she said.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Commentary: Ayoub: Now comes the governing part
description: Last week’s national “blue wave” stayed mostly off on Nebraska’s reliably red shores. The changing tide, however, moved closer.  That was not only evident in Democrat Denise Powell’s victory in the 2nd Congressional District, the state’s “Blue Dot,” but also in the vote totals of three closely watched races: for governor, U.S. senator and 1st […]
text:
The final day of the 2024 session of the Nebraska Legislature. (Paul Hammel/Nebraska Examiner)Last week’s national “blue wave” stayed mostly off on Nebraska’s reliably red shores. The changing tide, however, moved closer. 
That was not only evident in Democrat Denise Powell’s victory in the 2nd Congressional District, the state’s “Blue Dot,” but also in the vote totals of three closely watched races: for governor, U.S. senator and 1st Congressional District representative. Each winner did so with less than 51% of the vote as of this writing. 
In the 2022 governor’s race, the winning percentage was 59; in the U.S. Senate races in 2024, one of which was a special election, the percentages were 53 and 62; and in the Ist District election in 2024 the percentage was 60.
Change is afoot elsewhere. The NINO (nonpartisan in name only) Nebraska Legislature will no longer sport 33 GOP senators, a political cudgel supermajority and enough to end a filibuster. GOP senators will now number 30 (that’s likely but unofficial at this time), enough votes if everyone toes the party line to change the body’s rules or override a veto, the latter perhaps moot because the state’s corner office has a very red door.
Draw your own conclusions about what last week’s results mean for Nebraska, but across the country, voters clearly had change on their minds. I’m not smart enough to know for sure what the exact takeaways were. My best guess is that what American voters (including some Nebraskans) told exit pollsters was what most reasonable Americans already knew. 
Governing poorly has consequences.
People are tired of high prices, an incomprehensible war and bewildering tariffs. They have had enough of Congress capitulating to the White House. While they want immigration problems solved, they are not here for the administration’s policy of cruelty and violence. They reject taking food and medical assistance from the working poor. They do not believe some of us are more equal than others, and so have grown weary of the undermining or erasing of policies that promote diversity. They want our history, all of it, to be taught exactly as it happened, not rewritten to assuage the uninformed and the iconoclastic. They want AI-peddling, ring-kissing, data-center-building tech bros to stay in their lane and out of voters’ backyards. Finally, and most emphatically, they want the corruption to end.
Winning elections is the easy part; governing is the hard part. The winds of change may be softer in Nebraska than the gales blowing in Texas, Kansas and Iowa. Still, how a new Nebraska Legislature reads the prevailing breeze will be key to its success as it faces a variety of issues, including the daunting task of making a state budget add up with current and forecasted deficits. 
How a new, blue Congress navigates the next two years with a lame-duck GOP president whose policies took a serious beating at the ballot box will require a steely but deft hand. As we said above, voters want affordability, an end to wars and tariffs, and a return to food programs and healthcare options. And maybe throw a little agency into their own lives.
Some have already counseled that any investigations should wait until affordability issues are addressed. Maybe, but part of Congress’ responsibility is oversight, which it derives from Article I in the Constitution, the necessary and proper clause. Plus, Congress can’t multitask? Really? One senator scoffed at the notion of having to choose, reminding us that they can indeed “walk and chew gum at the same time.”  
Finally, especially given the change that is afoot even here in Nebraska, I offer a modest proposal with apologies to Jonathan Swift. Every elected official has a team of advisers (or at least should), those who gather information, read the tea leaves and offer opinions on policy, legislation, public relations and the aforementioned wafting political winds. 
The wise among these leaders should always have a “devil’s advocate” among their most trusted inner circle, someone who says no to groupthink, who reminds decision-makers of the consequences — especially the unintended ones — of a new idea that might become law, who tells not just the other side of the story, but even promotes it. 
Here’s why: The headline is the blue wave, and, as in any election, we had winners and losers. But unlike football, a footrace or fiddling contest, where there are winners and losers, whoever prevails at the ballot box doesn’t get a trophy or a medal or even a record contract.
They get a job … the description of which includes representing the hopes and dreams not simply for those who voted for them, but also those who voted against them and even those who didn’t vote.

name: Oklahoma Voice
title: Oklahoma tribal town town sues Kalshi amid prediction market contract dispute
description: OKLAHOMA CITY — A small Oklahoma tribe is suing one of the nation’s largest prediction market companies in an effort to invalidate a business agreement that they claim was not authorized by its governing committee. The Alabama-Quassarte Tribal Town and Samuel Marshall Jr., who claims he is the rightful chief of the tribe of about […]
text:
The Alabama-Quassarte Tribal Town's flag flies Oct. 27, 2026 at the Indian Flag Plaza outside the state Capitol in Oklahoma City. (Photo by Emma Murphy/Oklahoma Voice)OKLAHOMA CITY — A small Oklahoma tribe is suing one of the nation’s largest prediction market companies in an effort to invalidate a business agreement that they claim was not authorized by its governing committee.
The Alabama-Quassarte Tribal Town and Samuel Marshall Jr., who claims he is the rightful chief of the tribe of about 400, sued Kalshi, its CEO Tarek Mansour, Wilson Yargee, and Michael Stopp to block a potentially lucrative agreement that allows the tribe to develop and operate a prediction market app, known as PokkeTrades. Prediction markets allow people to wager on pretty much everything from the outcome of sporting events to political races to the weather.
The lawsuit asks a tribal judge to declare that the Alabama-Quassarte Tribal Town is not bound to any agreement for PokkeTrades and that Yargee, who claims he’s the legitimate chief, and his administration have no authority to authorize it. 
The tribe and Marshall wrote in its lawsuit filed in Muscogee (Creek) Nation District Court that Yargee and Stopp did not have permission from the Alabama-Quassarte Tribal Town’s governing committee to enter into the agreement with Kalshi. 
The lawsuit alleges Marshall is the legitimate chief, not Yargee. Yargee was removed from office in 2021 and has been falsely representing himself as the chief of the tribal town based about 90 miles southeast of Oklahoma City in Wetumka, the lawsuit alleges.
Oklahoma tribal leadership fight puts Kalshi’s prediction markets at center of dispute

It also alleges that the tribe’s governing body never ratified the agreement Yargee entered into with Kalshi, making it invalid.
Yargee’s agreement with Kalshi has forced Marshall and town officials to spend time and money correcting the record, disrupted business relationships, “damaged its commercial goodwill” and created confusion about town leadership, according to the complaint. The tribe is seeking a temporary restraining order, compensation for damages and correction of Yargee’s claims, among other requests. 
The tribe’s lawsuit also draws on an 1825 law from the Creek Nation that prohibited “bad talk” against the chief. Marshall requests that the court recognize this as a “civil Bad Talk claim” against the defendants who misrepresented their roles, therefore injuring the Alabama-Quassarte Tribal Town and chief. 
The Alabama Quassarte Tribal Town’s enrolled members hold dual citizenship at the Muscogee (Creek) Nation. The tribe was one of several tribal towns part of what was previously known as the Muscogee Nation Confederacy. 
Yargee though claims he is the rightful chief of the tribe. He previously told Oklahoma Voice that as chief, he had the right to enter into the agreement. 
Tribal election results were not immediately publicly available, but both Marshall and Yargee claim to have won reelection in 2025, and the Bureau of Indian Affairs lists both men as chief.
Kalshi, who promoted the gaming partnership with the tribe last month as one of its first partnerships with Native American tribes, stands by its agreement, said Jacki McGavick, a Kalshi spokesperson, on behalf of the company and Mansour.
She said the tribe’s governing council signed off on the agreement.
Prediction markets ‘undermine’ Oklahoma tribal gaming compacts, association says

Stopp, a citizen of the Cherokee Nation who serves as Yargee’s vice president of economic development, said in a statement on behalf of himself and Yargee that this is just the latest lawsuit filed by Marshall’s administration. 
Stopp said he and Yargee expect the court to dismiss the case as it has dismissed previous cases brought by Marshall’s administration. 
A previous lawsuit filed in this court between Marshall and Yargee over rightful leadership was dismissed over a lack of jurisdiction because both parties failed to waive their right to sovereign immunity, which protects recognized tribes from federal, state and tribal lawsuits without their explicit consent. Marshall has waived his and the town’s sovereign immunity for this lawsuit. 
“It would be helpful for a court competent jurisdiction to stop the Marshall faction from continuing to make these claims,” Stopp said. 
He said that if the court doesn’t immediately throw out the case, they will reevaluate their legal strategy which could include a waiver of sovereign immunity.

title: Commentary: Only ripples from the blue wave reached Oklahoma, but the GOP should acknowledge the erosion
description: Before the dust even had a chance to settle in last week’s elections, Republican House Speaker Kyle Hilbert proclaimed the results “demonstrate that Oklahomans continue to believe in the conservative principles, priorities and leadership that have helped move our state forward.” Republicans may have emerged maintaining control of all statewide and federal of[...]
text:
Voters fill out ballots for the midterm election at the Millwood Field House on Nov. 3, 2026, in Oklahoma City. (Photo by Emma Murphy/Oklahoma Voice)Before the dust even had a chance to settle in last week’s elections, Republican House Speaker Kyle Hilbert proclaimed the results “demonstrate that Oklahomans continue to believe in the conservative principles, priorities and leadership that have helped move our state forward.”
Republicans may have emerged maintaining control of all statewide and federal offices and commanding supermajorities in the Legislature, but voters didn’t actually signal that they embrace the GOP’s “conservative principles, priorities and leadership.”
In fact, I think they did the opposite. If Republicans are too shortsighted to recognize the as-yet small speck on the horizon is actually a freight train of doom hurdling toward, then they’re going to be in big trouble over the next decade.
The 2026 elections should be construed as a warning shot across the bow for the GOP. A prudent leader would consider it a sign that it’s time for the party to take some time to rethink whether its  “priorities” and “conservative principles” actually align with what voters want and need.
Here’s why:

Five Republican state House incumbents lost to Democrats on election night. Typically Democrats don’t even win contests for seats in both chambers that the incumbent is vacating. For five incumbent Republicans to be unseated by Democrats is unusual and a red flag that the tide is beginning to shift.
The state’s most populous counties — Tulsa and Oklahoma — turned blue Tuesday night. Those counties also said “no thanks” to some of their current Republican state lawmakers. Oklahoma County residents actually elected a Democratic slate of candidates and booted their longtime Republican county assessor from office. A political expert once told me that shifts in voting patterns in Oklahomans living in urban and suburban areas are typically harbingers of broader political change in the state. When those areas change from blue to red or red to blue, the rest of the state slowly follows.  
Republicans almost lost control of two seats in the U.S. House. Democrat Jena Nelson fell only about 3,300 votes short of upsetting Republican U.S. Rep. Stephanie Bice in Oklahoma’s 5th Congressional District, which includes parts of Canadian, Oklahoma, Logan, Lincoln, Pottawatomie, and Seminole counties. For context, the contest drew over 264,500 voters. Bice barely won despite the GOP-controlled Legislature’s previous efforts to gerrymander the district to guarantee Republican victories. In the 1st Congressional District, Republican Mark Tedford managed to win by only about 10,700 votes in an area that represents Tulsa, Creek, Rogers and Wagoner counties.
Voters again squashed legislators’ state questions. For the third time in as many months, Oklahoma voters rejected the “conservative principles” that state lawmakers claimed that their supporters espoused. It turns out that Oklahomans don’t want Republicans to be able to put their fingers on the scale when it comes to judicial selections or want state officials to muck around with property taxes — the primary local revenue stream that schools, counties and municipalities rely on to keep the lights on. And interestingly, those “conservative principles” that legislators were convinced Oklahomans wanted didn’t just lose by a little. Voters destroyed them. The effort to rig the judicial selection process lost by 480,000 votes. A question that would have reduced how much property taxes could grow lost by over 91,000 votes. Lawmakers would be wise to keep that in mind when Republican Governor-elect Mike Mazzei starts putting pressure on them to eliminate property taxes for some Oklahomans, and the next time they’re tempted to put issues on the ballot. Voters are proving to be increasingly skeptical of legislative ballot measures.
Texas. Voters living in what has long been considered a Republican stronghold, elected a slate of Democrats to legislative, statewide, and even the U.S. Senate. It was part of a partisan shift that occurred across the country states that have long been red.  

In short, any prudent Republican should view last Tuesday as a sign that when the GOP plows ahead with these so-called “conservative principles” the loss of five legislative seats may likely be only the beginning.
Oklahomans are sick and tired of being among the worst in the nation for public education outcomes, healthcare, incarceration rates and pretty much everything else that impacts people’s quality of life. They’re sick of politically connected people getting special treatment. They’re sick of officials diverting public money to pay for private education while watching their local schools subsiding on scraps. They’re sick of lawmakers putting measures on the ballot in an attempt to change things voters have already put in the state Constitution. 
And they’re exhausted by the continuing increase in prices of everything from their insurance to a tank of gas to nearly everything on their grocery list.
They want our state and federal leaders to focus on what actually matters. They want them to espouse the now ancient Republican value of local government control, which means to stop screwing around with revenue streams that run the level of government we all see close.
They want smaller class sizes and better public schools.
They want this to be a state where college graduates want to remain five years after graduating. Right now, an increasing number are fleeing for greener pastures, which is not a good sign.
To do that will mean making financial investments, not cutting taxes.
Because it will cost money to keep hospitals open, fix our roads and bridges, retain quality teachers and cut class sizes. 
They’ll need to respect voters who voted to expand Medicaid. 
And they’ll have to prove that they listen to the voters that put them there instead of the lobbyists funding their campaigns or an out-of-touch future governor who casually spent almost $13 million of his own money on the election like it was nothing while most people are struggling in this economy. 
There is time to divert that freight train of doom, but to do that Republicans have to look a little bit deeper than the fact they again won all statewide offices Tuesday night. And they’ll have to move away from their hero-like worship of President Donald Trump, stop being his backup band the Trumpettes and think about what our state really needs.
If Republicans can’t do that, in two years, their legislative losses are going to be more than five seats. In four years, it could cost them even more: congressional or statewide offices (Remember: Bice initially ran for a congress in a district that a Democrat won in 2018.).
Oklahoma voters are tired of losing. They want to be winners just like the GOP candidates were last week.
And if things aren’t getting better in two or four years, they will have no choice but to blame those so-called Republican “conservative principles” and the officials who purport to espouse them.

title: Idaho Legislature’s budget committee meets in Moscow, Lewiston this week
description: Members of the Idaho Legislature’s joint budget committee are meeting in Moscow and Lewiston for three days this week as they gear up for the 2027 legislative session.  Although the Idaho Legislature is not in session, the Joint FInance-Appropriations Committee, or JFAC, normally conducts a spring and fall tour at locations around the state during […]
text:
The door to the Idaho Legislature's Joint Finance-Appropriations Committee room at the Idaho State Capitol building is pictured on Jan. 6, 2023. (File photo by Otto Kitsinger for the Idaho Capital Sun)Members of the Idaho Legislature’s joint budget committee are meeting in Moscow and Lewiston for three days this week as they gear up for the 2027 legislative session. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Although the Idaho Legislature is not in session, the Joint FInance-Appropriations Committee, or JFAC, normally conducts a spring and fall tour at locations around the state during the legislative off season.
JFAC is a powerful legislative committee made up of 10 members each from the Idaho House of Representatives and Idaho Senate. Each year, the committee is responsible for setting every budget for every state agency and department. 
Last year, JFAC and Gov. Brad Little enacted budget cuts for almost all state agencies and departments. Other than K-12 public schools, most state agency budgets were cut by 4% in the fiscal year 2026 budget and 5% in the fiscal year 2027 budget. 
JFAC will begin working on the new fiscal year 2028 budget in January.
As preparation for the work that will come during the regular legislative session, JFAC members will participate in budget briefings, audit updates and working tours to inspect state facilities during this week’s meetings.
Deep dives on the Idaho Department of Health and Welfare budget request, the wildfire season and fire suppression costs, a briefing on new state correctional facilities and tours of the Port of Lewiston, Lewis-Clark State College and University of Idaho are planned throughout the week.
“The Joint Finance-Appropriations Committee is pretty much working year round because government is a year-round process and funding government and making sure it is funded appropriately demands a lot of time from the committee,” said Sen. Scott Grow, a Republican from Eagle who serves as co-chair of JFAC.

CONTACT US



This week’s meetings will not be livestreamed online, said Keith Bybee, the Idaho Legislative Services Office’s budget and policy analysis manager. That means the only option to follow the committee is to attend in person. 
JFAC’s first meeting of the week begins Tuesday at 3 p.m. Pacific Time Tuesday in the Idaho-Palouse Room at the Best Western University Inn, 1516 Pullman Road in Moscow (the full agenda and schedule is embedded at the bottom of this article).
Wednesday’s meeting begins at 8 a.m. Pacific Time inside the student union building on the University of Idaho’s Moscow campus.
JFAC will move to Lewiston on Thursday, starting at 8:30 a.m. Pacific Time at Independent School District No. 1 in Lewiston before moving on to the Idaho State Veterans Home, 821 21st Ave., in Lewiston. 
Grow said the working tours of state facilities, public schools, colleges and universities give legislative budget writers a chance to see first hand how government funding is put to use. 
“That gIves us opportunities to visit certain sites that are of interest in an effort to see how the appropriations have been utilized and to assure us that the money that was appropriated went for good and appropriate purposes in accordance with state law,” he said. 
 JFAC will have new members during 2027 Idaho legislative session

There will be changes coming to JFAC for the 2027 legislative session. Five of the 20 members of JFAC who served during the 2026 legislative session will not be returning in 2027, either because they retired, they lost their primary election in May or they lost in November’s general election. 
The JFAC members who will not return in 2027 include Sens. Jim Woodward, R-Sagle; Glenneda Zuiderveld, R-Twin Falls; Cody Galloway, R-Boise; Rep. Steven Miller, R-Fairfield and Rep. Dustin Manwaring, R-Pocatello. 
Grow said Republican legislative leaders will appoint new members to JFAC during the Idaho Legislature’s organizational session, which begins Dec. 3.
After that the 2027 regular session of the Idaho Legislature begins Jan. 11.

title: The first Wyoming Boys’ School trial starts today. Follow along with our coverage.
description:
The trial concerns the case of Blaise Chivers-King, one of six former boys’ school residents who accused school staff of physical and psychological abuse. Another former resident’s claims of improper isolation will go to trial at the end of the month.
The post The first Wyoming Boys’ School trial starts today. Follow along with our coverage. appeared first o[...]
text:
Do you have questions about this story? Or information to share? Reach out to Maya Shimizu Harris at maya@wyofile.com.
After more than two years of litigation, the first trial concerning alleged abuse at the Wyoming Boys’ School begins today. 
This trial concerns the case of Blaise Chivers-King, who is one of six former boys’ school residents who lodged complaints against the facility in 2024, accusing staff of physical and psychological abuse. The school, which detains delinquent boys ages 12 to 21, is a 38-acre residential facility near Worland that’s overseen by the Wyoming Department of Family Services. 
Chivers-King, who served two stints of roughly 11 months each at the Boys’ School between the ages of 15 and 17, alleged Wyoming Boys’ School staff violated his 14th Amendment rights by placing him in isolation, using excessive force and infringing on due process. U.S. District Judge Scott Skavdahl ruled in October that some, but not all of his claims, could go to trial.
The defendants, which include the Wyoming Boys’ School, the Wyoming Department of Family Services and individual boys’ school staff members, argued that “every instance of claimed ‘isolation’ served a legitimate purpose and was not excessive in relation to that purpose.” Staff who placed Chivers-King in isolation assert they should be protected by qualified immunity — a type of legal immunity that protects government officials from lawsuits under some circumstances.
Skavdahl disagreed, pointing to evidence that some uses of isolation “were, or became, simply punishment or unrelated to management of a safety threat.” He emphasized how staff placed Chivers-King “in isolation for predetermined amounts of time, which is at least arguably unrelated to the legitimate purpose of managing a child who is physically violent or attempting suicide.” That Chivers-King remained in isolation even after he changed his behavior, Skavdahl noted, could raise questions for a jury about its use for a legitimate purpose. 
Last month, Skavdahl denied the defendants’ request to bar the term “solitary confinement” during trial, though he said he would “listen carefully” to ensure the term isn’t used to “inflame the jury.” 
The defendants will also be required to bring physical examples of items related to former resident Blaise Chivers-King’s claims of excessive force and isolation, including a “spit mask,” mechanical restraints and riot gear, as well as a mattress and magnets used in the school’s detention rooms.
Skavdahl ruled Wednesday that some of the claims of improper isolation by another former resident, Dylan Tolar, can go to trial. While Tolar alleged four boys’ school staff members violated his 14th Amendment rights by putting him in isolation, the claims against just two of those staffers — Elsa Olson and John Schwalbe — will go to trial. Although Olson and Schwalbe never placed Tolar on detention status, which is the facility’s “most restrictive disciplinary status,” “whether conditions constitute impermissible isolation is based on facts, not a facility’s (or an expert’s) labels,” Skavdahl wrote in his order. 
The judge wrote that “a rational jury could conclude Olson and Schwalbe impermissibility placed Mr. Tolar in punitive isolation” because that isolation was similar to what’s described in other juvenile isolation cases: “a long stretch of time in which a child is not allowed out of his room and may be restricted in other ways as to entertainment, exercise, and the like.” 
Tolar’s trial is scheduled to start Nov. 30. 
I’ll be at the U.S. District Court of Wyoming in Casper this week keeping you up to date on what’s happening with the Chivers-King trial. You can follow my coverage here at WyoFile.
