name: Georgia Recorder
title: Democrats take control of Georgia’s powerful utility regulator
description: This coverage is made possible through a partnership between WABE and Grist, a nonprofit environmental media organization. Beginning in January, three of the five officials on the Georgia Public Service Commission will be Democrats. It will be the first time the party has controlled the powerful energy regulation board in 30 years.  The commission, which […]
text:
Peter Hubbard, Democratic member of the Public Service Commission, joined Atlanta's former mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms, the Democratic candidate for Governor, at a press conference in downtown Marietta on Sept. 14, 2026. Alander Rocha/Georgia RecorderThis coverage is made possible through a partnership between WABE and Grist, a nonprofit environmental media organization.
Beginning in January, three of the five officials on the Georgia Public Service Commission will be Democrats. It will be the first time the party has controlled the powerful energy regulation board in 30 years. 
The commission, which regulates utilities including the state’s largest electric provider, Georgia Power, has come under more scrutiny in recent years due to rising power bills and the high energy demands of data centers. 
On Tuesday, Peter Hubbard was re-elected to his seat and Shelia Edwards won her race for an open seat. The third Democrat, Alicia Johnson, was not up for election this year. Georgia PSC commissioners serve six-year terms.  
Now, Democrats say they plan to focus on affordability, clean energy and closer scrutiny of Georgia Power. 
“There’s a long laundry list of things that need to be looked into,” Hubbard said. “We’ll have to triage, in fact, and decide how best to move forward.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
One of his first priorities will be launching an affordability docket, he said — a series of hearings that would delve into the reasons for high power bills and ways to save customers money. Hubbard said he and his fellow Democrats also plan to bring close scrutiny to upcoming Georgia Power requests around making more energy and adjusting customer rates. 
But any changes, especially to power bills, will likely take time. 
“We may not be able to expect immediate effects on our wallets,” said Emory University associate professor Kristin Phillips, who studies energy burden and the PSC. “But I think we can expect immediate change in the types of decisions that are made.”
Affordability and high energy bills were driving issues in the campaigns both this year and last year, the two elections that together resulted in the new Democratic majority on the commission.
“We knew that we had to connect the dots between energy and affordability,” Brionté McCorkle of Georgia Conservation Voters said during a media briefing after the election. Her group campaigned for the Democratic candidates and worked to draw attention to the PSC elections. “It’s not just this obscure regulatory body like it used to be treated. Its decisions directly affect household budgets, communities, health and our energy future.”
Chris Womack, the CEO of Southern Company, Georgia Power’s parent company, also acknowledged the central importance of affordability during the company’s third-quarter earnings call on Thursday. But Womack said he’s confident the utility can address those concerns with the new commissioners.
“If you look at what we have been doing with rate freezes, with benefits, with how we are providing benefits from growth to customers — existing customers — as well as to the communities, we think that’s a strong platform to stand on,” he said.
Data centers, power bills and transparency
Since the data center boom in Georgia began, Georgia Power has maintained that the increased revenue from the energy-hungry facilities would more than pay for the new infrastructure needed to serve them. The utility argues that should keep rates lower for residential and small business customers. The utility calls this “downward pressure.” It doesn’t mean, though, that rates will go down for everyone else, but rather that any increases would be offset by the influx of revenue from data centers. 
The utility recently doubled down on that promise as part of its deal to serve a massive new OpenAI data center planned near Savannah. The deal, Georgia Power said, would bring $15 not of savings but of downward pressure per month for what Georgia Power calls the “typical” residential customer. 
Georgia Power also credited the increased revenue from data centers for the temporary rate freeze approved last year. But the rate freeze received criticism from some consumer and environmental groups because when it was announced, the deal essentially preempted previously planned PSC hearings that would have given advocates a chance to verify the utility’s financial claims. Advocates felt the process left them unable to confirm whether the company was delivering on its promises and fully shielding ordinary customers from data center costs. 
It’s part of a broader criticism often leveled at the PSC and Georgia Power: lack of transparency. 
The OpenAI contract was entirely redacted; a summary was provided to the public after the deal was approved. Specific details on other issues – from service contracts, to deals to buy energy, to construction costs – are often redacted from the utility’s public filings under the auspices of trade secrecy. Critics argue that while much of the information is indeed trade-secret, the redactions may go too far, and that PSC proceedings and Georgia Power operations in general should be clearer and more open to the public. Commission chair Jason Shaw acknowledged in an interview with WABE earlier this year that the commission needs to “do a better job of forcing” Georgia Power to make more details of its contracts public.
“I absolutely think transparency is potentially one of the biggest impacts here,” said Phillips of the election results. “It has been often on advocates to push on the way that the PSC communicates about the decisions that it’s making, and I’m hoping that there will be more clarity and transparency.”
The Democrats on the commission have promised to bring increased scrutiny to the next rate-setting process, scheduled for 2028, along with Georgia Power’s long-term plans to make and deliver energy, its forecasts about rising demand and other issues. Hubbard has also proposed conducting a rate case for the state’s natural gas utilities, which he said hasn’t been done in over a decade. And he said they’ll push for other changes going forward.
“We’ll continue with an agenda next year and the year after that to take advantage of this four-year period when we have the majority and can push for long-lasting reforms and shifting the direction of the state in terms of energy,” Hubbard said.

name: Michigan Advance
title: Michigan voters support more education funding, but how to pay for it is complicated
description: Jen Stroven, an organizer for Kalamazoo’s Yes For Families campaign, knew what she was up against: ‘Affordability, affordability, affordability.’  Asking voters to raise their own taxes to lower child care costs, expand access, and raise teacher wages may have seemed like a tall order at a time when the increased cost of living is a […]
text:
Getty ImagesJen Stroven, an organizer for Kalamazoo’s Yes For Families campaign, knew what she was up against: ‘Affordability, affordability, affordability.’ 
Asking voters to raise their own taxes to lower child care costs, expand access, and raise teacher wages may have seemed like a tall order at a time when the increased cost of living is a top issue on voters’ minds. But Stroven was confident the 0.5-mill property tax proposal would pass and she was right. In August, 63% of voters in Kalamazoo County approved the eight-year initiative that will add an average of $50 a month to their property tax bills. 

Stroven said that even for those voters who didn’t have young kids, they were able to see the economic benefit for communities and businesses that are losing workers because of lack of affordable childcare. She said they also understood how far-reaching the impact could be from the benefits to families to childcare workers, to the kids themselves. 
“It seemed for most folks to be a worthwhile investment,” Stroven said. 
The success of the Kalamazoo millage may come at a particularly cash-strapped time for voters but its passage is part of a larger trend both statewide and nationally of a shift in thinking from childcare and early childhood education as a personal responsibility to a public good. Kent County approved an early childhood millage in 2018; Leelanau County followed in 2019.
If voters can coalesce around early childhood education as a social good, whether or not funding for K-12 education can receive similar support is a little more complicated. 
Jen Stroven from the Kalamazoo Yes for Families Campaign. (Photo provided)
The legacy of Proposal A
For better or worse, K-12 educational funding in Michigan changed dramatically in 1994. Before, each school district relied heavily on local property taxes for funding. Unsurprisingly this led to massive inequities: Cities with a lot of property wealth could easily fund high teacher salaries, extensive programming and small class sizes with even smaller tax rates, while districts with low property values and rural communities were underfunded. 
In late 1993, the state Legislature removed the local property tax system, followed several months later by the voter-approved Proposal A constitutional amendment restructuring how Michigan funds K-12 public school operations. 
Since then, the Legislature distributes the exact same amount for each student in all schools through the School Aid Fund. Revenue for the fund comes mostly from sales taxes with small portions of revenue from income and property taxes.

Inequities still exist: Districts can pass voter-approved millages for capital expenses, such as school bonds and sinking funds to build new buildings or improve old ones. This means that some districts have state-of-the-art school buildings while students in other districts are stuck in crumbling schools.
David Arsen | Michigan State University
But all Michigan districts are legally restricted from asking voters to fund operational expenses like hiring more teachers, increasing salaries or even basics like paying a building’s utility bills. This funding paradox can create an incongruent situation like what’s currently playing out in Ann Arbor: a budget crisis with teacher layoffs while new school buildings are erected from a 2018 millage. 
On one hand, the Proposal A funding model has created more solidarity among districts, said David Arsen, a Michigan State University professor who specializes in education policy and school finance. But the downside, he says, is that communities lose the ability to respond locally to their own needs even if voters would be willing to tax themselves as they were in Kalamazoo. 
Why are schools still underfunded? 
In July, Michigan lawmakers celebrated a per-pupil funding increase from $10,050 to $10,300, along with other notable educational investments from the School Aid Fund, including an expansion of the Great Start Readiness Program to fund PreK for All and free school meals. Still, school funding hasn’t kept up with inflation and the changing economy. 
A recent poll commissioned by the K-12 Alliance of Michigan found that half of surveyed voters said that their local school districts have funding shortages for the resources they need.
Not keeping up with inflation
While $10,300 per student may sound like a lot, that number hasn’t kept pace with inflation according to research from the Education Policy Innovation Collaborative at MSU.  When adjusted for inflation, Michigan now spends less on school operations than it did decades ago. In 2002, the School Aid Fund provided an inflation-adjusted average of $13,858 per student.

 Decreased enrollment 
As a result of declining birth rates, population loss and other factors, public school enrollment in Michigan has declined by nearly 20%, or more than 335,000 students, since 2002. 
Tying funding to the number of students means that when enrollment drops, money disappears, even if costs increase. Schools have many fixed costs that can’t fluctuate with enrollment. A loss of even 20 students across all grade levels means a district loses hundreds of thousands of dollars while its operational costs, such as heating and cooling, running bus routes and paying school nurses, remain fixed or even increase with inflation. 
Compounding enrollment losses over several years force districts to cut essential staff and increase class sizes just to keep their budget balanced, even as per-pupil funding numbers are increased. 

 The problem with sales tax
Arsen explains that because the state sales tax is the primary source of revenue for the School Aid Fund, the education system loses out when there is a shift in consumer behavior and the tax code doesn’t keep up.
“The sales tax, which is the main source of revenue to the school aid fund, is based on the goods economy. There are a whole host of things in services that are not taxed. And so as the economy itself shifts from goods-producing to more services, that source of income doesn’t keep pace,” Arsen said. 
 Where is the money going to come from?

The good news for schools is that voters generally agree that funding education should be a priority, and as supporters of  the Kalamazoo millage demonstrated — a case can be made that well-educated kids are essential for the future of the state. However, figuring out where the money will come from remains a challenge. 
“We can get consensus in Michigan on equitable and adequate funding. What we have not been able to do yet is get agreement on where the revenues will come in order to fund that,”  Arsen said.
Molly Sweeney, organizing director of 482Forward, a member of the Invest in MI Kids ballot proposal coalition tells reporters the group plans to begin circulating petitions. July 31, 2025 | Photo By Kyle Davidson/Michigan Advance


The 2025 Invest in MI Kids campaign was an attempt at a solution. The campaign aimed to get a constitutional amendment on the 2026 ballot to place a 5% surcharge on single filers earning more than $500,000 and joint filers earning over $1 million. 
The initiative would have raised between $1.5 and $2 billion annually to lower student-to-teacher ratios, expand technical education and improve teacher retention. 

The campaign faced several obstacles, including pushback and procedural delays along with a high signature threshold. Though the campaign collected more than 250,000 signatures, it fell short of the goal and suspended operations in March, saying it would look toward the 2028 election cycle instead. 
Despite not making this year’s ballot, campaign manager Jessica Newman, co-director of the Michigan Education Justice Coalition, still thinks there’s a path to future success.
Jess Newman with Invest in MI Kids (Photo provided)
“This is a state that is ready to tax the rich, it’s ready to fund our public goods and services, and I wouldn’t take our failure to get on the ballot as evidence of that at all,” she said.  
Newman is not alone in that belief. Stroven and Arsen agreed that education funding is increasingly a bipartisan issue in Michigan. 
As Invest in MI Kids looks to the 2028 ballot, the campaign is now considering several other funding options beyond an increased income tax on high earners. Funding options that the campaign proposed in a survey to past canvassers include repealing data center property and sales tax exemptions, raising the corporate income tax rate, introducing a wealth proceeds tax, introducing a digital advertising tax and extending the sales tax to include services. 
Disclosure: The author was a volunteer signature collector for the campaign in 2025.
Voters in Kalamazoo and other counties approved taxes to pay for childcare. If Invest in MI Kids manages to get a proposal on the ballot next year, will Michiganders vote to fund education statewide? Public opinion seems to indicate they might. 
According to the EPIC survey, 65% of voters support an increase in education spending and put it on the top of their list of priorities, above even healthcare and fixing the roads.  
Newman remains hopeful. “I don’t have kids, but I understand that public schools are a public good that help every single person in the community.”
Support for this reporting came from The Better Life Lab at New America.

name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: Incoming Dem Ohio Secretary of State will do what she can to roll back GOP voting restrictions
description: As Democrats swept to historic victories Tuesday, a win in the Ohio Secretary of State race might start the process of rolling back years of Republican restrictions on voting that were predicated on voter fraud that didn’t exist. Allison Russo, a member of the state House of Representatives, defeated Republican Robert Sprague by 3.5 percentage […]
text:
Ohio Secretary of State-elect Allison Russo. (Photo by Nick Evans/ Ohio Capital Journal)As Democrats swept to historic victories Tuesday, a win in the Ohio Secretary of State race might start the process of rolling back years of Republican restrictions on voting that were predicated on voter fraud that didn’t exist.
Allison Russo, a member of the state House of Representatives, defeated Republican Robert Sprague by 3.5 percentage points to become secretary of state, the office that oversees Ohio’s elections and business registration.
Now she has a chance to continue a fight she began while she was in the legislature — to protect voting access for Ohioans.
“The thing that motivated me (to run) was understanding how important this office is for voting rights and for access to our elections,” Russo said in a phone interview. “I’ve known for a long time that this is an office I wanted to run for, and that we needed someone there to be an advocate for voters and voting.”
She was elected as part of a rout that broke total Republican control statewide offices in Ohio and left the GOP with only one statewide, non-judicial office — that of state auditor. 
As the GOP gained power in Ohio over the past 20 years, its leaders have entrenched that power through measures that critics said were antidemocratic. 
They severely gerrymandered the state legislature and Ohio’s congressional districts and then ignored seven orders of the Ohio Supreme Court saying that the gerrymanders were unconstitutional. 
And outgoing Secretary Frank LaRose repeatedly ratcheted down voting access on claims that the goal was to fight voter fraud. Yet his office’s own numbers demonstrated that it only might have happened 0.0005% of the time in the 2020 election. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
And more recent reporting for the Capital Journal shows there have been just nine convictions for illegal voting out of 35 million votes. That’s 0.0000003 convictions per vote cast.
Nevertheless, LaRose implemented rules and Republicans passed laws that shortened the early voting calendar, shortened deadlines around absentee voting and restricted the number of drop boxes and early-voting sites to one per county — regardless of whether the county is home to millions who tend to vote for Democrats or just 13,000 who tend to vote for Republicans.
Ohio Republicans also enacted one of the strictest voter ID laws in the United States.
All of those things culminated in the last night of early voting in Columbus, where voters had to stand in line for at least an hour after the polls had officially closed.
Russo said such waits are unacceptable, but as secretary of state, she has to deal with the law as it is.
“We have to work with existing state law whether I like that existing state law or not,” she said. “That said, we have a secretary of state (LaRose) who we’ve seen go beyond the plain language of the law and sometimes make existing, unfavorable law even worse. 
“So we are going to be looking very closely at the directives that have been previously issued. We’re going to work with our local elections officials to understand which ones are problematic to implement because they’re unclear, the legality may be problematic, or there are resource issues. That will be one of the first orders of business.”
As for drop boxes and early voting sites and hours, Russo said she’ll do what she can.
“There is some discretion for the secretary of state over the hours and how you use those days and the hours that are available to voters,” she said. “We’re going to be looking at what we can do there, because I share the concern that many Ohioans had when they saw those long lines. We do not want voters to be discouraged if they show up. And they should not have to wait that long.”
The secretary of state also has considerable power over the mechanics of citizen-initiated laws and constitutional amendments. She ensures they follow the single-subject rule and otherwise pass legal muster — including by verifying petition signatures.
And crucially, she proposes the language that will appear on the ballot to the Ohio Ballot Board.
In 2024, a group led by former Ohio Supreme Court Justice Maureen O’Connor, a Republican, proposed a constitutional amendment that sought to end gerrymandering by creating an independent, bipartisan panel to draw legislative and congressional districts. 
LaRose proposed three pages of ballot language with a title claiming that under the amendment, the panel was “required to gerrymander” the districts. Republicans on the ballot board adopted the language and the amendment failed in the same election that gained Donald Trump a second term as president.
There has been talk of trying to get a similar amendment on the ballot ahead of the 2030 census. Russo said it could be one of several in the next two years.
“I suspect there will be a number of ballot issues that will come forward over the next couple of years to address many of these concerns that voters have in this space,” she said. “Whether it be redistricting (or gerrymandering) reform, or voting rights — or it could be education funding — I suspect it will be a number of issues. As secretary of state, my involvement will be when those issues come forward.”
Would she commit to proposing straightforward, unbiased ballot language regardless of the content of the statute or amendment?
“Absolutely,” Russo said. “I talked a lot about that on the campaign trail — the need to have a more transparent process with ballot language. There has to be ample public notice about the ballot language to keep it simple and clear and easily understood. 
“Because listen, when you complicate ballot language, not only does it confuse voters, it also contributes to these long lines when voters have to stand there and read a lot of language and try to comprehend what it means.”

title: Report shows Ohio has permanent housing beds for less than 10% of people experiencing homelessness
description: Ohio only has enough permanent housing beds for 8% of all Ohioans experiencing homelessness, according to a new report.  In total, Ohio has 935 available permanent housing beds, according to a new report from the National Alliance to End Homelessness. “(Homeless service providers are) providing critical life-saving services to people in need of housing on a [...]
text:
File photo from Derek Miles for Colorado Newsline, States Newsroom.Ohio only has enough permanent housing beds for 8% of all Ohioans experiencing homelessness, according to a new report. 
In total, Ohio has 935 available permanent housing beds, according to a new report from the National Alliance to End Homelessness.
“(Homeless service providers are) providing critical life-saving services to people in need of housing on a day-to-day basis, and that work is made much more difficult by the fact that they don’t actually have the resources to do that work effectively,” said Daniel Soucy, research analyst at National Alliance to End Homelessness. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Ohio has less than one bed per every ten people experiencing homelessness, according to the report. 
“We would never ask an emergency room doctor to do surgery without a hospital room to do that surgery in, but we consistently ask homeless service providers to try and end homelessness without enough housing and enough shelter to do that,” Soucy said. 
Marcus Roth, spokesperson for the Coalition on Homelessness and Housing in Ohio, said the report is concerning. 
“Funding and resources for Ohio’s homelessness system is being dwarfed by increasing need,” he said. 
“The real problem is the lack of resources for the system, combined with economic factors such as rising rents that are making options for people to avoid homelessness scarcer and scarcer.” 
In 2024, 32,000 Ohioans entered the homeless system, but less than half of them were able to get into permanent housing, Roth said. 
“Ohio’s homeless system is effective at getting people out of homelessness with very few resources, but it can’t keep up with the flow of people into homelessness,” he said. 
There were 12,196 people experiencing homelessness in Ohio in 2025 — a 3% increase from 2024, according to the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development annual Homelessness Assessment Report. 
HUD’s Point-in-Time count are one-night estimates of sheltered and unsheltered people experiencing homelessness that took place in January 2025. 
About 20% of those experiencing homelessness in Ohio were unsheltered, according to HUD’s report. 
“It’s unsafe,” Soucy said. “It has impacts on people’s long-term health, and it’s an issue that we need to address urgently.” 
There has been a persistent shortage of shelter beds for more than a decade, Soucy said. 
“Asking service providers to end unsheltered homelessness, to find everybody a place to live when those resources just don’t exist, is not possible,” he said.
Ohio has about 63 shelter beds available per 100 people experiencing unsheltered homelessness, Soucy said. 
No state had homeless response systems with enough permanent housing for everyone experiencing homelessness at the time of HUD’s Point-in-Time count.
“We’re asking service providers to end homelessness with not even nearly enough resources,” Soucy said. 
Permanent housing ends homelessness, the housing advocates said.  
“What that usually looks like is private apartments that are owned by private landlords collaborating with homeless services agencies, so that they will help accept clients, people that are coming out of shelter,” Roth said. 
“What’s happened, though, with the increase in rent prices we’ve seen the last several years is that fewer and fewer landlords are willing to do that because they can make so much more money by just going to the private market, raising rents, and it’s leaving a real dearth of options for getting people out of homelessness.”
Ohio has a shortage of 266,000 affordable and available rental units, according to the 2026 Gap Report by the National Low Income Housing Coalition and COHHIO. 
A full-time Ohio worker needs to be making at least $23.82 an hour to be able to afford a “modest” two-bedroom apartment, according to the National Low Income Housing Coalition and COHHIO’s annual Out of Reach report.
Local, state, and federal lawmakers need to invest more in homeless response systems and permanent housing, Soucy said. 
“We need to ensure that there is enough permanent housing for everybody who is experiencing homelessness,” he said. “That means investments and resources and funding for these systems.”

title: Racine mayor Cory Mason won’t run for reelection
description: Racine Mayor Cory Mason won’t run for a fourth term, he announced Friday, making room for new leadership in Wisconsin’s fifth-largest city. Mason made the announcement Friday, on the eve of the 20th anniversary of his first election, when he won the race to represent the city in the state Assembly Nov. 7, 2006. Mason, […]
text:
Racine Mayor Cory Mason, photographed in 2024. (Photo by Erik Gunn/Wisconsin Examiner)Racine Mayor Cory Mason won’t run for a fourth term, he announced Friday, making room for new leadership in Wisconsin’s fifth-largest city.
Mason made the announcement Friday, on the eve of the 20th anniversary of his first election, when he won the race to represent the city in the state Assembly Nov. 7, 2006.
Mason, a Democrat, left the Assembly in 2017 after running in a special election to succeed John Dickert as mayor of Racine, a nonpartisan office. Dickert left in mid-term to take another job. Mason went on to win a full four-year term in 2019 and again in 2023.
“After 20 years, it’s time to pass the torch of leadership to the next generation,” Mason said in an interview.
Mason said he will remain in office until his current term ends in April. The  decision not to run again was one he and his family made recently, he said. Mason and his wife, Rebecca, a Racine estate planning and elder law attorney, have three children in high school.
“It’s important to have work-life balance, and I’m looking forward to the next chapter where I can have a little bit more of that moving forward,” Mason said.
Mason will leave office in the first months of unified Democratic control of the governor’s mansion and both houses of the state Legislature for the first time since Republicans won all three in 2010. That could open the door to policies that Democrats have advocated for years to no avail, such as sending more shared revenue dollars to cities including Racine.
It’s a contrast to most of Mason’s tenure in the Assembly, dominated particularly by the fight over Act 10, the law that then-Gov. Scott Walker introduced early in his first term stripping most collective bargaining rights from public employees except for police and firefighters.
Reflecting on his tenure as mayor, Mason identified nearly 20 accomplishments, leading with the completion of a community center and health clinic to serve a northwest side district of Racine. That same district is also the site of a major affordable housing project. 
Mason also listed a city work internship for young people, a jobs program to connect potential workers with construction trades and reductions in gun violence.
Still in progress is a longer-term project that he hopes will get picked up by the next mayor: establishing commuter rail service connecting Milwaukee and cities to the south, Racine and Kenosha.
Federal funds provide the bulk of the financing, which Mason said is a slow-moving process. Two decades ago, a similar commuter rail project for the corridor foundered when Republican state lawmakers balked at the plan.
“You need a muscular and robust partnership with the Wisconsin Department of Transportation to make a project to this scale go forward,” Mason said. “So we’re very excited about Gov. David Crowley for many reasons,” including his openness to improved public transportation, “and then having a Legislature that cares deeply about it.”
Trevor Jung, who won his race for the state Senate on Tuesday, is currently Racine’s transit director. “I know he shares my passion for this project and I’m really excited for him to advocate for this up in Madison,” Mason said.
Mason didn’t discount a return to politics, but turned aside speculation about possible races in the next four years.
Asked whether he might join the incoming Crowley administration, he said, “I don’t have anything definitive lined up, but I’ve not ruled anything out either.”
There’s one exception — becoming a lobbyist. “I did rule that out as the next thing that I would do,” Mason said. “But that notwithstanding, you know I’m excited to figure out what the next chapter of my life looks like.”

name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: Commentary: Acton win heralds new policy era for Ohio
description: After last week’s election results, Ohio will be returning to divided government for the first time in half a generation. Less than three hours after polls closed in Ohio, the Ohio Capital Journal called the race for governor. At the time I wrote this commentary, former state health director Amy Acton leads Vivek Ramaswamy by […]
text:
Dr. Amy Acton became the first Democrat in 20 years to lead Ohio after winning the governor’s race Tuesday, Nov. 3, at a rally in Cleveland. (Photo by Nick Evans/Ohio Capital Journal)After last week’s election results, Ohio will be returning to divided government for the first time in half a generation.
Less than three hours after polls closed in Ohio, the Ohio Capital Journal called the race for governor. At the time I wrote this commentary, former state health director Amy Acton leads Vivek Ramaswamy by nearly 8 percentage points with 99 percent of the total votes counted.
Acton has put forth a platform of policy priorities that look to reorient state policy, and successes in the Ohio House of Representatives give her a bloc that can back up her veto pen. As Candidate Acton moves to Governor Acton, there are a number of policy issues where we could see changes that would impact people’s lives in a concrete way.
 Education and Property Taxes

Ohio has been grappling with this tradeoff over the past few years. Record increases in housing valuations have led to a backlash against property taxes at the same time that the state has been working to equalize its school funding. Acton has prioritized fair school funding but will have to contend with headwinds with school finance’s most important tool in Ohio: property taxes.
Acton will face this challenges in the first few months of her governorship, with school funding questions being central to state budget negotiations.
 Poverty Reduction

The Acton campaign has emphasized anti-poverty tax credits as a “day one” priority for the administration. These are changes that will have to happen in collaboration with a potentially hostile General Assembly. While Governor DeWine was successful in negotiating an expansion to the Earned Income Tax Credit early in his first term, he introduced a Child Tax Credit last year that was immediately removed from the budget by House leaders.
This is a potential place for collaboration between Acton and legislative leaders. Leaders are interested in tax relief, and if that can be brought about through support for low-income households, this could be an opportunity for compromise during budget negotiations.
 Health Care

Governor Kasich famously bucked his party a decade ago by engineering a quiet approval for Medicaid expansion in the state, bringing around $8 billion of federal dollars for healthcare services into the state per year and providing health insurance coverage to 670,000 Ohio residents. Since then, legislators have worked to reduce the state’s investment in Medicaid, including passing a budget clause last year that will immediately remove coverage for those residents if the federal government changes policy to provide a dollar less than it provides for Medicaid today. I’m 
Acton has proposed medical debt relief, reducing administrative barriers to Medicaid enrollment, and using state purchasing power to reduce prescription drug costs. While some of this could be focuses for the state budget, many health care strategies may be possible through executive action. The options could grow in the second half of her term if Democrats take the White House in 2028, opening options for new waivers with the federal Department of Health and Human Services.
 Energy

Acton has proposed a moratorium on data center development and requiring developers to cover their own energy costs. She has also said she wants to appoint people to the public utilities commission that focus on ratepayer protection. This is likely to be an ongoing discussion as the question of data center development is not going away in Ohio any time soon. With the widespread backlash against data center development, there are opportunities for the new administration to work together with legislative leaders to ensure the benefits of new development outweigh their costs.
The first test of Ohio’s new divided government will come during next year’s budget negotiations. Acton will have opportunities to shape education, taxation, health care and energy policy, but each step she takes will come with fiscal and political tradeoffs. How those tradeoffs are resolved will determine how much this election concretely changes the lives of Ohio residents.

name: Florida Phoenix
title: Commentary: Florida bucked the trend toward sanity
description: Not subtle. Not nuanced. Americans launched an almighty middle finger at the Mob Boss of Mar-a-Lago, repudiating him and his congressional Flying Monkey squad. The Bible-spouting Pharisee Mike Johnson will no longer be Speaker of the House; the sclerotic Chuck Grassley will no longer chair the committee that placed Brett Kavanaugh and Neil Gorsuch on […]
text:
Republican Byron Donalds celebrates his win in the Florida governor race on Nov. 3, 2026, flanked by his wife, Erika, and running mate Bryan Ávila. (Photo via Donalds Facebook page)Not subtle. Not nuanced.
Americans launched an almighty middle finger at the Mob Boss of Mar-a-Lago, repudiating him and his congressional Flying Monkey squad.
The Bible-spouting Pharisee Mike Johnson will no longer be Speaker of the House; the sclerotic Chuck Grassley will no longer chair the committee that placed Brett Kavanaugh and Neil Gorsuch on the U.S. Supreme Court; and no longer will Congress sign off on obscene funding for the Iran war.
MAGA myrmidons crashed and burned in Trump-voting states across the nation — not Florida, of course, but we’ll talk about that in a minute.
Ohio, for example, where tech bro Vivek Ramaswamy saw nothing wrong with running an attack ad starring the estranged mother of opponent Amy Acton, a woman who defended her husband even though he’d been indicted for raping Amy when she was 12.
Or Texas, for God’s sake. Texas, a state so red it puts cheap Santa suits to shame, spurned Ken Paxton, Trump’s hand-picked Senate candidate.
The epically sleazy Paxton, who was impeached by his own party, got taken to the woodshed by a fresh-faced seminarian with a strong resemblance to Opie Taylor.
Elon Musk must be sick as a parrot. He burned through millions of dollars trying to get his Texas supplicants elected, to no avail. Now, SpaceX and Tesla stock is heading downhill and Texas’ new Democratic government is likely inclined to investigate him, his dodgy finances, his campaign donations, and his environmentally disastrous space city.
Now that Texas is no longer friendly to the bazillionaire oligarch and professional baby-daddy, what do you want to bet Musk moves to Florida?
All the best authoritarian creeps end up here: Trump, his boys, the Kushners, Jeff Bezos, and Flávio Bolsonaro.
But Iowa? Kansas? Seriously? Kansas hasn’t sent a Democrat to the Senate since 1932.
New new South
South Carolina hasn’t chosen a Democratic senator since Fritz Hollings was re-elected in 1998. It’s got one now.
The South, land of slavery-excusing, abortion-banning, vaccine-hating, and mandating religious instruction in public schools is getting bluer.
They’re still counting in the Mississippi Senate race, where Democrat Scott Colom leads incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith. His lead is small, but y’all, this is Mississippi, a state Trump won by more than 20 points in 2024.
In North Carolina, voters flipped a U.S. Senate seat, gave Democrats the majority in the state House of Representatives, and made substantial gains in the state Senate.
In Georgia, the top offices are now as blue as deep water.
Democrats hold both U.S. Senate seats, have taken control of the state House of Representatives, and elected the nation’s first Black woman governor.
Then there’s Florida, which never fails to disappoint.
While most the country rejected Donald Trump’s toxic regime, Florida bucked the trend toward sanity and stuck with Republicans.
Byron Donalds made history as the state’s first Black governor.
This should be a proud accomplishment, except the man is a Trumpist to the core.
During the campaign, he inched away — a little — from references to Trump’s endorsement.
Trump’s approval rating was (and is) in the low-to-mid 30s.
However, once Donalds won, the sucking-up resumed. The man who likes to call Trump “Daddy,” declared: “Mr. President, I want you to hear from Florida that we are still red!”
And Trump is still a racist.
Even Florida shifted
Florida could have made more history by electing Angie Nixon, who’d have been our first Black senator.
Instead, we chose former Attorney General Ashley Moody, appointed to serve out Marco Rubio’s term after he was elevated (if that’s the right word) to be Trump’s secretary of state.
James Uthmeier, appointed to fill the attorney general post after Moody decamped for D.C., won his election, too.
He’s a self-proclaimed devout Christian, yet remains proud of “Alligator Alcatraz,” that giant human rights violation of a prison camp in the Everglades.
Government inspectors (Trump administration inspectors!) found the facility abused detainees, some of whom accused the state of “torture.”
Uthmeier can now continue his mission to shut down drag shows, ban Judy Blume novels, instruct bishops in Roman Catholic theology, and defend himself against accusations of misdeeds in the HOPE Florida scandal.
Still, Florida was not a total bust for Democrats.
These races were far closer than they should have been, given how this state has been blindly electing Republicans for the past 30-odd years.
Angie Nixon was less than three percentage points behind Ashley Moody. That’s a major shift: Marco Rubio beat Val Demings by 6.5 percent in 2022 and Rick Scott’s 2024 margin over Debbie Murcasel-Powell was over 12 points.
The last time he ran, Ron DeSantis romped (an unseemly image, but still), beating Charlie Crist by nearly 20 points.
David Jolly got within 1.3 percentage points of Donalds.
As for Uthmeier, his win over José Javier Fernandez was thread-slim, despite having more than three times as much campaign cash.
There’s more (qualified) good news for Dems.
If Republicans prevail in the two neck-and-neck races that are, at the time of writing, still too close to call, the party make-up of Florida’s congressional delegation will remain the same as it was last year.
‘Oops’
But Republicans thought they could grab even more seats.
Remember that redistricting stunt they pulled to pad their numbers and get rid of the likes of Kathy Castor, the long-time representative from Tampa Bay?
It didn’t quite go as planned.
Three of the four redrawn districts went to Democrats; incumbent Darren Soto leads in the fourth.
Nationwide, what the gerrymandering Republicans thought was a sure bet to net them more seats blew up in their faces.
Most of their redrawn districts went to Democrats.
As the Texan sage and failed presidential candidate Rick Perry once said, “Oops.”
Despite Florida’s Cabinet remaining DeSantisite, Republicans have lost their supermajority in the House and their total control of the Senate is teetering on the brink after Maitland Mayor John Lowndes whipped incumbent DeSantis acolyte Jason Brodeur, one of the most powerful politicos in the state.
The question will be: Will Florida Republicans get a clue and realize they’re not as popular as they used to be?
During a post-election press conference, DeSantis congratulated Florida (and, by extension, himself) for bucking the national trend, while warning the midterms were “as close to an extinction-level event for Republicans in many parts of the country as we have seen probably in the last 100 years.”
Scary! His party has lost two key states, Ohio and Texas: “If the Republican Party doesn’t have Texas as an anchor, then we are not going to be viable moving forward.”
Texas was always what Florida wanted to be when it grew up.
But, as DeSantis boasted, “Our line of scrimmage held better here in Florida.”
Amendment 3
He’s even more pleased Amendment 3, his pet anti-local government project, passed.
Appealing to greed usually works: Voters have chosen to dismantle our property tax system.
Homeowners will be happy to get the extra cash, though the one-third of Floridians who rent won’t get anything out of this.
And nobody will like it when their local taxes and fees shoot up to fund basic services, when the potholes don’t get fixed, law enforcement loses officers, firefighters get laid off, libraries and neighborhood clinics close, cultural events are canceled, and parks neglected.
None of that matters to DeSantis. Amendment 3 is his calling card for another presidential bid, an accomplishment he thinks he can run on.
But Florida might not remain the Ghost of Texas Past DeSantis and the Republicans want it to be.
This year shows even the reddest of reds can fade.
The presidential race in 2028 may bring another Democratic opportunity in Florida.
Ashley Moody must run again to keep her U.S. Senate seat. It’s possible she’ll again face Angie Nixon.
Given the stinking miasma of the Trump administration will still be hanging over Republicans in general, and Moody in particular, Nixon could prevail this time.
Perhaps the Florida Democratic Party — long a by-word for dysfunction — will look across the border at Georgia, where Black women hold the top state offices, and learn.
The national Democratic Party may finally (finally!) invest in the state, recruiting good candidates, growing the voter base one citizen at a time, and spending actual money here.
It won’t be easy, obviously, but the midterms have blown a chill wind through Republican Florida.
As the good old Game of Thrones saying goes, “Winter is coming.”

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: CT Republicans need a reckoning, not excuses
description: If CT voters were convinced we offered a credible alternative, more would have supported us.
text:
Connecticut Republicans didn’t just lose an election Tuesday. We suffered a political slaughter the likes of which we have never seen. 
While a national Democratic wave contributed to the outcome, the magnitude of our defeat demands more than excuses. It demands an honest reckoning.

Timothy Herbst

First, Ryan Fazio deserves our gratitude and respect. When others declined to step forward, Ryan accepted the enormous challenge of running for governor in an unfavorable political environment. He worked tirelessly, traveled the state, and made a serious case for fiscal responsibility and economic opportunity. He knew the odds and answered the call anyway. His courage, commitment, and extraordinary work ethic deserve admiration.
But honoring Ryan’s effort cannot substitute for examining why Republicans lost so decisively.
Perhaps the greatest frustration is the disconnect between voters’ concerns and their choices at the ballot box. Connecticut residents repeatedly identified taxes, the cost of living, and exorbitant utility bills among their most pressing problems. Yet those concerns did not translate into accountability for the party that has controlled the governorship and both legislative chambers since 2011.
Donald Trump didn’t create Connecticut’s public benefits charge on electric bills. State policymakers did. Trump didn’t design Connecticut’s tax structure or determine Hartford’s spending priorities. Connecticut’s elected leaders did. Trump didn’t enact the state laws that have stripped control of zoning from local communities. Gov. Ned Lamont and Democratic legislators did.
Donald Trump certainly didn’t create Connecticut’s longstanding and shameful achievement gap in our public schools. That problem predates his presidency by decades and remains unresolved after 16 years of Democratic control in Hartford. And now, with proposals for regionalized school districts back on the table, I fear Hartford may seek to strip communities of local control over their schools as well.
At some point, Lamont and Democratic legislative majorities must be held accountable for the problems they have failed to solve. Certainly, national economic forces matter. But opposition to Donald Trump appears to have overwhelmed almost everything else. For many voters, national political passions superseded an examination of Connecticut’s governing record.
Yet Republicans cannot simply blame Trump or the electorate. If voters were convinced we offered a credible alternative, more would have supported us.
That is our failure to address.
The Republican Party needs rebuilding from the bottom up. It starts with our Republican Town Committees and the members representing each district on the Republican State Central Committee. Many have served faithfully for years, even decades, and deserve appreciation. But 20 years in the same position should not be mistaken for 20 years of progress.
Republicans in every district must examine who represents them on State Central. Are they recruiting new people, bringing fresh ideas, expanding our reach, and building a party capable of winning? Or have these positions become comfortable seats occupied by the same familiar faces election after election?
There is another fundamental problem that Republicans must confront: the tremendous disconnect between our Republican elected officials, our Republican Town Committees, and the Republican State Central Committee. I witnessed this firsthand when I ran for governor eight years ago. Too often, these groups operate in separate silos rather than functioning as parts of a unified political organization. Elected officials, party leaders, and grassroots activists should be working toward common objectives, communicating regularly, and supporting one another. If we cannot get on the same page within our own party, how can we possibly expect to prosecute a successful statewide campaign in an increasingly difficult political environment?
And then there is the destructive culture of infighting that has plagued Connecticut Republicans for far too long. Democrats certainly have their own personality conflicts, ideological divisions, and internal disagreements. But when an election approaches, they generally find a way to put those differences aside and unite around the common objective of winning. 
Connecticut Republicans, by contrast, too often form a circular firing squad, spending more time attacking fellow Republicans than challenging the opposing party. Personal grievances, factional rivalries, and old political scores become more important than the larger mission. This mindset has to be expurgated from the Connecticut Republican Party once and for all. Healthy debate and honest disagreement make a political party stronger. Personal vendettas and political score-settling only make it weaker. We will never build a credible governing alternative until we learn that winning elections requires discipline, mutual respect, and a willingness to put the party’s broader interests ahead of individual egos.
We need new blood, new energy, and a new generation willing to do the hard work of rebuilding. Town committees must become engines of candidate recruitment, fundraising, and community engagement. District Republicans must take responsibility for choosing State Central representatives committed to growing the party rather than preserving the status quo.
There may be one silver lining in this otherwise disastrous election. With overwhelming legislative majorities, Connecticut Democrats, particularly their progressive wing, may interpret the results as permission to pursue a more ambitious agenda. I suspect progressives like Josh Elliott will view this election as a mandate to push their agenda further left. Governor Lamont strikes me as a genuinely nice man. But being a nice man and having the political will to stand up to the most ideological members of your own party are two different things. Whether he will exercise that restraint remains an open question.
Republicans should prepare for renewed debates over taxes on investment income and high earners, costly energy mandates, government spending, and further erosion of local decision-making authority. These are potential battles, not inevitable outcomes. We must challenge proposals on their merits and offer practical alternatives.
The political landscape will eventually change. Donald Trump will not be a presidential candidate in 2028. Although his influence will persist, Democrats cannot assume that opposition to him will indefinitely overshadow scrutiny of their own governing record.
But Republicans cannot simply wait for Democrats to overreach.
We must rebuild a coalition that includes independents and the pragmatic, fiscally responsible Democrats once represented by Joe Lieberman. These voters want affordable electricity, reasonable taxes, safe communities, good schools, and competent government. Our message must be grounded in common sense and kitchen-table economics, not national grievances or ideological purity tests. We must demonstrate that Republicans can govern better, not merely complain louder.
Ryan Fazio did his part. Now the rest of us must do ours.
No one is entitled to a seat on State Central. No one is entitled to lead simply because they’ve always been there. And no Republican should confuse loyalty to the party with loyalty to the people who currently occupy its positions.
The time for excuses is over. The time for new blood is now. If we aren’t willing to clean house and make meaningful changes within our own party, we have no business asking Connecticut voters to trust us to lead the state.
Timothy M. Herbst was the First Selectman of Trumbull from 2009-2017 and ran for Governor of Connecticut in 2018.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Election season is done. Holiday season is approaching. And lawmakers still have dozens of big decisions to make.
description: It’s a new phenomenon for the Legislature to have this much unfinished business this close to the end of the two-year session.
text:
THERE’S NO PLACE like the State House for the holidays.
It’s easy to forget amid all the hubbub of a national blue wave and a nine-question state ballot, but with the election now past, the Legislature has a long list of business left to accomplish in the eight holiday-punctuated weeks remaining before the 2025-2026 term draws to a close.
“Long” might actually be an understatement. There are 12 House-Senate negotiating panels still working to finalize compromise bills, plus a late-moving spending proposal needed to close the state’s financial books. But because legislative leaders prefer to cram multiple topics into each omnibus package, the number of discrete policy decisions still in play reaches into the dozens.
By our count, there are more than 40 significant policy choices the Democrats who control Beacon Hill need to make before the final gavel rings out on January 5, 2027, ranging from whether to upzone the entire state for duplex development to whether to ban the sale of dogs, cats, and rabbits in pet stores. Any bill left unfinished by the term’s end will expire, and lawmakers will need to start the process from scratch after they’re sworn in for the 2027-2028 session.
Our tally may be exhausting, but it is not exhaustive. We did not include every one of the discrepancies in spending between House and Senate legislation, which are more granular.
It’s a lot to track, even for professional Beacon Hill-watchers.
Because almost everything is now in the hands of conference committees, the actual policy decisions will essentially be made behind closed doors by only a handful of Democrats. Each panel is working to iron out differences between the underlying House and Senate versions of a bill; once its members reach agreement, the rest of the Legislature will only get a chance to vote up or down on the final accord — usually with no more than a day or two’s notice on the actual substance — without making any further changes.
House Speaker Ron Mariano said Friday that the negotiating teams are ” making progress and working hard.”
“It’s important to understand that these are complex policy decisions that take time, and often many conversations and meetings to resolve,” Mariano said in a statement to CommonWealth Beacon. Stretching the timeline, he added, gives lawmakers “more time to work diligently to reach the best possible policy outcomes — understanding that the content of the final product is far more important than reaching an agreement quickly solely for the sake of doing so.”
It’s a new phenomenon for the Legislature to have this much unfinished business this close to the end of the two-year session. For decades, lawmakers set themselves an earlier deadline, writing into their internal rules that no formal sessions can take place after July 31 in the second year of the term. Roll call votes can only happen in a formal session, so the rule effectively meant the only lawmaking that could occur after the cutoff date needed to be uncontroversial enough to win unanimous support.
Prior generations of lawmakers created the deadline almost immediately after a stinging controversy about lame-duck session shenanigans. Weeks after the 1994 election, with only a bit more than a month left in the legislative term, Republican Gov. Bill Weld suddenly filed legislation authorizing a 55 percent pay raise for lawmakers even though, as CommonWealth’s Dave Denison put it, he was previously “on record as being cool to the idea.” The Legislature quickly approved the measure, and days later, they also advanced a tax cut bill that had been quietly amended to include a capital gains tax cut — a Weld priority that had long failed to gain traction.
After drawing intense criticism for what struck many as a quid pro quo exchange, lawmakers the following year codified a new rule: Formal sessions, and therefore major business of any kind, must end by July 31 in the term’s second year. Republican Rep. David Peters of Charlton, who self-identified as “one of the loudest critics of the system,” at the time called the new deadline “one of the most significant reforms I’ve seen since I’ve been in the building,” according to a 1995 State House News Service report.
Three decades later, the current crop of legislative leaders decided the rule was worth tweaking after a pair of especially chaotic sprints to the finish line. In both 2022 and 2024, the House and Senate headed into July 31 with several major bills stuck in conference committee. Still hoping to strike deals, lawmakers kept the sessions going well past sunrise on August 1, then adjourned with some matters still unresolved.
This term, lawmakers agreed to a different approach. The Legislature’s new rules still require major bills to get an initial round of approval in both the House and Senate by July 31, but as long as conference committee negotiations started by that date, lawmakers can reconvene in a formal session any time before the term ends to greenlight a final compromise version.
Lawmakers sent 12 different matters into conference committees by the deadline this term. None produced any agreements by Election Day, leaving essentially the entire pile of business that was unfinished on August 1 to be decided in lame-duck sessions — including a potential rewrite of a public records ballot question voters just approved in a landslide.
“The whole point behind the July 31 extension for conferences was to take the pressure off the last couple of weeks and say, ‘We’re close here, if we meet a few more times on this, we can wrap this up before the end,’” Mariano said in the summer.
It’s safe to say the pressure is back on.

text:
A voter fills out a ballot at the Portland Expo in Maine’s June 9, 2026, primary election. (Photo by Jim Neuger / Maine Morning Star)I hope this column will rescue the ballot of someone you know from being discarded.
You can help.
The 2026 election has not ended.  There are 61 counties in North Carolina where voters with ballots in limbo could decide who wins or loses. The close contests include three Congressional races, several contests for seats in the General Assembly, and more than a dozen local elections, from school board to district attorney.
NC elections board moves to make it easier to toss voters’ ballots

More than 35,000 provisional ballots are still being evaluated by local election officials to see if the person qualifies to vote. Maybe their name didn’t show up on the registration rolls for one reason or another, so they had to cast a provisional ballot. Or they didn’t have an approved photo ID to show the poll worker.
These voters have until noon Tuesday to contact their county board of elections and provide additional information or confirm the official’s research that they are qualified to vote.
Another 700 or so voters who submitted a ballot by mail also need to take immediate action before Tuesday at noon. Some glitch – perhaps an unsealed envelop or missing identity information – is holding up the final decision on whether their ballot will count.
Some of these voters have been contacted by strangers affiliated with a partisan or nonpartisan group. But they may not trust that messenger or may not think it’s worth the time to fix something that shouldn’t be a ballot-counting barrier anyway.
That’s where you come in. Search this list of affected voters in your county. If you know someone on it, please be a trusted messenger and urge them to take action.  It may not be clear what needs fixing – the key is they should immediately contact their county board of elections and learn what is needed. Right away.
One more group of about 250 voters are also on the searchable list.  They used “same-day registration” to register and vote during early voting.  But a verification mailing to them bounced back, so the board of elections may disqualify their ballot – unless they take action by Thursday at noon.
Please go to the names on the list in your county and look for people you know.  There are still undecided contests from Congressional seats to the local courthouse and school board.  Let your friend know that her or his ballot can still count — and could decide who wins and who loses an important election.

name: VTDigger
title: My teeth could kill me
description:
I’ve survived avalanches and earthquakes, but a lack of dental care could be what finally does me in.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  My teeth could kill me.
text:
Dear Editor,
I’ve experienced avalanches, tornadoes, earthquakes, high-voltage shocks and aggressive toxins. And always gotten through. Usually shaken but escaping being stirred into nothingness. Ribs, arms, fingers, legs, back, neck — I’ve broken them all. And while not fun, none of them were dead ends. The hassle and patience of healing was always just a hiccup in my adventures. 
Twenty-five years ago, while training for an extreme skiing competition in Crested Butte, Colorado, I broke my back and neck. “Just” hairline fractures, though my brain was knocked around a bit. As I was getting carted off to the hospital, all I could think was, “At least I didn’t blow a knee,” a common career-ender for alpine professionals. Back then, I was not thinking, “At least I didn’t break a tooth.”
I should have been. My body withstood remarkable abuse for decades. But my teeth are possibly what will kill me. 
Bad teeth are not just a cosmetic issue. An infection could give me mortal sepsis. And my only access to dental care is the emergency room. 
Modern health coverage considers teeth essentially disconnected from the rest of the body. And here is how extreme it has gotten: A concussion triggered seizures that resulted in falls that broke teeth. Many tens of thousands of dollars have been spent to fix up my entire body — except the teeth I broke.
I cannot get dental coverage, or come close to being able to afford it out of pocket. I’ve looked carefully for a solution — from free clinics and dental school programs to Medicare and private insurance — but my only options are luck, care, home remedies and the emergency room. If an infection starts to push me into mortal danger? Then health insurance will, hopefully, save my life. But all this will do is treat the symptoms and reset the clock for a new emergency. Such duct-taping of underlying problems is costing us all a lot of money. Much more than if we simply recognized that teeth, like bones, are simply part of our body.

READ MORE

You could be in full-body traction, perhaps from doing something moronic like driving drunk, or tumbling down an avalanche chute. But having bad teeth, even from an accident outside your control? That will create more social barriers and earn more scorn than a body cast. And I’ve been brainwashed by our culture just as much as anyone else: The shame of showing my mouth in public outweighs the pain of simply being alone. 
I hope that a wave of rationality is coming and that we build a structure where we can thrive and help each other stay healthy. A framework of compassion over profit. 
Meanwhile, I count myself lucky. Unlike others in an even worse position, I have food, water and warmth. I also have Tylenol, tooth drops, good books and hope. I know that problems with my teeth are minuscule compared with the health brutality many people are experiencing. I still believe that we, America, are going to reprioritize things and figure these issues out together.
Todd Murchison
Brattleboro, Vt.
