name: Michigan Advance
title: Commentary: The true guardians of our democracy
description: As the dust settles on the 2026 blue wave tsunami of a national election, the predictable wave of political analysis and backslapping has begun.  Pundits and the political class will spend weeks dissecting voter shifts, messaging strategies and polling margins.  Here in Michigan and across the country, an important story of this election isn’t just […]
text:
Election workers collect absentee ballots outside the Department of Elections in Detroit on Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Janelle D. James/Michigan Advance)As the dust settles on the 2026 blue wave tsunami of a national election, the predictable wave of political analysis and backslapping has begun. 
Pundits and the political class will spend weeks dissecting voter shifts, messaging strategies and polling margins. 
Here in Michigan and across the country, an important story of this election isn’t just about who won or lost. It is about how the election was run: smoothly, securely, and with an unwavering commitment to the fair and transparent democratic process.
For that, we must thank our secretary of state, now governor-elect, Jocelyn Benson and her exceptional team, as well as municipal clerks, poll workers and precinct volunteers across America — and specifically here in Michigan — who managed the logistical marvel of our vital voting system.
This year’s success was also fortified by an extraordinary, collaborative effort that took place far outside the standard political arenas. To truly appreciate why our system held strong, we must also thank former Democratic Gov. Jim Blanchard, who served as ambassador and was my former boss; former Republican Gov. John Engler; former Republican U.S. Rep. and state Senate Majority Leader Michael Bishop; and former Lt. Gov. John Cherry, a Democrat. and the leaders of the Detroit Regional Chamber.
In an era deeply fractured by political tribalism, these bipartisan leaders showed our state—and the country—a master class in pragmatic statesmanship. 
As leaders of the bipartisan Democracy Defense Foundation in Michigan, these former political rivals chose to stand shoulder to shoulder in defense of our democracy.
Rather than retreating into comfortable partisanship, they put their collective weight behind a singular, vital mission: upholding public trust in our election infrastructure and protecting the integrity of the vote.
Throughout the campaign cycle, they traveled the state, hosting forums, speaking with the media, and utilizing new polling to directly address and de-escalate public anxieties surrounding voter safety and ballot security. Their  message was simple yet profound: Our election systems are decentralized, heavily scrutinized and robustly protected by our own neighbors. By auditing the facts and calling for civic responsibility, they helped lower the temperature of the public discourse. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
They reminded us that while we can disagree passionately about policy, we must remain unified in our respect for the democratic process.
Crucially, this message found a powerful amplifier in the Michigan business community, spearheaded by the Detroit Regional Chamber. Under the leadership of longtime President and CEO Sandy Baruah and his outstanding team, the business sector recognized that a stable democracy is the literal bedrock of a strong state and prosperous economy. 
The chamber did not sit on the sidelines. Instead, it mobilized its expansive network to transform corporate civic engagement into a tangible, frontline reality.
Through focused election briefings and executive webinars, the chamber consistently educated regional leaders on the extensive, multi-layered safeguards built into Michigan’s voting framework. More importantly, it issued a direct call to action for employers. 
Jointly they prodded chamber members and the citizens of Michigan to move beyond passive observation and actively encourage their workforces to serve as local poll workers and precinct watchers. The business community responded in kind. By providing employees with the flexibility, and in some cases dedicated time off, to work the polls, regional employers helped solve a critical staffing puzzle for local clerks.
The result of this combined effort was palpable on Election Day. Because of the infrastructure championed by our local clerks, reinforced by the structural support of the chamber and the bipartisan shield, our precincts operated with transparent efficiency. Voters stood in lines managed by well-trained volunteers, ballots were counted meticulously, and the system functioned exactly as it was designed to do.
Democracy is not a self-sustaining machine; it requires continuous care, human labor, and a shared cultural agreement that the rules matter. 
This November, Michigan and America proved that when political rivals lock arms and the business community and others align their collective  resources with civic duty, we can withstand the forces of lies and cynicism.
To the thousands of election workers who checked IDs and handed out “I Voted” stickers, we thank you. And to Jim Blanchard, John Engler, former Rep. Michael Bishop, former Lt. Gov John Cherry and the Detroit Regional Chamber, thank you for reminding us that defending our democracy is a job that belongs to all of us. 
You didn’t just protect an election; you strengthened the very fabric of our state and nation.

name: California
title: ‘Soul-hurting pain’: Victims’ families enraged at Newsom’s death row decision
description: Families of those killed by death row inmates react to California Gov. Gavin Newsom commuting their sentences to life in prison.
text:
In summary
Families of those killed by death row inmates react to California Gov. Gavin Newsom commuting their sentences to life in prison.


They’ve lived through the worst horrors a family can endure, and they were promised their murdered loved ones would receive justice through an execution.They suffered through years, if not decades, of appeals and hearings where they were forced to hear the stories of their loved ones’ violent deaths graphically retold again and again.
They watched courts — and then Gov. Gavin Newsom — suspend executions. The last one was carried out in 2006, before he was elected, despite California voters repeatedly reaffirming their support for the death penalty over the past 50 years.
And then on Thursday, they learned that Newsom, in one of his final acts as governor, had commuted the death sentences to life in prison for each of the 548 murderers on death row.
“These are not just numbers on a legal document,” said Sandy Friend, whose eight-year-old son was raped, tortured and murdered by a man facing a death sentence. “Each case has a family left behind. Each case has a story of a horrific, violent end to someone’s loved one. To wipe all of that away with one stroke of a pen, without looking at the details or looking into the eyes of the families, was completely unthinkable.” 
Newsom in an open letter about the commutations said the decision was among the most difficult of his career, “not because I doubt its necessity for our state but because I know its announcement may surface excruciating memories for victims’ families.”
The California Supreme Court will have to sign off on the commutations for around 400 of the prisoners who were convicted of multiple felonies. 
After Newsom’s announcement, CalMatters spoke with Friend and two others whose loved ones were victims of California killers sentenced to death.Their reactions ranged from acceptance to fury.
A little boy’s mother feels ‘soul-hurting pain’
On May 16, 1996, eight-year-old Michael Lyons was walking home from his Yuba City elementary school when Robert Boyd Rhoades grabbed him and drove him to a secluded spot along the Feather River. 
Rhoades raped and tortured the boy for the next 10 hours. 
When detectives found his body, it was naked from the waist down, his Batman shirt pulled over his head. He’d been cut and stabbed 70 to 80 times, according to Friend, the boy’s mother. 
When Friend went to see his body, investigators would only let her see his face and one hand.“I could see those scrape marks — those knife wounds — across his little face,” she wrote in an essay posted on the Criminal Justice Legal Foundation’s website. “That image will forever be the last image of his beautiful face I would ever see.”

A family photo of Michael Lyons. Photo courtesy of Sandy Friend

In text messages Friday with CalMatters, Friend called Newsom’s decision a betrayal of everything she and other victims’ families have gone through. 
“I feel a deep, soul-hurting pain and an angry, screaming feeling inside,” she said. “We fought for justice, and now one man has swiped away these monsters’ true sentences in one moment, just like the monsters who took our loved ones’ voices and silenced our loved ones.”
Friend said she is worried that Rhoades may some day walk free, despite Newsom’s insistence that these murderers never will. 
Recent experience makes her believe those concerns are valid.
It was only last December that Rhoades, now 73, had his most recent effort to lower his sentence rejected. 
Rhoades tried to use a law Newsom signed in 2021 allowing inmates to petition to have certain sentences reduced, one of several laws the Legislature and California voters have passed over the years to increase opportunities for parole and early release. 
Michael’s family prevailed, but it was a painful experience. Once again, Friend and Michael’s loved ones had to go to court to relive the worst days of their lives. 
“He was a little boy. He was my son,” Friend said. “He had a voice, and that voice deserved to be heard, just as the voices of the hundreds of other victims and their loved ones deserved to be heard.”
A grieving sister bears governor no ill will
LaVerne Brison’s sister, Cynthia Annette Johnson, was one of the 14 victims of serial rapist and murderer Chester Dewayne Turner, who prowled south Los Angeles in the 1980s and 90s.
Turner preyed on vulnerable women in the Figueroa Corridor, an area notorious for sex work, drug use and violent crime during the crack epidemics.Detectives found the body of Johnson, 30, in February 1997 in nearby Green Meadows
Brison, a 75-year-old retired nurse who now lives in Georgia, said she has no hard feelings toward Newsom for his decision. She never expected Turner to be executed in her lifetime. 
“I don’t put the blame on (Newsom),” she said. “After all, he just inherited it. If he didn’t do anything, what was the next governor going to do?”
She has mixed feelings about the death penalty.
At right, Chester Dewayne Turner and attorney John Tyre, left, listen as a jury sentences Turner on murder charges in Superior Court in Los Angeles on May 15, 2007. Turner was convicted of the murders of 11 people over more than a decade. Photo by Francine Orr-Pool, Getty Images
She knows how imperfect the justice system can be. Another man was initially charged with Johnson’s murder before being exonerated, according to the Los Angeles Times. Turner was eventually tied to Johnson’s murder through DNA evidence.
“I was a nurse. I saved lives. I don’t believe in killing,” Brison said. “But there are people who deserve it. And he’s one of them.”
When he was done with his victims, Turner tossed their bodies like trash. One of Turner’s victims was found in a portable toilet.
Brison said she knows of others in her situation who have spent their lives filled with grief, rage and frustration as they waited years hoping for their loved one’s killer to be executed. 
She’s not one of them.
Brison said she chooses to picture Turner, who’s now 60 and housed at California State Prison, Los Angeles County, rotting in a cell — when she thinks of him at all.
“I choose not to waste any time on him,” she said. “I don’t let him invade my thoughts. He’s not worth it. He really isn’t worth it.”
‘He would have made a spectacular father’
Phyllis Loya, a 78-year-old former attorney, is furious at Newsom for disrespecting her son’s memory and for adding more trauma on top of everything she and other victims’ families have endured.“It was a deliberate political decision, and he could care less about what happens to victims,” she said. “He doesn’t want our input. He doesn’t want to hear our stories. He doesn’t want to consider us.” 
Her son, Larry Lasater, 36, an officer with the Pittsburg Police Department, got the call on April 23, 2005 to be on the lookout for two armed suspects who’d just robbed a bank branch inside a grocery store.Officers spotted their stolen getaway car and tried to pull it over. It crashed. The two suspects got out and took off running down a trail. 
Lasater and other officers chased the suspects. One of them was hiding in the brush, armed with a 9mm Glock handgun. 
That suspect, 18-year-old Alexander Rashad Hamilton, fired four shots, two of which hit Lasater. Hamilton continued firing at other officers until the gun’s magazine was empty before he surrendered.At his sentencing hearing, Hamilton said he was fine with being sentenced to death. He had no interest in hearing from Lasater’s family, telling the judge, “Let me get on my way,” the San Francisco Chronicle reported.
Hamilton is now 39 and housed at Richard J. Donovan Correctional Facility in San Diego.
Lasater left behind a wife who gave birth to their son 2 ½ months after his death.Loya said her son lived his life in service to others and to his country. 
Her voice shook as she described how her son, a U.S. Marine reservist, had volunteered to lead the Marines in his former tank unit in Iraq shortly before his death.“He was a wonderful son, and a brother, and a grandson, and he would have made a spectacular father,” she said.

name: Washington State Standard
title: How Election Night felt on UW’s campus
description: Washington voters had until 8 p.m. Tuesday to return their ballots in an election featuring three statewide initiatives and five of the nine state Supreme Court seats.  But it was the ballot initiatives – including measures to ban trans girls from sports, to repeal the state income tax on millionaires, and to change parental rights […]
text:
A ballot drop box at the University of Washington’s voting center on Nov. 4, 2026.
(Summer Brown/Washington State Standard)Washington voters had until 8 p.m. Tuesday to return their ballots in an election featuring three statewide initiatives and five of the nine state Supreme Court seats. 
But it was the ballot initiatives – including measures to ban trans girls from sports, to repeal the state income tax on millionaires, and to change parental rights in schools – that drove some people to cast their votes just before the deadline. 
By 6:30 p.m., the University of Washington’s voting center was packed with last-minute voters. Lines stretched down multiple floors. 
Nea Fox, 29, who has lived in Roosevelt since 2024, voted against Initiative 638, which is what originally led her to the voting center. The measure and various candidate races were at the top of her mind as she slipped her ballot into the drop box.
“I think it’s absolutely horrible,” Fox said.  
The now passed initiative bars transgender girls from competing in girls’ K-12 sports. Students who want to play on girls’ teams will now need a health care provider to verify their sex assigned at birth to participate.
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
Some Gen Z adults said they were voting for the first time, or more consistently than before, because of what they were seeing on social media.
“A lot of pressure against leftist icons, like Hasan Piker and Zohran Mamdani, have made me more adamant to vote,” Fox said. “Currently, there is a genocide and I feel complicit in it. [Voting] clears my conscience of that.”
Patrick Jean-Philippe, who recently moved to Seattle from Florida, said people should use their right to vote, especially in a state as accessible as Washington. Jean-Philippe said he moved here because he saw legislation that aligned more closely with his personal values.
“Washington is one of the easiest states to vote in,” Jean-Philippe said. “The fact I moved here a month ago, and my first bill was enough for me to vote here, that’s not the case in many states.”
Jean-Philippe, a first-generation Haitian-American, said people should vote, since not everyone gets the same freedom and liberty as those living in America do. 
“Voting is the only means any of us have to influence any of these huge circumstances that feel out of our control,” Jean-Philippe said. “Some people don’t think it’s much, and to be honest, I don’t think it’s enough, but voting is all you got.”
Although many Washingtonians believed the state would stay blue, even on local initiatives and propositions, they still cast their votes to show support. 
“I believe in the power of local elections,” Fox said. “If everyone thought that your vote didn’t matter, nothing would change.”
Throughout early voting to Election Day, many Gen Zers dropped off their first-ever ballot. Alexandra Padua, 18, a first-year University of Washington student, walked out of the voting center with an ‘I voted’ sticker displayed clearly on her chest. Padua said voting is both difficult and rewarding. 
“[Voting] was very new for me and honestly very hard,” Padua said. “I mean, it determines your rights and it’s a decision that you’re able to contribute to.” 
Many voters praised the state’s accessibility, citing mail-in voting and a plethora of voting centers across the state. Some areas also have accessible voting units, or AVUs, which are wheelchair accessible and give voters with disabilities privacy. 
Despite this, some Washingtonians also feel that the state could do a better job informing the public about what is on the ballot, and when midterm elections take place. 
“I do wish I was more aware of [midterm elections],” Padua said. “But I did my research and I am happy with what I selected.”
Even when voting feels redundant or useless, Padua said, it allows her to decide who governs the country and state and what gets enacted into law. 
“It feels great to vote,” Padua said. “It’s a right that you have to take advantage of.”
Summer Brown is a reporter for University of Washington’s Community News Lab, a project of the UW Journalism and Public Interest program.

name: VTDigger
title: Spiritual adviser to death row inmates visits Middlebury
description:
The Rev. Jeff Hood came to Addison County last week, where he spoke with community members about capital punishment and his work as a spiritual adviser.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Spiritual adviser to death row inmates visits Middlebury.
text:
Rev. Jeff Hood visits Middlebury Chapel during a trip to Addison County last week. Hood was in town for a screening of “The Spiritual Advisor,” a 23-minute documentary produced by Middlebury College professor James Chase Sanchez that follows Hood and his role as a spiritual advisor in the days leading up to the 2024 execution of Emmanuel Littlejohn in Oklahoma. Photo courtesy of Jeff Hood

This story by Marin Howell was first published in the Addison Independent on Nov. 5, 2026.
MIDDLEBURY — The Rev. Jeff Hood didn’t go to seminary expecting to end up on death row, but that’s exactly where he’s spent the past several years — building relationships with people sentenced to die and advocating for their lives.
More than a dozen times, he’s stood with incarcerated individuals in the execution chamber.
His role in such cases is captured in “The Spiritual Advisor,” a 23-minute documentary produced by Middlebury College professor James Chase Sanchez (A Pound of Snow Productions) that follows Hood in the days leading up to the 2024 execution of Emmanuel Littlejohn in Oklahoma.
A Middlebury College screening of the film brought Hood to Addison County last week, where he spoke with community members about capital punishment and his work as a spiritual adviser.
“My ministry and my vocation is very centered on this idea that we are closest to God when we are closest to love because God is love,” Hood told the Independent. “I feel like my ministry has always been centered on going to places where love seems the most absent, and I think that’s what has drawn me to work on death row, is that these spaces are amongst the most marginalized and forgotten places in our country.”
Hood, 42, is an Old Catholic priest and an anti-death penalty activist based in Little Rock, Ark. A 2022 U.S. Supreme Court ruling cleared the way for him and other spiritual advisers to touch and pray aloud over prisoners inside the execution chamber.
Since then, Hood has been present for 14 executions in five states.
“You get out of the chamber and you look in the newspaper or you look around, 98-99% of the people in that state have no idea that this took place the night before,” he said. “I feel like part of my job is to say, ‘It did happen, I was there, and it matters.’”
He described another aspect of his job as being present, talking with those he works with over the phone and making visits.
“When one of them gets an execution date, I spend the last two weeks of their lives pretty much with them every day,” Hood said. “Everybody thinks, ‘Oh, it’s just about reading scripture,’ and it’s like, the scriptures don’t mean s*** if you’re not present for somebody. Who cares what you think about God if you’re not going to be present for them?”
While Hood acknowledges there are innocent individuals on death row, he’s under no illusion that’s always the case. He’s sat with people convicted of gruesome crimes, and there are other aspects of this work that keep him up at night.
“I woke up last night, and I had this image of one of my guys who was executed a few weeks ago, Jamaal Howard, I was there in the chamber with him in Texas. I had this nightmare of him looking at me and saying, ‘Jeff, why didn’t you help me?’” Hood recalled. “I don’t know how to live past those nightmares. I have them all the time.”

Rev. Jeff Hood, left, has spent recent years as a spiritual advisor to people on death row, building relationships with them and advocating for their lives as they near their execution date. He is pictured here with Jamaal Howard, who was executed in Texas on Oct. 7. Photo courtesy of Jeff Hood

What keeps him going in this work despite that?
“I think about my family, obviously, a lot,” he said. “I feel like I’m creating a world that will be more gentle for them.”
He noted two of his sons are autistic.
“I know that they do not function in a way that is acceptable, often, in terms of where we live and wider society,” he said. “I have this sneaking suspicion that if we can learn how to treat those that we think are the most horrible amongst us then we will be kinder and gentler to everyone.”
“I want my kids to know that I never was afraid to stand on the side of love,” Hood continued. “That I never was afraid to stand on the side of the forgotten, the pushed out, the marginalized.”
His role has also taught him about life and humanity.
“When we go to places in which cruelty is at its maximum, we find the places where kindness and compassion can be at its maximum,” he said. “If we can find humanity in monstrosity then we have a cure for monstrosity and that is being human to those we have determined are not human.” 
Hood founded the Execution Intervention Project, a nonprofit that opposes the death penalty and supports those condemned to die and their loved ones. He emphatically speaks out against the use of capital punishment and has petitioned state officials to stay the executions of those he’s worked with.
Last month, Hood’s efforts helped Eric Reid — incarcerated in Arkansas and convicted of capital murder for the deaths of his wife and daughter — reach a deal that replaced his death sentence with life in prison.
“I tell people all the time that you can’t teach people not to kill each other by killing each other,” he said. “Every time we perform an execution, we’re telling people it’s OK to kill each other if the offense is great enough.”
Recent surveys show many Americans agree with that sentiment. A report released by the Pew Research Center in August found two-thirds (66%) of Americans favor the death penalty for individuals convicted of murder and that overall support of capital punishment was up six percentage points from five years ago.
“Majorities favor the death penalty and say it is morally justified, yet many do not think it deters serious crimes,” the report reads.
Sanchez acknowledges not everyone will agree with Hood but has found many moved by his work and related issues since the film’s premiere last year.
“At the opening screening in New York, an elderly woman stopped the director and I in the hall after the screening to announce that we had changed her mind about the death penalty,” he said. “Of course, the goal of the film is not advocacy per se, but to create an art piece that might shape or reshape ideologies and views of our world is meaningful to us. I have met many people who have changed their views of the death penalty or who never cared about it and now deeply care about it because of the film. That’s what documentaries should do.”
Sanchez said around 100 people attended last week’s screening in Dana Auditorium, which was followed by a Q&A featuring Hood and director Joel Fendelman.
“Many students had questions about the filmmaking, but there were many questions by students, faculty, and the general public about Jeff’s work. The screening and his talk afterward opened people’s eyes to the realities of this world, and people were thoroughly engaged in untangling it,” Sanchez said. “For instance, I remember someone asking how hard it is to go back and forth between executions and being a family man and the toll it takes on Jeff, and the thoughtfulness of that question shows a depth of engagement.”
The film is available to watch for free on Rolling Stone’s website and YouTube page, as well as on the Documentary+ streaming service.
“We are working on a feature film based on the short, as we follow Jeff for five executions, including the first nitrogen hypoxia execution in 2024. The feature focuses on the ping pong effect of Jeff’s life, focusing on him as a father and husband in parallel with his spiritual advising,” Sanchez said, noting anyone interested in learning more or supporting the effort can reach out to him directly at james@poundofsnow.com.
In addition to last week’s screening, Hood spoke with multiple classes during his time in Middlebury.
“I hope (the screening) and the conversations I’ve had in classes are helping people to get a certain depth of understanding of the cruelness of the death penalty, so that they might be advocates for life,” Hood said. “It seems that I didn’t really learn how to live until I started watching all of these people be murdered, and it seems that me sharing these stories help people to understand what this looks like, so that they might be able to get a deeper appreciation of what their life can look like and how they can bring meaning to their life.”
Through such conversations, Hood has found that many are unaware the death penalty is still being used in the U.S. His presence — dressed in a long, clerical robe known as a cassock — has sparked discussion on other topics, as well.
“There’s also been a number of people who are like, ‘People are still religious?’” Hood said with a laugh. “I start talking about God, and I might as well be talking about extraterrestrials.”
It’s been an opportunity, Hood noted, to share with others how faith fuels his work.
“I do think that’s been a cool part of this because it’s been able to share, ‘Hey there are people of faith who do really amazing things because they are motivated by their faith,’” he said. “And they’re not always the people who are telling you they’re going to hell, they’re also the people who are trying to solve the hells that they find here on earth.”
“I feel like that says a lot about what I do,” Hood continued. “I go to hell to try to put some fires out for all of us.”

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: TIF: State hearing reflects love, hate and suggestions to retool development incentive
description: LINCOLN — A pros-and-cons discussion about one of Nebraska’s most controversial yet championed economic development tools took center stage at a legislative hearing Friday: Is TIF out of control? What, if any, changes should lawmakers pursue? TIF stands for tax-increment financing, and state Sen. Danielle Conrad of Lincoln had called for a review of state […[...]
text:
The Midtown Crossing redevelopment was among Omaha tax-increment financing-assisted projects. This view looks west near 31st and Farnam Streets along the spine of the retail and residential area. (Cindy Gonzalez/Nebraska Examiner)LINCOLN — A pros-and-cons discussion about one of Nebraska’s most controversial yet championed economic development tools took center stage at a legislative hearing Friday: Is TIF out of control? What, if any, changes should lawmakers pursue?
TIF stands for tax-increment financing, and state Sen. Danielle Conrad of Lincoln had called for a review of state laws governing the incentive — particularly related to the blighted and substandard designation on TIF-eligible areas and notification to affected neighborhoods.
State Sen. Danielle Conrad of Lincoln speaks at a news conference related to reviewing state rules and regulations. Jan. 16, 2025. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
Conrad told the Urban Affairs Committee that Legislative Resolution 415 was prompted by concerns from north Lincoln constituents. But she said residents elsewhere, including Omaha’s south and midtown areas, also are in the midst of divisive TIF-related matters.
Several state lawmakers have previously raised red flags about potential overuse or abuse of the incentive. Conrad pointed out Nebraska Auditor Mike Foley’s report two years ago documenting that more than a half-billion dollars in property tax collections were redirected over a five-year period to fund urban redevelopment throughout Nebraska — marking a “remarkable increase” in TIF use that risks further upward pressure on local property taxes.
No one Conrad has spoken to advocates getting rid of the public funding mechanism, as she said they recognize it can spur development and economic growth. 
“But what I fear has happened with this tool is that it has veered from its original purpose of community betterment and become just really, truly another giveaway for big developers and big corporations at the expense of community,” Conrad said.
 Blighted, substandard

In addition to apartment buildings and commercial projects, TIF is tapped increasingly to add housing, including for-sale owner-occupied homes, in rural areas, said Christy Abraham of the League of Nebraska Municipalities.	

How TIF works:
For up to 20 years, the extra property taxes generated by new improvements on TIF sites are diverted to help private developers pay eligible costs of transforming the area.
Critics have objected in part because local taxing jurisdictions forgo that increased property tax while the developer’s loan is being paid off. Some also question whether city councils have grown too lenient in bestowing the required designation of an area as blighted.
The value of a site that existed prior to TIF approval is essentially “frozen” during the TIF loan period, and the fixed property tax revenue generated from it continues to be collected from the owner and distributed to the usual recipients. After the developer’s loan is paid off, all property taxes flow to traditional tax recipients. The idea is that the project site would then be worth more.
State law says the venture must be in a blighted area and deemed not possible to be developed “but for” the subsidy.



The tax-increment financing program was authorized in the 1980s by the Nebraska Legislature as a way to boost development and jobs in areas deemed to be blighted and substandard. In essence, it allows a developer, with approval by the respective city, to use future property tax gains to subsidize development costs in designated blighted and substandard areas. 
Among dominant concerns raised during the hearing that stretched more than two hours was the “blighted and substandard” description attached to eligibility. 
Speakers generally agreed the terminology brings a stigma to homeowners and businesses in the boundaries. 
State Sens. Stan Clouse of Kearney, a committee member, and Mike Jacobson of North Platte, who testified, were among those who said they “hate” that terminology but support the financing tool. 
Bridget Hadley, a deputy planning director who oversees the TIF program for the City of Omaha, said her team instead tries to use “community redevelopment area,” as she recognizes the “substandard” term is offensive to those who live in the designated zone.
Both Clouse and Jacobson said they’ve seen positive payoffs in their areas as a result of TIF. After the TIF loan is paid off in the 15- or 20-year period, Clouse said, the project’s full value is on the property tax rolls.
Jacobson called himself a “big believer” in the incentive because cities do not have to spend funds and they benefit from growth spurred by the TIF project. 
“It’s as clean as it can possibly be,” he said.
 Thaw the freeze

Doug Kagan of Nebraska Taxpayers for Freedom warned of  “reckless use” of TIF, questioning whether municipalities approve the financing for projects that developers would have done anyway. He said the incentive has led to “outrageous distortion of property tax use.”
Residents of historic neighborhoods, including Kalili Haszar of Lincoln, urged lawmakers to examine how some TIF-enabled apartment structures are gentrifying vintage neighborhoods filled with longtime and hardworking homeowners and residents.
“Stop incentivizing their destruction,” she said. Haszar is president of the Clinton Neighborhood Organization, formed in 1966 and known as the state’s oldest organized neighborhood association.
Representatives of neighborhood groups said municipalities should find ways to involve neighbors more and earlier in the blighted and substandard designation process. 
An idea that picked up steam during the discussion was to stop freezing the base value of a project site when a TIF zone is created.
Currently when a TIF redevelopment plan is approved, the county assessor freezes the taxable value of the property at its pre-development assessed value. The property owner continues to pay standard property taxes, and those taxes calculated only on the frozen base value continue to flow to traditional tax entities like schools, cities, counties as they did before.
Alan Seybert suggested that the base amount should instead grow with surrounding property values, a notion that several said was worthy of further consideration, including state Sen. John Cavanaugh, a member of the committee.
Testimony and information provided during the hearing is expected to inform possible legislation next year.
Conrad, sponsor of LR 415, said she was impressed by the diverse voices and opinions. What she heard, she said, reinforces that “the status quo should not stand.”

name: Idaho Capital Sun
title: Who voted early in Idaho’s election? Mostly Republicans.

text:
Ada County election workers process hundreds of absentee ballots for the 2026 general election on Oct. 1, 2026. (Photo by Kyle Pfannenstiel/Idaho Capital Sun)In Idaho, more than a third of votes in Tuesday’s election were cast before Election Day.
Over 290,000 of the more than 731,000 ballots cast in the election were through early and absentee voting, according to data from the Idaho secretary of state’s office. That’s 100,000 more of those types of voting than were submitted during the state’s last election for statewide offices in 2022, according to the state election agency.
Those forms of voting — available without a need to state a reason — allow voters to cast ballots either in person or by mail before Election Day. (Technically, some of these absentee ballots were submitted on Election Day. In Idaho, absentee ballots may be submitted until polls close at 8 p.m. local time on Election Day.)

 Republicans make up over half of Idaho’s early and absentee voters, state data shows. Democrats vote early and absentee at higher rates.

Looking at state election data, the political makeup of the voters who cast ballots through early and absentee voting largely mirrors the state’s pool of more than 1 million registered voters, state data shows. With one caveat: Democrats vote early and absentee at higher rates.
Here’s how it breaks down:

About 59% of early and absentee voters this election were Republicans, which is slightly below the party affiliation of all registered voters, which is nearly 62% Republican. 
Unaffiliated voters make up nearly 22.3% of early and absentee voters, which is slightly lower than their nearly 24.6% share of Idaho’s total registered voters.
Democrats make up nearly 18% of early and absentee voters. That’s a bigger rate of Idaho’s total registered Democrats, which is nearly 12%.
Voters affiliated with third parties — the Constitution and Libertarian parties — make up a combined 0.76% of Idaho’s absentee voters. They make up less than 1.5% of all registered voters.

There is also an age skew. Older voters, who make up most of Idaho’s total voters, vote early and absentee at higher rates than younger voters, the data show. 

Voters at least 45 years old make up 61.8% of the state’s registered voters, but cast 79% of the state’s early and absentee ballots this election.
Voters age 44 and younger voted absentee and early less this year. They make up nearly 38.2% of registered voters, but just 21% of this year’s pre-Election Day votes. 
Voters aged 18 to 29 appeared the least likely to vote absentee and early this year. They cast only 7% of ballots early and absentee. But they make up 15.5% of registered voters, a higher share of the state’s overall voter pool than Idahoans age 75 and older, who make up nearly 13.8% of registered voters.

It’s too early to tell how each of these demographics turned out to the polls this year. The secretary of state’s office hasn’t yet released more detailed information on the voters who showed up on Election Day.
 So, why did early election results show some Democrats in the lead?

After polls close on Tuesday, and results start rolling in, absentee and early votes are some of the first to be counted, election officials say. The initial results this year showed Democrats leading in many statewide races — and even Proposition 1 in the lead. A few hours later, the actual outcomes became clear — Republican incumbents had sailed through reelection; voters had rejected Prop 1, an abortion ballot initiative; but voters in the state’s few competitive legislative districts elected six more Democrats to the Statehouse. 
Idaho Secretary of State Phil McGrane, a Republican, takes questions from an Idaho News 6 reporter at a GOP election night watch party on Nov. 3, 2026, in Downtown Boise. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun)
But if the pool of voters who vote early and absentee somewhat reflects the state’s overall voter pool, why was there a disconnect in the initial results? Secretary of State Phil McGrane said it’s complicated.
“When you see those first results, it’s not accounting for all of them,” he said in an interview.
If people look at early results in more rural, Republican areas, they’ll see Republicans in the lead, he said. If they look at the state’s few purple areas, they might see something different.
“We saw high turnout early on in Blaine and in Teton counties, and it makes sense that you would see higher Democratic turnout” there, he said.
